evidence.snippet: Using exome sequencing, we identify SERAC1 mutations as the cause of MEGDEL syndrome, a recessive disorder of dystonia and deafness with Leigh-like syndrome, impaired oxidative phosphorylation and 3-methylglutaconic aciduria
evidence.explanation: Gene-discovery study establishing SERAC1 as the causal gene.

evidence.snippet: Both mutations were found to lead to decreased or absent expression of SERAC1
evidence.explanation: Two hepatopathy-associated alleles were linked to reduced protein expression.

evidence.snippet: By interacting with the mitochondrial serine transporter protein SFXN1, SERAC1 facilitated and was required for SFXN1-mediated serine transport from the cytosol to the mitochondria
evidence.explanation: The single experimental study behind the emerging serine_transport_mtdna hypothesis identifies SERAC1 as an activator required for SFXN1-mediated serine transport.

steps/1.description: Biallelic pathogenic variants reduce SERAC1 function. Some tested truncating alleles lower protein expression, but absence of protein or mislocalization is not established for every allele.

evidence.snippet: Complementation of patient fibroblasts with wild-type human SERAC1 by lentiviral infection led to a decrease and partial normalization of the mean ratio of phosphatidylglycerol-34:1 to phosphatidylglycerol-36:1
evidence.explanation: Wild-type complementation partially rescues the patient-cell lipid ratio.

evidence.snippet: no LPG acyltransferase activity has been identified from SERAC1 to date
evidence.explanation: The 2023 LPGAT1 study distinguishes remodeling involvement from demonstrated catalytic activity.

steps/2.description: Patient fibroblasts show an increased PG-34:1/PG-36:1 ratio, partly corrected by wild-type SERAC1. These data establish involvement in remodeling; direct LPG acyltransferase activity of purified SERAC1 has not been established.

evidence.snippet: decreased concentrations of phosphatidylglycerol-36:1 species, resulting in an altered cardiolipin subspecies composition
evidence.explanation: The discovery study links altered PG species with cardiolipin composition.

steps/3.description: Cardiolipin acyl-species composition changes in SERAC1-deficient fibroblasts. This observation does not establish a decrease in the overall rate of cardiolipin remodeling.

evidence.snippet: We also detected low concentrations of bis(monoacyl-glycerol)-phosphate, leading to the accumulation of free cholesterol, as shown by abnormal filipin staining
evidence.explanation: Patient fibroblasts showed reduced BMP and cholesterol accumulation.

steps/4.description: Reduced BMP accompanies SERAC1 deficiency in patient fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: By interacting with the mitochondrial serine transporter protein SFXN1, SERAC1 facilitated and was required for SFXN1-mediated serine transport from the cytosol to the mitochondria
evidence.explanation: The experimental study identifies SERAC1-dependent SFXN1 transport.

steps/5.description: Experimental work places SERAC1 in an outer-membrane complex with SFXN1 that facilitates serine import. Outer-membrane localization is compatible with an ER-mitochondria contact-site role.

evidence.snippet: Loss of SERAC1 impaired the one-carbon cycle and disrupted the balance of the nucleotide pool, which led to primary mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion in mice, HEK293T cells, and patient-derived immortalized lymphocyte cells due to insufficient supply of nucleotides
evidence.explanation: This proposed sequence was studied in mice and cellular models; it is not a universal clinical finding.

steps/6.description: SERAC1 loss impairs mitochondrial one-carbon metabolism in the experimental serine-transport model.

evidence.snippet: Loss of SERAC1 impaired the one-carbon cycle and disrupted the balance of the nucleotide pool, which led to primary mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion in mice, HEK293T cells, and patient-derived immortalized lymphocyte cells due to insufficient supply of nucleotides
evidence.explanation: This proposed sequence was studied in mice and cellular models; it is not a universal clinical finding.

evidence.snippet: both in vitro and in vivo supplementation of nucleosides/nucleotides restored mtDNA content and mitochondrial function
evidence.explanation: Preclinical rescue supports nucleotide limitation in the experimental systems.

steps/7.description: Loss of SERAC1 disrupts nucleotide availability in experimental systems; nucleotide or nucleoside supplementation rescues downstream mtDNA and mitochondrial function.

evidence.snippet: Loss of SERAC1 impaired the one-carbon cycle and disrupted the balance of the nucleotide pool, which led to primary mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion in mice, HEK293T cells, and patient-derived immortalized lymphocyte cells due to insufficient supply of nucleotides
evidence.explanation: This proposed sequence was studied in mice and cellular models; it is not a universal clinical finding.

evidence.snippet: including hepatic mitochondrial DNA depletion in one patient
evidence.explanation: Human liver depletion is consistent with, but does not prove, the experimental transport mechanism.

evidence.snippet: long-range PCR and qPCR analyses of the patient's blood excluded any mtDNA deletions or depletions
evidence.explanation: Normal blood findings limit generalization across patients and tissues.

steps/8.description: Depletion occurs in Serac1-deficient mice, HEK293T cells and patient-derived immortalized lymphocytes. Hepatic depletion has also been observed clinically, but normal blood or muscle testing in other cases shows that it is not universal across tissues or patients.

evidence.snippet: We also detected low concentrations of bis(monoacyl-glycerol)-phosphate, leading to the accumulation of free cholesterol, as shown by abnormal filipin staining
evidence.explanation: Patient fibroblasts showed reduced BMP and cholesterol accumulation.

steps/9.description: Unesterified cholesterol can accumulate or be distributed abnormally in patient fibroblasts. Filipin staining is variable and can be normal in both mild and classic presentations.

evidence.snippet: In the patient fibroblasts, no SERAC1 protein was detected, the mitochondrial network was severely fragmented, and the cristae morphology was altered
evidence.explanation: These findings concern fibroblasts from one severe neonatal case.

steps/10.description: A severely fragmented mitochondrial network was observed in fibroblasts from a lethal neonatal case; this is a cellular finding rather than proof of a universal intermediate.

evidence.snippet: In the patient fibroblasts, no SERAC1 protein was detected, the mitochondrial network was severely fragmented, and the cristae morphology was altered
evidence.explanation: These findings concern fibroblasts from one severe neonatal case.

evidence.snippet: The ultrastructural findings included abnormal circular mitochondrial cristae
evidence.explanation: Liver ultrastructure corroborates a mitochondrial structural abnormality.

steps/11.description: Altered cristae were observed in patient fibroblasts and circular cristae in a separate liver biopsy.

evidence.snippet: The calcium buffer function between cytoplasm and mitochondria was deficient
evidence.explanation: Calcium buffering was abnormal in patient fibroblasts.

steps/12.description: Calcium buffering between cytoplasm and mitochondria was deficient in a severe patient fibroblast line. Reduced calcium influx is a proposed contributor to respiratory dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: In liver mitochondria, complexes I, III, and IV were clearly decreased
evidence.explanation: Respiratory-complex abnormalities were observed in one neonatal liver.

evidence.snippet: Plasma and cerebrospinal fluid lactate, plasma alanine, and respiratory chain complexes in fresh muscle were normal
evidence.explanation: Normal muscle findings do not exclude SERAC1 disease.

steps/13.description: Respiratory-complex deficiencies vary by tissue and patient. One neonatal liver showed reduced complexes I, III and IV, whereas fresh muscle complexes were normal in another confirmed case.

evidence.snippet: All affected children displayed biochemical features consistent with mitochondrial OXPHOS dysfunction
evidence.explanation: A four-patient hepatopathy series supports mitochondrial dysfunction.

steps/14.description: Impaired oxidative phosphorylation is a variable cellular consequence of SERAC1 deficiency. Lipid, calcium and mtDNA pathways are candidate contributors whose relative roles in human tissues remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: In stage 1, T2 signal changes of the pallidum are present. In stage 2, swelling of the putamen and caudate nucleus is seen
evidence.explanation: Defines the staged anatomical progression across 30 patients.

steps/15.description: MRI shows evolving basal-ganglia abnormalities, with early pallidal signal changes, putaminal and caudate swelling with relative dorsal-putaminal sparing, and later atrophy. The characteristic putaminal eye is stage dependent and is a strong diagnostic clue; molecular testing confirms the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Sixty‐one of 62 (98%) individuals had 3‐MGA‐uria
evidence.explanation: Primary retrospective cohort; denominator is specific to this feature.

steps/16.description: Urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid was elevated in 61/62 tested individuals (98%) in the 67-person cohort. Concentrations fluctuate, and a normal measurement does not exclude the disorder.

evidence.snippet: Forty‐eight of 61 individuals (79%) were diagnosed with sensorineural hearing impairment
evidence.explanation: Primary retrospective cohort; denominator is specific to this feature.

steps/17.description: Sensorineural hearing impairment was diagnosed in 48/61 (79%) in the 67-person cohort. It may be congenital or progressive and can follow a normal newborn screen. The later 36-person hearing cohort does not establish a uniform anatomical site.

steps/18.description: Dystonia occurred in 53/65 (82%) of the 67-person cohort, with median onset at 18 months. Later-onset presentations also occur.

evidence.snippet: All patients presented a distinctive brain MRI pattern with five characteristic disease stages affecting the basal ganglia, especially the putamen
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of 43 MRI studies in 30 patients.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI studies were available for 55/67 individuals. In all individuals, alterations of the basal ganglia at different stages were observed.

steps/19.description: Stage-dependent basal-ganglia MRI changes, including a putaminal eye of relatively spared tissue, were found in the systematic imaging series. The eye is not present at every age; later stages show atrophy. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Severe neonatal liver dysfunction was reported in 30/62 (48%) individuals. Nine of these 30 (30%) individuals fulfilled the criteria of neonatal liver failure

steps/20.description: Severe neonatal liver dysfunction occurred in 30/62 (48%) in the cohort. Nine of those 30 fulfilled neonatal liver-failure criteria; that 30% subgroup rate must not be applied to all affected individuals. Hepatic abnormalities often improved after infancy.

evidence.snippet: Metabolic acidosis, mild hyperammonemia and lactic acidemia were accompanied with clinical findings in newborn period

steps/21.description: Lactic acidosis is reported during metabolic crises, but normal lactate occurs in confirmed cases. The cohort rate for elevated serum lactate should not be interpreted as a rate for acidosis.

edges/18.description: Hearing impairment is a clinical consequence associated with SERAC1 deficiency; its anatomical and molecular basis remains uncertain.

evidence.explanation: The classification supports a secondary phospholipid-associated aciduria.

edges/19.description: MEGDEL belongs to the secondary acidurias associated with mitochondrial phospholipid dysfunction; the exact route to organic-acid accumulation is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Using exome sequencing, we identify SERAC1 mutations as the cause of MEGDEL syndrome, a recessive disorder of dystonia and deafness with Leigh-like syndrome, impaired oxidative phosphorylation and 3-methylglutaconic aciduria
evidence.explanation: Gene-discovery study establishing SERAC1 as the causal gene.

evidence.snippet: Homozygosity mapping identified a candidate locus on 6q25.2-6q26
evidence.explanation: Independent mapping of the disease locus to the SERAC1 region.

evidence.snippet: No correlation has been recognized between the genotype and clinical phenotype.
evidence.explanation: The full case discussion summarizes the lack of a general genotype-phenotype correlation, consistent with the full GeneReviews chapter.

genes/0.notes: SERAC1 encodes a protein involved in phosphatidylglycerol remodeling and mitochondrial physiology. Disease-associated variants include truncating, splice, missense and multiexon deletion alleles. The effect on RNA, protein abundance and cellular function depends on the allele and has not been measured for every reported variant. A general genotype-phenotype correlation has not been established. LPGAT1-deficient mice reproduce several overlapping findings, but this does not establish LPGAT1 as a human MEGDEL gene.

evidence.snippet: Care is best provided by a multidisciplinary team including a metabolic pediatrician, pediatric neurologist, dietician, and physical therapist when possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends coordinated supportive care.

treatments/0.description: Care is supportive, coordinated across metabolic medicine, neurology, nutrition, rehabilitation, audiology and other specialties according to involvement. No disease-modifying human treatment has been established.

evidence.snippet: In addition, protein intake was stopped, and the patient anabolized with intravenous glucose. Temporary stabilization could be achieved after four days
evidence.explanation: Describes the metabolic crisis protocol and its partial effect.

treatments/1.description: Urgent specialist management addresses hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia, coagulopathy and other organ dysfunction. In one severe neonatal case initially managed as a suspected urea-cycle disorder, protein was temporarily withheld, intravenous glucose and ammonia-lowering therapies were given, and continuous dialysis controlled ammonia. This empiric crisis regimen is not a disease-specific treatment protocol.

evidence.snippet: Due to high ammonia level, continuous hemodialysis was established immediately after admission
evidence.explanation: Reports hemodialysis used specifically to control hyperammonemia.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Continuous hemodialysis removes ammonia during the hepatic crisis.

evidence.snippet: Twenty-two individuals received hearing rehabilitation with conventional hearing aids, followed by cochlear implant (CI) surgery in six. One of these six individuals acquired spoken language, which lessened in clarity as disease progressed.
evidence.explanation: Primary hearing-rehabilitation cohort defines limited and variable language benefit.

treatments/2.description: Hearing aids and cochlear implants have been used, but expected benefit should be discussed with audiology and the family. In a 36-person retrospective hearing study, 22 received hearing aids and six subsequently received implants; only one implanted individual acquired spoken language, which became less clear with progression. Improved environmental interaction can still be meaningful. The auditory lesion is not consistently localized.

evidence.snippet: Twenty-two individuals received hearing rehabilitation with conventional hearing aids, followed by cochlear implant (CI) surgery in six. One of these six individuals acquired spoken language, which lessened in clarity as disease progressed.
evidence.explanation: Primary hearing-rehabilitation cohort defines limited and variable language benefit.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Auditory augmentation may improve access to sound; clinical language benefit is variable and often limited.

evidence.snippet: The ICU period was smooth, and she was released the next day. The anaesthetic plan was tolerated without any complications.
evidence.explanation: Single-case perioperative outcome; no comparative safety inference.

treatments/3.description: One two-year-old undergoing cochlear implantation tolerated ketamine and dexmedetomidine induction with dexmedetomidine maintenance. This case supports feasibility in that individual; it does not establish an optimal anaesthetic regimen, comparative safety or a specific malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility in MEGDEL.

evidence.snippet: Management of neonatal hypoglycemia; feeding therapy and gastrostomy tube as needed
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends feeding support.

evidence.snippet: Thirty‐seven of 58 individuals (64%) were given tube feeding.
evidence.explanation: Tube feeding was common in the primary cohort.

treatments/4.description: Assess growth, nutritional intake and swallowing safety. Feeding therapy and enteral support, including gastrostomy when needed, address inadequate intake or unsafe feeding.

evidence.snippet: Depolarizing muscle relaxants as succinylcholine must not be administered in any patient with myopathy due to their upregulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in skeletal muscle
evidence.explanation: The case report summarizes a wider myopathy precaution; it does not establish a MEGDEL-specific absolute contraindication.

evidence.snippet: It is recommended to refrain from administering propofol by continuous infusion after induction of anaesthesia due to concerns about propofol infusion syndrome in this vulnerable population
evidence.explanation: Gives the propofol restriction and its stated rationale.

evidence.snippet: Preoperative fasting is reduced to 2 h, if possible, to avoid hypovolemia and hypoglycemia
evidence.explanation: The fasting precaution, which matters here because catabolic stress precipitates decompensation.

treatments/5.description: Plan anaesthesia individually with attention to organ involvement, glucose, hydration, temperature and postoperative recovery. The MEGDEL case report discusses limiting fasting, avoiding prolonged propofol infusion and avoiding succinylcholine in patients with myopathy based on wider mitochondrial-disease practice; these are extrapolated precautions, not MEGDEL-specific comparative evidence.

evidence.snippet: each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of inheriting biallelic pathogenic variants and being affected
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recurrence risk assumes both parents are known carriers.

evidence.snippet: Once the SERAC1 pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: Family testing requires known pathogenic variants.

treatments/6.description: When both parents carry a pathogenic SERAC1 variant, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of an affected child. Confirm familial variants and phase, offer carrier testing to at-risk relatives, and discuss prenatal or preimplantation testing when appropriate.

evidence.snippet: Oral baclofen was given to 15 individuals. It was reported as having a positive effect in 11 individuals, whereas in 2 no change was observed, and in another 2, clinical deterioration of spasticity was seen.
evidence.explanation: Uncontrolled retrospective response data.

evidence.snippet: some individuals have experienced (temporary) improvement of spasticity with oral or intrathecal baclofen treatment
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews summarizes symptomatic use.

treatments/7.description: Oral or intrathecal baclofen may improve spasticity, sometimes temporarily. In the historical cohort, oral baclofen was reported beneficial in 11 of 15 individuals, ineffective in two and associated with worsening in two; responses require individual assessment.

A teenage case improved from BFMDRS 30.5 to seven at two years without correction of scoliosis. A separate adult report describes benefit at six months, but its preceding genetic report classified p.Arg411Cys as a VUS. Both are uncontrolled observations, with limited generalizability to severe infantile disease.

treatments/9.description: Physical therapy and positioning or mobility equipment support function and reduce orthopedic complications; tailor the program to progressive motor limitations.

evidence.snippet: Occupational therapy is recommended for difficulty with fine motor skills that affect adaptive function
evidence.explanation: Full GeneReviews recommends assistance with adaptive tasks.

treatments/10.description: Occupational therapy supports fine-motor activities and adaptive equipment.

evidence.snippet: An AAC evaluation should be completed by a speech-language pathologist who has expertise in the area. This evaluation typically takes into account cognitive abilities, sensory impairments, and motor skills to determine the most appropriate form of communication.

treatments/11.description: Provide educational support and speech-language assessment, including augmentative and alternative communication tailored to cognition, hearing and motor abilities.

evidence.explanation: Specialist-directed symptomatic treatment.

treatments/14.description: Monitor glucose in infantile MEGD(H)EL and assess growth, nutrition, swallowing, neurological progression, communication, hearing, musculoskeletal and vision problems, and family needs at visits and at least annually. Monitor liver dysfunction with hepatology input.

ER-mitochondria contact-site and outer-membrane localization are not mutually exclusive. evidence.snippet: Although cognitive function and hearing loss were not assessed in the affected dogs, the canine disorder appears to closely resemble early-onset MEGDHEL syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly identify unassessed model features.

open_questions/1.rationale: The canine paper establishes a movement disorder and neuropathological overlap. Hearing and cognition were unassessed; liver and organic-acid measures were not reported. Direct phenotyping is needed before using this model for those disease manifestations. Normal findings would limit those particular model outcomes, not refute human disease mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: Intriguingly, the genealogies reveal that obligate L68Q carriers born 1825 to 1900 experienced a drastic reduction in life span, from 65 years to the present-day average.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the historical shift in carrier life span that defines this environmental observation.

evidence.snippet: We have used the full length cystatin C cDNA probe (Abrahamson et al., 1987) to demonstrate a mutation in the codon for leucine at position 68, which abolishes an Alu I restriction site in cystatin C gene of the HCCAA patients.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the codon-68 CST3 mutation as the initiating lesion in HCCAA patients.

evidence.snippet: The same mutation in cystatin C, L68Q, has been found in all patients examined so far pointing to a common founder.
evidence.explanation: Establishes L68Q as the single founder allele shared by all examined patients.

steps/2.description: A single T-to-A substitution in codon 68 of CST3 replaces leucine with glutamine in cystatin C. Every known HCCAA carrier is heterozygous for this one Icelandic founder allele, so the disorder has a uniform initiating genetic lesion.

evidence.snippet: A gamma-trace variant protein is the major constituent of the amyloid fibrils in patients from Iceland with hereditary cerebral hemorrhage with amyloidosis.
evidence.explanation: Identifies variant cystatin C (gamma-trace) as the amyloid subunit in patient tissue, establishing it as the amyloidogenic precursor.

evidence.snippet: The structure of the three-dimensional domain-swapped dimers shows how the L68Q mutation destabilizes the monomers and makes the partially unfolded intermediate less unstable.
evidence.explanation: Crystallographic work provides the destabilization mechanism that makes the L68Q precursor misfolding-prone.

steps/3.description: Variant cystatin C is the amyloidogenic precursor of this disease, the disorder-specific substitution for the module's generic destabilized precursor. The variant protein purified from patient amyloid is cystatin C (gamma-trace) carrying the position-68 substitution, and structural work shows the mutation destabilizes the folded monomer.

evidence.snippet: The concentration of cystatin C in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of HCCAA patients is markedly diminished and cultivated monocytes from affected individuals accumulate cystatin C.
evidence.explanation: Documents both the reduced extracellular (CSF) pool and the cellular accumulation that define this node.

steps/4.description: Variant cystatin C accumulates within cells rather than being secreted, which depletes cerebrospinal fluid cystatin C and is proposed to raise the local concentration that drives aggregation. This is a secretion/trafficking arm that runs alongside the intrinsic destabilization arm.

evidence.snippet: The dimerization occurs through three-dimensional domain swapping, a mechanism for forming oligomeric proteins.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the specific misfolding/oligomerization mechanism substituted for the module's generic beta-sheet oligomerization step.

evidence.snippet: Higher aggregates may arise through the three-dimensional domain-swapping mechanism occurring in an open-ended fashion in which partially unfolded molecules are linked into infinite chains.
evidence.explanation: Extends the dimer mechanism to higher-order aggregates, the amplifying step of the chain.

evidence.snippet: One of the most important drivers of the disease is the aggregation of L68Q-hCC into amyloid oligomers, as the monomer does not accumulate in the cerebral vasculature.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the oligomer, rather than the monomer, as the disease-driving species, which is what makes this node the therapeutic target.

steps/5.description: Cystatin C dimerizes by three-dimensional domain swapping, in which two partially unfolded monomers exchange structural elements to reconstitute monomer-like domains. Open-ended propagation of the same mechanism links molecules into higher aggregates. Oligomer formation - not the monomer - is the species that accumulates in the cerebral vasculature.

evidence.snippet: Cystatin C was deposited in all brain areas, grey and white matter alike, most prominently in arteries and arterioles; capillaries and veins were not, or minimally, affected.
evidence.explanation: Post-mortem topographical mapping establishes the arterial selectivity of deposition in patient brain.

evidence.snippet: We found that cystatin C amyloid immunoreactivity was present not only in cerebral cortical and leptomeningeal vessels, but also in white matter parenchymal vessels.
evidence.explanation: Immunohistochemistry documents the anatomical distribution of cystatin C amyloid across cortical, leptomeningeal, and parenchymal vessels.

evidence.snippet: This study shows for the first time, that cystatin C does not exclusively form CAA and perivascular amyloid but also focal deposits in the brain parenchyma.
evidence.explanation: Extends deposition beyond the vessel wall to parenchymal focal deposits.

steps/6.description: The rate-limiting lesion of HCCAA. Variant cystatin C amyloid deposits selectively in the walls of brain arteries and arterioles - grey and white matter alike, and in leptomeningeal as well as parenchymal vessels - while capillaries and veins are spared. Perivascular and parenchymal focal deposits also occur.

evidence.snippet: Cystatin C deposition within the vascular media and adventitia, with associated vessel wall injury as manifested by sm cell loss, represents microvascular degeneration that leads to cerebral hemorrhage.
evidence.explanation: Names smooth muscle cell loss as the vessel wall injury that leads to hemorrhage.

evidence.snippet: To evaluate possible cytotoxicity in this condition solubilized cystatin C amyloid extracted from HCHWA-I leptomeninges was applied to cerebral smooth muscle cells in culture and was found to kill the cells.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the direct cytotoxicity mechanism; note this is a culture experiment, so the in vivo magnitude of this contribution is not established.

steps/7.description: Smooth muscle cells are progressively lost from the media and adventitia of affected vessels. Solubilized cystatin C amyloid extracted from patient leptomeninges kills cultured cerebral smooth muscle cells, supplying a direct cytotoxic mechanism for the withdrawal of these cells observed in patient tissue. The denuded, structurally incompetent wall is what fails under pressure.

evidence.snippet: Our results show that excess deposition of extracellular matrix proteins in cerebral arteries of HCCAA is a prominent feature of the disease and may play an important role in its pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes excess matrix deposition as a prominent structural feature of the affected arteries.

evidence.snippet: The amyloid deposition in the vessel walls causes thickening of the walls leading to occlusion or rupture and resulting in brain hemorrhage.
evidence.explanation: Connects wall thickening to the two vascular outcomes, occlusion and rupture.

steps/8.description: Continued amyloid and extracellular matrix deposition - collagen IV, aggrecan, thickened laminin, intimal thickening over a frayed elastic layer - progressively expands and stiffens the arterial wall. This is the disorder-specific form of the module's progressive tissue amyloid accumulation, and it is what converts molecular aggregation into a structural vascular lesion.

evidence.snippet: The neuroinflammatory response was limited to the close vicinity of affected arteries and perivascular as well as parenchymal focal deposits.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the restricted spatial distribution of the neuroinflammatory response.

steps/9.description: A spatially restricted neuroinflammatory reaction forms a glial scar within and around affected arteries and their perivascular and parenchymal focal deposits. The response is local rather than diffuse, tracking the deposits themselves.

evidence.snippet: The density of fibroblasts in the upper dermis of carrier skin was increased, whereas the distribution of other cell types examined did not differ compared with control biopsies.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the selective fibroblast change in carrier skin.

evidence.snippet: The pathogenesis of the disease in carriers is very similar in the CNS and in the skin based on autopsy studies, thus skin biopsies can be used to monitor the progression of the disease by quantifying the cystatin C immunoreactivity.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the CNS-skin correspondence that licenses skin biopsy as a disease monitor.

evidence.snippet: Although the amyloid can be detected outside the brain, the clinical manifestation is restricted to the brain, and usually consists of repeated hemorrhages leading to paralysis.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that despite systemic deposition, clinical disease is restricted to the brain.

steps/10.description: Variant cystatin C also deposits outside the central nervous system - skin, lymph nodes, testis, spleen, salivary glands, adrenal cortex. In skin it begins in the dermal-epidermal basement membrane, colocalizes with collagen IV, and is associated with increased upper-dermal fibroblast density. Clinically this arm is essentially silent, but it is the basis for skin biopsy as a staging and pharmacodynamic assay.

evidence.snippet: The disorder has an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance and causes fatal brain hemorrhage in normotensive young adults.
evidence.explanation: States the defining clinical consequence, including its occurrence in normotensive individuals.

evidence.snippet: Haemorrhages were observed in all patients and occurred in all brain areas, variable between patients. Microinfarcts were observed in 34.6% of patients.
evidence.explanation: Post-mortem series quantifying hemorrhage occurrence and the microinfarct fraction.

evidence.snippet: Most L68Q carriers have clinical symptoms characterized by recurrent hemorrhages and dementia, between the age of 20-30 years.
evidence.explanation: Establishes recurrence and the accompanying dementia in the typical age window.

steps/11.description: The clinical end state. Amyloid-laden arteries rupture, producing intracerebral hemorrhage in normotensive young adults. Hemorrhages recur with increasing frequency and severity, accompanied by dementia and paralysis, and are fatal at a mean age of about 30 years. Microinfarcts are also found in a substantial minority at autopsy.

evidence.snippet: It has an amino acid substitution (glutamine for leucine) at position 58 (position 68 in gamma-trace numbering), which is near the proposed active site of related proteins
evidence.explanation: Locates the amino acid substitution in the amyloid-forming variant protein purified from patient tissue.

edges/2.description: The L68Q substitution sits near the inhibitory region of cystatin C and yields a conformationally destabilized variant protein.

evidence.snippet: The structure of the three-dimensional domain-swapped dimers shows how the L68Q mutation destabilizes the monomers and makes the partially unfolded intermediate less unstable.
evidence.explanation: Links monomer destabilization directly to the domain-swapped dimer that initiates aggregation.

edges/3.description: Destabilization of the monomer favours the partially unfolded intermediate that permits three-dimensional domain swapping.

The evidence is insufficient to assert a tumor-predisposition phenotype or surveillance recommendation, and a mechanistic link to heterochromatin or telomere dysfunction remains unestablished.

evidence.snippet: Homegrown (not commercial) maize kernels from case households had higher concentrations of aflatoxins than did kernels from control households [geometric mean (GM) = 354.53 ppb vs. 44.14 ppb; p = 0.04].
evidence.explanation: The case-control exposure contrast, which is what makes this an established cause rather than a suspected one.

evidence.snippet: Case patients stored wet maize (OR = 3.5; 95% CI, 1.2-10.3) inside their homes (OR = 12.0; 95% CI, 1.5-95.7) rather than in granaries more often than did controls.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the modifiable post-harvest practices, which is where prevention acts.

evidence.snippet: The disease was associated with the consumption of maize contaminated heavily with Aspergillus flavus. Analysis of contaminated samples showed that affected people could have consumed between 2 and 6 mg. of aflatoxin daily over a period of a month.
evidence.explanation: An independent outbreak with an estimated ingested dose, which is the closest thing to a dose-response figure available for human disease.

steps/1.description: Aflatoxin B1 arriving at the liver is oxidised by cytochrome P450 to the reactive exo-8,9-epoxide. This step is shared with chronic aflatoxin carcinogenesis; everything downstream of it in this entry is not.

evidence.snippet: From 1 to 3% of ingested aflatoxins irreversibly bind to proteins and DNA bases to form adducts such as aflatoxin B1-lysine in albumin (Skipper and Tannenbaum 1990).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the fraction that forms adducts and names the specific albumin adduct used as the biomarker.

evidence.snippet: Disruption of proteins and DNA bases in hepatocytes causes liver toxicity (Tandon et al. 1978).
evidence.explanation: States the link from adduct formation to hepatotoxicity. Note this sentence is itself a citation to earlier work within the cited paper, so it reports rather than demonstrates the step.

steps/2.description: A small but fixed fraction of ingested aflatoxin binds irreversibly to protein and DNA. The albumin adduct is the measurable one and, because it is not repaired, it persists with the half-life of albumin itself — which is what makes it a usable exposure biomarker weeks after the meal.

evidence.snippet: Acute aflatoxicosis manifests as acute hepatic failure and jaundice, caused by toxic metabolites that lead to hepatic necrosis through mechanisms involving DNA damage, oxidative stress, and lipid peroxidation.
evidence.explanation: Names the injury mechanisms that lead to necrosis, distinct from the mutagenic route.

evidence.snippet: Disruption of protein synthesis and immune suppression further contribute to disease severity, and impaired production of clotting factors leads to coagulopathy and bleeding risks (Benkerroum, 2020).
evidence.explanation: Adds protein-synthesis disruption and gives the route to coagulopathy, which is curated as a phenotype of this node's consequence.

steps/3.description: The cytotoxic arm that distinguishes acute aflatoxicosis from the chronic carcinogenic route. Adducted macromolecules disrupt protein synthesis, and DNA damage, oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation act alongside it. This node exists because it is the acute-specific mechanism: none of it is the TP53 mutagenesis that drives the chronic arm curated in Aflatoxin_Related_HCC.

evidence.snippet: Acute exposure to high levels of aflatoxin B1, one of the most toxic mycotoxins, can result in severe poisoning, defined as acute aflatoxicosis, which manifests as acute hepatic failure followed by death in severe cases.
evidence.explanation: States the acute exposure to hepatic failure route that this node and the next one decompose.

steps/4.description: Centrilobular hepatocyte death at acute dose. Split from acute hepatic failure, which is the organism-level consequence, because the two sit at different biological scales and the second follows from the first.

evidence.snippet: During January-June 2004, an aflatoxicosis outbreak in eastern Kenya resulted in 317 cases and 125 deaths.
evidence.explanation: The scale and lethality of the reference outbreak.

evidence.snippet: Aflatoxicosis can progress to potentially lethal acute hepatitis with vomiting, abdominal pain, hepatitis, and death (Etzel 2002).
evidence.explanation: Describes the clinical progression of the acute syndrome.

evidence.snippet: As a result, symptoms of acute aflatoxicosis include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, diarrhoea, oedema, jaundice, convulsions, intestinal bleedings, and even death in severe cases (Kamala et al., 2018).
evidence.explanation: The basis for the gastrointestinal edges out of this node. Graded INDIRECT and OTHER because the sentence is the review's narrative summary of a secondary source rather than a result of the review itself, and "as a result" is the only thing that places these symptoms downstream of hepatic failure.

evidence.snippet: Seven patients had serum samples analyzed at the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI), and all were negative for viruses known to cause hepatic disease in Kenya (e.g., yellow fever; Rift Valley fever; dengue; acute hepatitis A, B, and C; West Nile virus; and Chikungunya and Bunyamwera) (American Public Health Association 2000).
evidence.explanation: Supports the description's claim that hepatotropic viral causes were excluded, and is the diagnostic basis for treating this as a toxic rather than infectious hepatitis.

steps/5.description: Organ-level failure: jaundice, coagulopathy, ascites and death. The clinical presentation is nonspecific enough that the 2004 outbreak was investigated as acute jaundice of unknown origin, with the seven patients who had serum tested negative for every hepatotropic virus known to circulate in the region.

evidence.snippet: our case definition was restricted to acute jaundice of unknown origin (i.e., no history of cirrhosis or obstructive liver disease) leading to hospitalization
evidence.explanation: Gives the operational case definition used in the reference investigation.

evidence.snippet: Common symptoms included vomiting (77-100 %), jaundice (88-100 %), and abdominal pain (8-87 %).
evidence.explanation: Frequency support. Jaundice was reported in 88-100% of cases across the outbreaks pooled by the systematic review, which is why the band is VERY_FREQUENT rather than OBLIGATE.

steps/6.description: The presenting sign and the basis of the outbreak case definition — acute jaundice of unknown origin, without a history of cirrhosis or obstructive liver disease.

evidence.snippet: Aflatoxicosis can progress to potentially lethal acute hepatitis with vomiting, abdominal pain, hepatitis, and death (Etzel 2002).
evidence.explanation: Lists vomiting among the progressive features.

evidence.snippet: Common symptoms included vomiting (77-100 %), jaundice (88-100 %), and abdominal pain (8-87 %).
evidence.explanation: Frequency support. Vomiting was reported in 77-100% of cases. The range straddles the FREQUENT/VERY_FREQUENT boundary; VERY_FREQUENT is recorded because the mass of the range and every individual outbreak in the review's symptom table sit above 80%.

steps/7.description: Part of the early gastrointestinal presentation.

evidence.snippet: Aflatoxicosis can progress to potentially lethal acute hepatitis with vomiting, abdominal pain, hepatitis, and death (Etzel 2002).
evidence.explanation: Lists abdominal pain among the progressive features.

evidence.snippet: Common symptoms included vomiting (77-100 %), jaundice (88-100 %), and abdominal pain (8-87 %).
evidence.explanation: Frequency support. Abdominal pain ranged from 8% to 87% across outbreaks. That spans three FrequencyEnum bands, so the reported range is recorded verbatim rather than compressed into one of them.

steps/8.description: Part of the early gastrointestinal presentation.

evidence.snippet: Parts of Western India have experienced an outbreak of hepatitis affecting man and dogs and characterised by jaundice, rapidly developing ascites, portal hypertension, and a high mortality-rate.
evidence.explanation: Describes the syndrome in an independent outbreak, including the cross-species occurrence.

evidence.snippet: Other symptoms include fever (between 46 and 65 %), diarrhoea (between 31 and 50 %), ascites (50 %), scrotum swelling (8 %), rectal bleeding, easy bruisability, constipation, dyspnea, hypothermia, shock, fits (85 %) and coma (32 %).
evidence.explanation: Frequency support. Ascites was reported in 50% of cases in the outbreak series the systematic review pooled, placing it in the FREQUENT band.

steps/9.description: Rapidly developing ascites with portal hypertension characterised the western India outbreak, which affected dogs as well as people.

evidence.snippet: Disruption of protein synthesis and immune suppression further contribute to disease severity, and impaired production of clotting factors leads to coagulopathy and bleeding risks (Benkerroum, 2020).
evidence.explanation: Names the mechanism and the manifestation. Graded OTHER because the sentence is the review's narrative summary citing a secondary source, not a result the review itself produced.

evidence.snippet: Other symptoms include fever (between 46 and 65 %), diarrhoea (between 31 and 50 %), ascites (50 %), scrotum swelling (8 %), rectal bleeding, easy bruisability, constipation, dyspnea, hypothermia, shock, fits (85 %) and coma (32 %).
evidence.explanation: The observed bleeding phenotype in pooled outbreak cases. INDIRECT because the review reports rectal bleeding and easy bruisability as symptoms without reporting a coagulation measurement, so the coagulopathy is inferred from the bleeding rather than measured.

steps/10.description: Impaired clotting from loss of hepatic clotting-factor synthesis, presenting as bleeding and easy bruising. Asserted in the entry's own description and now modelled: it is the clinical arm of the failure node that supportive care is actually directed at, since fresh frozen plasma is given for it.

evidence.snippet: Other symptoms include fever (between 46 and 65 %), diarrhoea (between 31 and 50 %), ascites (50 %), scrotum swelling (8 %), rectal bleeding, easy bruisability, constipation, dyspnea, hypothermia, shock, fits (85 %) and coma (32 %).
evidence.explanation: Reports diarrhoea in 31-50% of pooled outbreak cases, which is the FREQUENT band.

steps/11.description: Part of the gastrointestinal presentation, reported alongside vomiting and abdominal pain.

edges/0.description: The epoxide binds covalently to DNA bases and to proteins, notably serum albumin.

edges/1.description: Disruption of hepatocyte proteins and DNA produces the cytotoxic injury. The intermediates that were previously left unnamed on this edge are now an explicit node, so the edge itself is direct.

edges/2.description: The combined injury kills hepatocytes outright at acute dose.

edges/3.description: Loss of hepatocyte mass beyond hepatic reserve produces organ failure.

edges/4.description: Loss of hepatocyte conjugating and excretory capacity.

edges/5.description: Failure of hepatic clotting-factor synthesis, the route the systematic review names explicitly.

edges/6.description: Portal hypertension and the fall in plasma oncotic pressure that follows loss of hepatic albumin synthesis are the intermediates. Both are named in the western India outbreak report as part of the same syndrome, neither was measured there, so they are recorded on the edge rather than modelled as their own nodes.

edges/7.description: The systematic review places vomiting downstream of the necrosis-to-failure chain, but does so narratively ("as a result") while citing a secondary source. Direct gastrointestinal toxicity of ingested aflatoxin is an untested alternative route and would not run through hepatic failure at all, so the intermediates are recorded as unknown rather than assumed.

edges/8.description: Same standing as vomiting: attributed to the hepatic chain by the review's narrative, with direct gastrointestinal toxicity unexcluded.

edges/9.description: Same standing as vomiting and abdominal pain.

evidence.snippet: The human gastrointestinal tract rapidly absorbs aflatoxins after consumption of contaminated food, and the circulatory system transports the aflatoxins to the liver
evidence.explanation: States the route from ingestion to the target organ where bioactivation happens.

edges/10.description: Ingested aflatoxin B1 is absorbed and carried by the portal circulation to the liver, which is where bioactivation occurs. This exposure is the disease; there is no other route to the mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Management consisted of supportive care including antibiotics and antifungal therapy, transfusion of red blood cells and fresh frozen plasma. His recovery was uneventful.
evidence.explanation: A single uncontrolled case. Graded INDIRECT because recovery after supportive care in one patient does not establish that the care caused the recovery.

treatments/0.description: There is no antidote. Management is supportive — transfusion of red cells and fresh frozen plasma for the coagulopathy, antimicrobials for intercurrent infection, and organ support. The single detailed case report describes recovery on this management, which is the most that can be claimed for it.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Supports organ function while the liver regenerates; it does not act on aflatoxin metabolism or adduct formation.

evidence.snippet: Mortality rates in the study of Tzee-Cheng et al. (1991) should be interpreted with caution, as co-intoxication with excessive levels of boric acid may have influenced the severity of the acute aflatoxicosis (Tzee‐Cheng et al., 1991).
evidence.explanation: Refutes attributing the 1991 series' neurological severity to aflatoxin alone, which is the reason this entry carries no encephalopathy phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Other symptoms include fever (between 46 and 65 %), diarrhoea (between 31 and 50 %), ascites (50 %), scrotum swelling (8 %), rectal bleeding, easy bruisability, constipation, dyspnea, hypothermia, shock, fits (85 %) and coma (32 %).
evidence.explanation: The neurological figures themselves. INDIRECT because the sentence reports fits and coma as observed symptoms without attributing them to a hepatic mechanism, which is precisely the gap.

open_questions/0.rationale: Encephalopathy is a standard feature of fulminant hepatic failure of any cause, and it would be easy to import it here on that basis. The cited corpus does not support it. Not one of the five references uses the phrase "hepatic encephalopathy". The only neurological figures in the literature — fits in 85 percent and coma in 31 percent of cases — come from a single 1991 series, and the systematic review that pools it says explicitly that that outbreak involved co-intoxication with boric acid and that its severity should be interpreted with caution. A phenotype was therefore not created: doing so would assert on a general clinical expectation what the sources actually contest. Resolving this needs neurological findings from an outbreak without a co-intoxicant.

open_questions/1.rationale: In the Kenyan case-control study, case patients were positive for hepatitis B surface antigen roughly ten times more often than controls. In chronic aflatoxin exposure an HBV interaction is well established for hepatocellular carcinoma, so it is tempting to carry that model across. But the acute finding rests on one study with wide confidence intervals, HBV and aflatoxin exposure are geographically confounded, and the mechanism that would make an HBV-infected liver more vulnerable to a single toxic insult is not the same as the mechanism of the chronic interaction. Recorded as open rather than imported from the HCC entry.

open_questions/2.rationale: Prevention, food standards and outbreak response all turn on this number and it is not known. The best human estimate comes from the 1974 western India outbreak — 2 to 6 mg daily for about a month, reconstructed from contaminated food samples rather than measured intake. The Kenyan outbreak reported maize concentrations up to 4,400 ppb but not consumption, so no dose can be derived. Every regulatory limit for aflatoxin in food is therefore anchored to carcinogenic risk from chronic exposure, not to the acute lethal dose.

open_questions/3.rationale: Pancytopenia with bleeding is described in a case report with confirmed serum aflatoxin, and it is not predicted by a purely hepatocentric model. It could equally reflect the coagulopathy and marrow suppression of any fulminant hepatic failure with sepsis. Distinguishing them would need haematological data from an outbreak cohort, which no published investigation reports. Kept as a phenotype with explicitly weak evidence rather than dropped or over-claimed.

evidence.snippet: We show that ALMS1 is widely expressed and localizes to centrosomes and to the base of cilia.
evidence.explanation: Cell localization experiments place ALMS1 at the centrosome and basal body, supporting a primary ciliary-basal body mechanism.

evidence.snippet: We have detected six different mutations (two nonsense and four frameshift mutations causing premature stop codons) in seven families, confirming that ALMS1 is the gene underlying Alström syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Human genetic evidence links ALMS1 loss to disease and anchors basal body dysfunction as the upstream defect.

steps/1.description: ALMS1 is a centrosome and ciliary basal body-associated protein. Loss of ALMS1 function disrupts basal-body dependent cellular organization across multiple tissues and acts as the upstream lesion for the sensory, renal, metabolic, and fibrotic components of Alstrom syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Diminished cone ERG b-wave response is observed early, followed by the degeneration of photoreceptor cells.
evidence.explanation: The Alms1 mouse model directly demonstrates progressive photoreceptor degeneration.

evidence.snippet: BACKGROUND: Alström syndrome (ALMS) is a rare autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the ALMS1 gene, characterized by progressive cone-rod dystrophy, early-onset obesity, cardiomyopathy, and multiorgan dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Large human cohort framing confirms progressive cone-rod dystrophy as a core disease manifestation.

steps/2.description: ALMS1 deficiency disrupts photoreceptor intracellular trafficking and drives progressive cone and rod degeneration, producing the characteristic retinal dystrophy of Alstrom syndrome.

evidence.snippet: These results identify previously unrecognized cochlear histopathologies associated with this ciliopathy that (i) implicate ALMS1 in planar cell polarity signaling and (ii) suggest that the loss of outer hair cells causes the majority of the hearing loss in Alström Syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Mouse inner-ear studies support outer hair cell loss as the proximal lesion driving ALMS hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: Absent otoacoustic emissions, intact speech discrimination, and disproportionately normal auditory brainstem responses suggest an outer hair cell site of lesion.
evidence.explanation: Human audiologic phenotyping independently supports an outer hair cell lesion.

steps/3.description: ALMS1 localizes to cochlear hair-cell basal bodies; its loss perturbs planar cell polarity and outer hair cell survival, producing progressive sensory hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: Hence, we show for the first time the relative AT failure in human obese cohorts to be a major determinant of accelerated IR without evidence of lipodystrophy.
evidence.explanation: Human metabolic phenotyping identifies relative adipose tissue failure as a proximal mechanism for insulin-resistant obesity in Alstrom syndrome.

steps/4.description: Obesity in Alstrom syndrome is accompanied by inadequate adipose tissue expansion and adipocyte dysfunction, producing a metabolically fragile state in which insulin resistance develops early and progresses rapidly.

evidence.snippet: alterations associated with ALMS1 depletion clustered around the processes of extracellular matrix regulation and lipid metabolism in both the transcriptome and proteome.
evidence.explanation: ALMS1 knockout fibroblast profiling directly links ALMS1 deficiency to extracellular matrix dysregulation.

steps/5.description: ALMS1 deficiency alters extracellular matrix regulatory programs, favoring collagen remodeling and fibroproliferative disease in liver and heart.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that in vitro knockdown of Alms1 in mice causes stunted cilia on kidney epithelial cells and prevents these cells from increasing calcium influx in response to mechanical stimuli.
evidence.explanation: Mouse kidney epithelial experiments show direct impairment of renal cilia morphology and mechanosensory signaling.

evidence.snippet: After adjusting for age, there were no significant associations of kidney dysfunction with type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension, cardiomyopathy or portal hypertension suggesting that kidney disease in AS is a primary manifestation of the syndrome due to lack of ALMS1 protein.
evidence.explanation: Human cohort data argue that kidney disease is a primary manifestation of ALMS rather than a secondary metabolic complication.

steps/6.description: Renal disease in Alstrom syndrome reflects a primary nephron ciliopathy rather than merely secondary metabolic injury, with progressive tubular ciliary loss and impaired mechanosensory signaling.

evidence.snippet: In this case, the cardiac manifestation in Alstrom syndrome is pEFE.
evidence.explanation: Pathology-confirmed case shows that infantile ALMS cardiomyopathy can present as primary endocardial fibroelastosis.

evidence.snippet: ALMS1-depleted cardiomyocytes exhibited enhanced proliferation activity.
evidence.explanation: Functional studies in patient-derived systems implicate direct cardiomyocyte remodeling effects of ALMS1 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Cardiomyopathy is common in adults with AS, complicated in a significant proportion by atherosclerotic coronary artery disease and restrictive cardiomyopathy, confirmed on CMR and invasive testing.
evidence.explanation: Adult cohort data show persistent structural and functional cardiac remodeling beyond infantile disease.

steps/7.description: Cardiac disease in Alstrom syndrome spans infantile fibroelastotic cardiomyopathy and later adult myocardial remodeling, with both cardiomyocyte and cardiac fibroblast abnormalities implicated.

evidence.snippet: The infantile cone-rod dystrophy with nystagmus and severe visual impairment is the earliest and most consistent clinical manifestation of ALMS.
evidence.explanation: Review of ALMS clinical data identifies cone-rod dystrophy as the earliest and most consistent feature.

steps/8.description: Early progressive retinal degeneration involving cones and rods, often beginning in infancy and driving lifelong visual disability.

evidence.snippet: Clinical manifestations included universal visual impairment (100%, 112/112), obesity (84.1%, 96/114), hearing loss (70.8%, 51/72), hepatic steatosis (66.7%, 40/60), and cardiac abnormalities (58.2%, 46/79).
evidence.explanation: Large cohort shows that visual impairment was universal among evaluated patients.

steps/9.description: Severe early-onset visual loss caused by progressive retinal degeneration.

evidence.snippet: Cone-rod dystrophy presents as progressive visual impairment, photophobia, and nystagmus usually starting between birth and age 15 months.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies nystagmus as an infantile manifestation of the cardinal retinal dystrophy.

steps/10.description: Infantile nystagmus accompanies the earliest cone-rod dystrophy and is an important diagnostic clue.

evidence.snippet: Cone-rod dystrophy presents as progressive visual impairment, photophobia, and nystagmus usually starting between birth and age 15 months.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly supports early photophobia within the retinal phenotype.

steps/11.description: Early photophobia accompanies progressive cone-rod dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: Our data show that hearing loss associated with AS begins in childhood and is a predominantly symmetric, sensory hearing loss that may progress to a severe degree.
evidence.explanation: Prospective audiology cohort defines the typical childhood-onset progressive sensory hearing phenotype.

steps/12.description: Progressive, usually symmetric sensory hearing loss beginning in childhood.

evidence.snippet: Clinical manifestations included universal visual impairment (100%, 112/112), obesity (84.1%, 96/114), hearing loss (70.8%, 51/72), hepatic steatosis (66.7%, 40/60), and cardiac abnormalities (58.2%, 46/79).
evidence.explanation: Large cohort shows obesity in more than 80% of evaluated patients.

steps/13.description: Early-onset obesity, often beginning in childhood and frequently truncal in distribution.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report on a monogenic form of IR-prone obesity, Alström syndrome (ALMS).
evidence.explanation: Human metabolic study explicitly frames ALMS as insulin-resistance-prone obesity.

steps/14.description: Early and often severe insulin resistance complicating obesity in Alstrom syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Insulin resistance is typically accompanied by the skin changes of acanthosis nigricans, and proceeds to T2DM in the majority by the third decade.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly links acanthosis nigricans to the insulin-resistant phenotype.

steps/15.description: Cutaneous acanthosis nigricans commonly accompanies severe insulin resistance.

evidence.snippet: Insulin resistance is typically accompanied by the skin changes of acanthosis nigricans, and proceeds to T2DM in the majority by the third decade. Nearly all demonstrate hypertriglyceridemia.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews' "nearly all" wording directly supports the very-frequent band.

steps/16.description: Hypertriglyceridemia is a highly penetrant metabolic manifestation.

evidence.snippet: In addition, infantile transient cardiomyopathy, early childhood obesity with hyperphagia, deafness, insulin resistance (IR), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), systemic fibrosis and progressive renal or liver dysfunction are common findings.
evidence.explanation: Clinical review supports type II diabetes mellitus as a common downstream metabolic manifestation of ALMS.

steps/17.description: Progressive hyperglycemia emerging as insulin resistance worsens over time.

evidence.snippet: Alström syndrome is a monogenic recessive disorder featuring an array of clinical manifestations, with systemic fibrosis and multiple organ involvement, including retinal degeneration, hearing loss, childhood obesity, diabetes mellitus, dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), urological dysfunction, and pulmonary, hepatic, and renal failure.
evidence.explanation: Large genotype-phenotype study identifies dilated cardiomyopathy as a core multisystem feature of ALMS.

evidence.snippet: RESULTS: 47 adults with AS (64% male; mean age 33 years; 66% white British) were studied. Seven (15%) survived infantile cardiomyopathy and 23 (49%) developed adult-onset cardiomyopathy.
evidence.explanation: Adult cardiovascular cohort shows cardiomyopathy is frequent across the lifespan.

steps/18.description: Infantile or later-onset myocardial disease with ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction; infantile episodes may partially recover while adult cardiomyopathy can progress.

evidence.snippet: Alström syndrome is characterized by cone-rod dystrophy, obesity, progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment, acute infantile-onset cardiomyopathy and/or adolescent- or adult-onset restrictive cardiomyopathy, insulin resistance / type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and chronic progressive kidney disease.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews explicitly includes adolescent- or adult-onset restrictive cardiomyopathy in the core clinical spectrum.

steps/19.description: A later-onset restrictive cardiomyopathy is part of the biphasic cardiac spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Eighteen percent met the definition for chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and proteinuria); all were adults with median age of 32.8 (20.6-37.9) years.
evidence.explanation: Prospective NIH cohort quantifies age-progressive chronic kidney disease in adults with ALMS.

steps/20.description: Age-progressive primary kidney involvement with declining kidney function and proteinuria in a subset of adults.

evidence.snippet: Clinical manifestations included universal visual impairment (100%, 112/112), obesity (84.1%, 96/114), hearing loss (70.8%, 51/72), hepatic steatosis (66.7%, 40/60), and cardiac abnormalities (58.2%, 46/79).
evidence.explanation: Large cohort demonstrates frequent hepatic steatosis in ALMS.

steps/21.description: Common metabolic liver involvement that often coexists with early fibrogenic liver stiffness abnormalities.

evidence.snippet: Patients with ALMS displayed enhanced steatosis, an early increased age-dependent LS that is associated with obesity and T2DM but also linked to genetic alterations, suggesting that ALMS1 could be involved in liver fibrogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Human liver stiffness and steatosis data support progressive fibrogenic liver involvement while qualifying the causal contribution of ALMS1.

steps/22.description: Progressive fibrogenic liver involvement can accompany steatosis and increasing liver stiffness.

evidence.snippet: Coupled with recent data on the complex phenotype of Bardet-Biedl syndrome, our findings imply an unexpected central role for basal body and centrosome dysfunction in the pathogenesis of obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes.
evidence.explanation: The localization study connects ALMS1 basal-body biology with obesity pathogenesis but does not resolve the intervening tissue and signaling mechanisms, so it only partially supports this indirect edge.

edges/1.description: Basal body and centrosome dysfunction in ALMS1-related ciliopathy contributes directly to the childhood obesity component of Alstrom syndrome.

evidence.snippet: relative AT failure in human obese cohorts to be a major determinant of accelerated IR
evidence.explanation: Human metabolic phenotyping supports adipose failure in ALMS, while the intervening route from basal-body dysfunction remains unresolved.

edges/2.description: ALMS1 loss compromises adipose tissue buffering capacity and promotes metabolically adverse obesity.

evidence.snippet: alterations associated with ALMS1 depletion clustered around the processes of extracellular matrix regulation and lipid metabolism in both the transcriptome and proteome.
evidence.explanation: ALMS1-depleted fibroblasts directly connect loss of the centrosomal protein to extracellular-matrix regulatory changes, although intermediate signaling is not resolved.

edges/3.description: Cilia-linked signaling defects alter matrix remodeling programs and favor multiorgan fibrotic disease.

evidence.snippet: in vitro knockdown of Alms1 in mice causes stunted cilia on kidney epithelial cells and prevents these cells from increasing calcium influx in response to mechanical stimuli.
evidence.explanation: Experimental Alms1 depletion directly impairs renal epithelial cilia and mechanosensory signaling.

edges/4.description: Renal tubular primary cilia lose normal maintenance and mechanosensory function.

evidence.snippet: Diminished cone ERG b-wave response is observed early, followed by the degeneration of photoreceptor cells.
evidence.explanation: Alms1 disruption produces early functional cone deficits followed by photoreceptor loss in vivo.

edges/5.description: Photoreceptor cells progressively fail when ALMS1-dependent ciliary trafficking is lost.

evidence.snippet: the loss of outer hair cells causes the majority of the hearing loss in Alström Syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The inner-ear model links ALMS1-dependent planar-cell-polarity disruption to outer-hair-cell loss.

edges/6.description: Hair-cell basal body dysfunction perturbs inner-ear sensory-cell polarity and survival.

evidence.snippet: relative AT failure in human obese cohorts to be a major determinant of accelerated IR
evidence.explanation: Human metabolic phenotyping directly identifies relative adipose-tissue failure as a determinant of accelerated insulin resistance.

edges/7.description: Limited adipose buffering capacity accelerates systemic insulin resistance.

evidence.snippet: Both extreme IR and β-cell failure are the two determinant factors responsible for the development of glucose metabolism alterations in ALMS.
evidence.explanation: Clinical review directly supports progression from severe insulin resistance and beta-cell failure to dysglycemia and type II diabetes in ALMS.

edges/8.description: Progressive insulin resistance drives diabetes as beta-cell compensation fails.

evidence.snippet: Patients with ALMS displayed enhanced steatosis, an early increased age-dependent LS that is associated with obesity and T2DM but also linked to genetic alterations, suggesting that ALMS1 could be involved in liver fibrogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Human liver phenotyping links steatosis and liver stiffness to obesity and T2DM while preserving an additional ALMS1-specific contribution.

edges/9.description: Severe insulin resistance and metabolically adverse obesity contribute to common steatotic liver disease.

evidence.snippet: Insulin resistance is typically accompanied by the skin changes of acanthosis nigricans
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly connects insulin resistance, the established intermediate, with acanthosis nigricans.

edges/10.description: Severe insulin resistance commonly produces acanthosis nigricans as a cutaneous marker.

evidence.snippet: Insulin resistance is typically accompanied by the skin changes of acanthosis nigricans, and proceeds to T2DM in the majority by the third decade. Nearly all demonstrate hypertriglyceridemia.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews places near-universal hypertriglyceridemia in the same insulin-resistance progression, supporting this clinically mediated edge.

edges/11.description: The severe insulin-resistant metabolic state is commonly accompanied by hypertriglyceridemia.

evidence.snippet: Patients with ALMS displayed enhanced steatosis, an early increased age-dependent LS that is associated with obesity and T2DM but also linked to genetic alterations, suggesting that ALMS1 could be involved in liver fibrogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Human elastography and ultrasound data support age-dependent fibrogenic liver involvement while appropriately qualifying the ALMS1-specific mechanism as suggested rather than proven.

edges/12.description: Dysregulated extracellular-matrix programs contribute to progressive liver fibrogenesis.

evidence.snippet: In this case, the cardiac manifestation in Alstrom syndrome is pEFE.
evidence.explanation: Pathology confirms fibroelastotic cardiac remodeling in ALMS, but a direct causal route from the broader extracellular-matrix program is not established.

edges/13.description: Abnormal matrix remodeling contributes to infantile fibroelastosis and later adult cardiomyopathy.

evidence.snippet: Alström syndrome is characterized by cone-rod dystrophy, obesity, progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment, acute infantile-onset cardiomyopathy and/or adolescent- or adult-onset restrictive cardiomyopathy, insulin resistance / type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and chronic progressive kidney disease.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies chronic progressive kidney disease as part of the core clinical spectrum.

edges/14.description: Primary renal involvement progresses with age to chronic kidney disease.

evidence.snippet: Diminished cone ERG b-wave response is observed early, followed by the degeneration of photoreceptor cells.
evidence.explanation: The Alms1 model directly links progressive photoreceptor loss with cone functional decline.

edges/15.description: Progressive cone and rod loss produces the hallmark retinal dystrophy.

evidence.snippet: The infantile cone-rod dystrophy with nystagmus and severe visual impairment is the earliest and most consistent clinical manifestation of ALMS.
evidence.explanation: Clinical evidence connects infantile cone-rod dystrophy with severe visual impairment.

edges/16.description: Early photoreceptor loss causes severe lifelong visual disability.

evidence.snippet: Cone-rod dystrophy presents as progressive visual impairment, photophobia, and nystagmus usually starting between birth and age 15 months.

genes/1.notes: Rare loss-of-function variants cause familial aortic valve developmental anomalies and calcification. A 2022 sequencing/systematic study found a pathogenic variant in one of eight recruited pedigrees and none in 381 sporadic BAV patients. Its approximately 2% familial and <0.1% sporadic literature estimates use heterogeneous congenital-heart-disease denominators, mainly of White ancestry; they are not population fractions of all aortic stenosis. Incomplete penetrance and uncertain variants remain important.

treatments/0.description: Replacement relieves severe valvular obstruction. Prosthesis choice incorporates anticoagulation, durability, future interventions and patient preferences; correction of the valve does not guarantee complete myocardial recovery.

Transfemoral access, coronary obstruction risk, annular anatomy and lifetime reintervention planning matter. Other candidates require individual Heart Team assessment; TAVI for bicuspid stenosis is a weaker recommendation in selected patients at increased surgical risk. Vascular injury, paravalvular leak and pacemaker risk differ from surgical risks.

evidence.explanation: Class I, level B recommendation; the complete clinical and hemodynamic context is required.

treatments/2.description: Intervention is recommended for symptomatic severe high-gradient stenosis, and for confirmed severe low-flow low-gradient disease with reduced ejection fraction. With preserved ejection fraction and low flow/gradient, severity confirmation and exclusion of competing explanations are essential. Expected benefit, life expectancy and procedural feasibility determine whether intervention is appropriate.

evidence.snippet: Intervention should be considered in asymptomatic patients (confirmed by a normal exercise test, if feasible) with severe, high-gradient AS and LVEF ≥50%, as an alternative to close active surveillance, if the procedural risk is low. IIa A
evidence.explanation: The 2025 conditional early-intervention recommendation, not a mandate to replace every asymptomatic valve.

evidence.snippet: Intervention is recommended in asymptomatic patients with severe AS and LVEF <50% without another cause.
evidence.explanation: Class I, level B ventricular-function indication.

treatments/3.description: The 2025 guideline supports intervention as an alternative to close surveillance in asymptomatic severe high-gradient stenosis with ejection fraction ≥50% and low procedural risk (Class IIa, A). Ejection fraction <50% without another cause is a Class I indication. Very severe hemodynamics, rapid progression with heavy calcification, markedly elevated natriuretic peptides or abnormal exercise blood pressure strengthen selection. Trials differ in age, valve anatomy, fibrosis enrichment, procedures and outcome definitions; there is no uniform mortality benefit across all asymptomatic populations.

evidence.snippet: Asymptomatic pa- tients with severe AS should be followed up at least every 6 months to allow detection of early symptoms
evidence.explanation: Regular clinical and echocardiographic surveillance in the guideline.

treatments/4.description: For patients managed without immediate intervention, educate patients and caregivers to report symptoms promptly and reassess severity and ventricular function. The 2025 guideline recommends at least six-monthly follow-up for asymptomatic severe disease, annual reassessment for moderate degenerative stenosis, and potentially two- to three-year intervals for younger patients with mild disease and little leaflet calcium. New symptoms prompt earlier reassessment.

evidence.snippet: Balloon aortic valvotomy may be considered as a bridge to SAVR or TAVI in haemodynamically unstable patients, and (if feasible) in those with severe AS who require urgent high-risk NCS.
evidence.explanation: Explicit bridge indication in the adult 2025 guideline.

treatments/5.description: In the adult severe-stenosis guideline, balloon valvotomy may be considered as a temporary bridge to SAVR or TAVI in hemodynamic instability or urgent high-risk noncardiac surgery (Class IIb, C). Benefits are limited and severe regurgitation is a risk; it is not a durable substitute for replacement in calcific adult disease. Pediatric congenital-valve decisions require their own clinical context.

evidence.snippet: Balloon aortic valvotomy may be considered as a bridge to SAVR or TAVI in haemodynamically unstable patients, and (if feasible) in those with severe AS who require urgent high-risk NCS.
evidence.explanation: Explicit bridge indication in the adult 2025 guideline.

Blood-pressure management addresses comorbidity and additional ventricular load; it has not been established to reverse the valve lesion and must not delay indicated replacement.

evidence.explanation: Symptom relief while addressing severe valve disease.
