evidence.snippet: Missense substitutions affecting DNA-binding residues were associated with diffuse mesangial sclerosis (74%), early steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome onset, and rapid progression to ESRD.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the genotype-phenotype association between DNA-binding-residue missense variants and the Denys-Drash renal phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Truncating mutations conferred the highest Wilms tumor risk (78%) but typically late-onset steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Records the contrasting truncating-variant phenotype, which is why Wilms risk cannot be read off the Denys-Drash label alone.

genes/0.notes: The recurrent hot spot lies in zinc finger III, encoded by exon 9. Genotype tracks with phenotype across the WT1 spectrum: missense substitutions at DNA binding residues give the diffuse mesangial sclerosis picture of Denys-Drash, truncating variants carry the highest Wilms tumor risk, and intronic KTS variants give the Frasier picture.

evidence.snippet: SRNS: avoid immunosuppressants; consider renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibition.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management recommendation for the glomerulopathy.

treatments/0.description: Renin angiotensin aldosterone system blockade is used to reduce proteinuria. Immunosuppression is explicitly avoided, since the glomerulopathy is genetic rather than immune mediated.

evidence.snippet: Avoid treating glomerulopathy with immunosuppressants, as they are not effective and potentially toxic.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews agents and circumstances to avoid statement.

treatments/1.description: An explicit agents to avoid recommendation. Immunosuppressants used empirically for steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome are ineffective here and carry toxicity, which is a practical reason to establish the WT1 genotype early.

evidence.snippet: Prevent whenever possible gonadoblastoma by prophylactic gonadectomy in those with a disorder of testicular development.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews prevention recommendation.

treatments/2.description: Removal of dysgenetic gonadal tissue in individuals with a disorder of testicular development, to prevent gonadoblastoma.

evidence.snippet: Wilms tumor every three months until age seven years
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews tumor surveillance interval.

treatments/3.description: Renal imaging every three months until age seven years. This entry classifies the syndrome as a cancer predisposition, so the tumor arm of the surveillance protocol belongs here alongside the proteinuria monitoring already recorded.

evidence.snippet: Treat Wilms tumor with standard oncology protocols and, when applicable, nephron-sparing surgery.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews treatment recommendation for the tumor.

treatments/4.description: Standard oncology protocols, with nephron-sparing surgery where applicable. The nephron-sparing qualifier matters more here than in sporadic Wilms tumor, because these patients are already losing renal function to the glomerulopathy.

evidence.snippet: Diaphragmatic hernia repair prior to the start of peritoneal dialysis.
evidence.explanation: Supports dialysis being anticipated in management by an inference step: the recommendation sequences other surgery around starting it rather than recommending dialysis outright.

treatments/5.description: Peritoneal or haemodialysis for the kidney failure that follows the glomerulopathy, typically within months of nephrotic syndrome onset. Timing of diaphragmatic hernia repair is explicitly sequenced around starting peritoneal dialysis.

evidence.snippet: End-stage renal disease was reached either concomitantly or within four months after onset of NS in seven of ten patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes by inference that definitive kidney replacement is part of the expected course: the paper reports how fast kidney failure arrives, not the transplant itself.

treatments/6.description: The definitive kidney replacement arm. Graft recurrence of the glomerulopathy is not expected, since the lesion is driven by the constitutional WT1 variant acting in the native kidney rather than by a circulating factor.

evidence.snippet: those designations are now recognized to be part of a phenotypic continuum and are no longer clinically helpful
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews statement that motivates this gap, quoted so the entry does not assert a nosology its own baseline source contradicts.

open_questions/0.rationale: The GeneReviews WT1 Disorder chapter states that the Denys-Drash and Frasier designations are no longer clinically helpful and describes one phenotypic continuum. MONDO still carries separate terms, and there is no MONDO umbrella term for the continuum to bind, so the knowledge base cannot simply follow the clinical reframing. The mechanistic distinction is also real, a zinc finger missense dominant negative versus an intron 9 splice isoform imbalance, so collapsing the entries would lose a genuine mechanistic contrast. This entry is retained on that basis, with kb/groupings/WT1_Disorders.yaml carrying the continuum, and the question is recorded rather than silently resolved.

evidence.snippet: a 8733 bp deletion, encompassing exon 4 of the heat shock protein cochaperone BCL2-associated athanogene 3 (BAG3), was found in seven affected family members and was absent in 355 controls
evidence.explanation: Identifies the founding BAG3 loss-of-function allele and its segregation with disease, establishing the trigger lesion of this entity.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that new comprehensive genomic approaches have identified rare variants in BAG3 as causative of DCM.
evidence.explanation: States the causal conclusion linking rare BAG3 variants to dilated cardiomyopathy.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion in CMD1HH is a loss-of-function variant in BAG3, encoding the heat shock protein co-chaperone Bcl2-associated athanogene 3. The founding allele was an 8733 bp deletion removing exon 4, and the disease allele class also includes frameshift, nonsense, and missense variants. Unlike the sarcomeric dilated cardiomyopathies, the affected protein is not part of the contractile machinery: BAG3 is a quality-control co-chaperone, so the lesion removes maintenance capacity rather than force-generating capacity.

evidence.snippet: Stv and its mammalian ortholog BAG-3 coordinate the activity of Hsc70 and the small heat shock protein HspB8 during disposal that is initiated by the chaperone-associated ubiquitin ligase CHIP and the autophagic ubiquitin adaptor p62.
evidence.explanation: Defines the BAG3-organized CASA machinery - Hsc70, HspB8, CHIP, p62 - that this node represents.

evidence.snippet: Instead of keeping Z disk proteins in a folded conformation, this machinery facilitates the degradation of damaged components, such as filamin, through chaperone-assisted selective autophagy (CASA).
evidence.explanation: States that the BAG3 machinery works by degrading damaged Z-disc components rather than refolding them - the distinguishing feature of this mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Under mechanical stress, the cochaperone cooperates with the small heat shock protein HSPB8 and the cytoskeleton-associated protein SYNPO2 to degrade force-unfolded forms of the actin-crosslinking protein filamin.
evidence.explanation: Specifies the mechanical-stress trigger and the filamin substrate of BAG3-initiated CASA.

steps/2.description: BAG3 initiates chaperone-assisted selective autophagy (CASA), the pathway that disposes of misfolded and mechanically damaged proteins. In striated muscle, BAG3 coordinates Hsc70 and the small heat shock protein HSPB8, with the chaperone-associated ubiquitin ligase CHIP and the autophagic adaptor p62, to degrade force-unfolded Z-disc components such as filamin so that they can be replaced. This machinery is required continuously because the Z-disc is under mechanical, thermal, and oxidative stress with every contraction. A BAG3 loss-of-function allele reduces the capacity of this disposal pathway; CASA is mechanistically distinct from chaperone-mediated autophagy.

evidence.snippet: Impaired CASA results in Z disk disintegration and progressive muscle weakness in flies, mice, and men.
evidence.explanation: States the direct structural consequence of impaired BAG3-dependent CASA - Z-disc disintegration and progressive weakness - across species including humans.

evidence.snippet: the Z disk, a protein assembly essential for actin anchoring in striated muscles, which is subjected to mechanical, thermal, and oxidative stress during contraction
evidence.explanation: Establishes why the Z-disc requires continuous quality control - it is the actin anchor and bears the mechanical stress of every contraction.

steps/3.description: The Z-disc is the anchor for actin thin filaments and the mechanical node of the sarcomere. When CASA cannot clear force-damaged components, they accumulate and the Z-disc disintegrates, producing progressive structural failure of the contractile apparatus. This has been shown across species - impaired CASA causes Z-disc disintegration and progressive muscle weakness in flies, mice, and humans - and in the heart it converts a maintenance defect into a contractile one.

evidence.snippet: Knockdown of bag3 in a zebrafish model recapitulated DCM and heart failure.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that loss of bag3 is sufficient to produce the dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure phenotype in vivo.

steps/4.description: Cumulative Z-disc and sarcomere degradation produces the defining structural remodeling of dilated cardiomyopathy: left ventricular chamber enlargement with wall thinning, myocyte loss, and interstitial fibrosis, with falling ejection fraction. Knockdown of bag3 in zebrafish reproduces this dilated phenotype and heart failure, confirming that loss of the co-chaperone is sufficient to generate the remodeling.

evidence.snippet: Dilated cardiomyopathy commonly causes heart failure and is the most frequent precipitating cause of heart transplantation.
evidence.explanation: States the heart-failure and transplantation burden that constitutes the clinical endpoint of this disease.

steps/5.description: The dilated, poorly contracting ventricle produces progressive systolic heart failure, the clinical endpoint of CMD1HH. Dilated cardiomyopathy is the most frequent precipitating cause of heart transplantation, and advanced BAG3-related disease follows the same course.

edges/1.description: Reduced BAG3 co-chaperone function degrades the CASA pathway that disposes of mechanically damaged Z-disc proteins.

edges/2.description: Without CASA-mediated turnover, damaged Z-disc components accumulate and the Z-disc loses structural integrity.

edges/3.description: Progressive structural failure of the contractile apparatus produces chamber dilation and falling systolic performance.

evidence.snippet: BAG3 | HGNC:939 | dilated cardiomyopathy | MONDO:0005021 | AD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen's Gene Curation Expert Panel classifies this gene-disease relationship as Definitive, which is the authority for curating the gene as CAUSATIVE rather than a candidate.

evidence.snippet: In a multigenerational family with autosomal dominant transmission, we employed whole-exome sequencing in a proband and three of his affected family members
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gene-disease relationship by exome sequencing in a multigenerational dominant family, which is the ascertainment behind the autosomal dominant mode recorded above.

treatments/0.description: Standard guideline-directed heart-failure therapy targeting the neurohormonal drive of adverse remodeling.

treatments/1.description: Advanced, refractory disease is an indication for transplantation.

evidence.snippet: identified the same mutation in another Taiwanese distal hereditary motor neuropathy pedigree with different ancestries and one additional Belgian distal hereditary motor neuropathy family of Caucasian origin
evidence.explanation: Establishes p.His257Arg as recurrent across unrelated pedigrees, which is what raised it above a private family variant.

evidence.snippet: The variant completely co-segregates with the dHMN phenotype in the family, and it was classified as likely pathogenic according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics standards and guidelines.
evidence.explanation: Second allele, independently classified against ACMG criteria.

steps/1.description: A single heterozygous missense allele in WARS1, encoding cytoplasmic tryptophanyl-tRNA synthetase. The recurrent p.His257Arg allele was identified across three unrelated pedigrees from two continents; p.Asp314Gly is a second, independently ascertained allele associated with a milder, later-onset phenotype. Both lie in the catalytic body of the enzyme.

evidence.snippet: Cell transfection studies demonstrated a dominant-negative effect of the p.His257Arg mutation on aminoacylation activity of TrpRS, which subsequently compromised protein synthesis and reduced cell viability.
evidence.explanation: Names the reduced activity and its immediate consequence.

steps/2.description: Charging of tRNA-Trp with tryptophan by cytoplasmic TrpRS is reduced. This is the canonical, housekeeping arm of the mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Further in vitro analyses showed that the WARS mutation could potentiate the angiostatic activities of TrpRS by enhancing its interaction with vascular endothelial-cadherin.
evidence.explanation: The disease-variant claim this node rests on.

evidence.snippet: Proteolytic removal of the N-terminal 93 amino acids gives rise to T2-TrpRS, which has potent anti-angiogenic activity mediated through its extracellular interaction with VE-cadherin.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the normal fragment biology that the disease variant acts on.

evidence.snippet: the core catalytic domains of human TyrRS and TrpRS function as angiogenic and angiostatic factors, respectively, whereas the full-length forms are inactive for this function
evidence.explanation: Confirms that the angiostatic activity is a property of the cleaved fragment, not of full-length TrpRS.

steps/3.description: Vertebrate TrpRS carries an N-terminal extension whose proteolytic removal yields the T2-TrpRS fragment, an angiostatic cytokine that acts extracellularly by binding vascular endothelial-cadherin (VE-cadherin). The full-length enzyme is inactive for this function. The dHMN9 variant enhances that interaction. Whether the relevant consequence in motor axons is vascular or a direct effect on the neuron is not established.

evidence.snippet: which subsequently compromised protein synthesis and reduced cell viability
evidence.explanation: Direct statement of reduced protein synthesis and viability.

steps/4.description: Translational output falls and cell viability is reduced. Motor neurons, with the largest axonal biosynthetic burden of any cell, are proposed to be the least tolerant of this.

evidence.snippet: His257Arg TrpRS also inhibited neurite outgrowth and led to neurite degeneration in the neuronal cell lines and rat motor neurons.
evidence.explanation: Both halves of this node - outgrowth failure and degeneration - are stated in one sentence of the source.

steps/5.description: Mutant TrpRS both prevents neurites from extending and causes established neurites to break down, in neuronal cell lines and in primary rat motor neurons. This is the most proximate cellular readout available for dHMN9; no human neuronal model has been reported.

evidence.snippet: length-dependent motor axonal degeneration with CMT examination score ranging from 6 to 10
evidence.explanation: Names the length-dependent motor axonal pattern in affected individuals.

steps/6.description: Distal degeneration of the longest motor axons, sparing sensory fibres in most reported patients. Electrophysiology shows a motor axonal pattern. Conformance is asserted for the axonal-degeneration node only; the module's demyelinating arm is not part of the dHMN9 phenotype. Annotated with *neuron projection maintenance* rather than the *neuron projection development* term used on the upstream cellular node. GO has no term for axon degeneration (the peripheral_axonal_degeneration module works around the same gap), and failure to maintain an already-formed axon is the closer reading for this node than failure to build one.

evidence.snippet: Distal hereditary motor neuropathy is a heterogeneous group of inherited neuropathies characterized by distal limb muscle weakness and atrophy.
evidence.explanation: Definitional: states distal weakness as the characteristic feature of the entity these WARS1 families were ascertained as having. The patient-specific evidence for this phenotype is the PMID:31069783 item below.

evidence.snippet: distal wasting and weakness, minimal sensory disturbance
evidence.explanation: Documents distal weakness in the p.Asp314Gly family specifically.

steps/7.description: Slowly progressive weakness of distal limb muscles, beginning in the feet and later involving the hands. This is the presenting and defining feature.

evidence.snippet: distal wasting and weakness, minimal sensory disturbance
evidence.explanation: Reports distal wasting in the p.Asp314Gly family itself.

evidence.snippet: Distal hereditary motor neuropathy (dHMN) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of inherited neuropathies characterized by distal limb muscle wasting and weakness with no or minimal sensory abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Definitional context: distal wasting is characteristic of the entity these WARS1 families were ascertained as having.

steps/8.description: Wasting of distal limb muscles accompanying the weakness, reflecting chronic denervation.

evidence.snippet: Cell transfection studies demonstrated a dominant-negative effect of the p.His257Arg mutation on aminoacylation activity of TrpRS, which subsequently compromised protein synthesis and reduced cell viability.
evidence.explanation: States the dominant-negative effect on the canonical enzymatic activity directly.

edges/1.description: The mutant subunit reduces aminoacylation activity of the enzyme beyond what one inactive copy would predict, i.e. it acts on the wild-type product rather than merely failing to contribute.

evidence.snippet: Further in vitro analyses showed that the WARS mutation could potentiate the angiostatic activities of TrpRS by enhancing its interaction with vascular endothelial-cadherin.
evidence.explanation: Directly reports potentiation of the non-canonical angiostatic function by the disease variant.

edges/2.description: The same variant enhances a non-enzymatic activity of TrpRS, so the allele is not only subtractive. This is the arm that makes dHMN9 more than a translation-capacity disorder.

evidence.snippet: which subsequently compromised protein synthesis and reduced cell viability
evidence.explanation: Links the aminoacylation defect to translational output in the same experiment.

edges/3.description: Reduced supply of charged tRNA-Trp limits elongation of any transcript containing tryptophan codons.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, these findings establish WARS as a gene whose mutations may cause distal hereditary motor neuropathy and alter canonical and non-canonical functions of TrpRS.
evidence.explanation: Supports that both functions are altered by the variant; graded PARTIAL because the causal step from the non-canonical arm to neurite damage is not demonstrated.

edges/4.description: Proposed second route to the neurite phenotype, alongside the translation arm. The published experiments establish that the variant both potentiates the angiostatic interaction and damages neurites, but do not show that the first causes the second.

evidence.snippet: His257Arg TrpRS also inhibited neurite outgrowth and led to neurite degeneration in the neuronal cell lines and rat motor neurons.
evidence.explanation: Reports the neurite phenotype produced by the same variant in the same study.

edges/5.description: Reduced biosynthetic capacity is the proposed proximate cause of failure to build and maintain neurites.

evidence.snippet: The clinical features included juvenile to adult onset (15-23 years), distal wasting and weakness, minimal sensory disturbance and length-dependent motor axonal degeneration with CMT examination score ranging from 6 to 10.
evidence.explanation: Documents length-dependent motor axonal degeneration in WARS1-variant patients.

edges/6.description: Cellular neurite failure scaled to the whole organism produces the length-dependent axonal pattern seen on nerve conduction studies.

evidence.snippet: Distal hereditary motor neuropathy is a heterogeneous group of inherited neuropathies characterized by distal limb muscle weakness and atrophy.
evidence.explanation: States the defining clinical consequence of the axonopathy.

edges/7.description: Denervation of distal muscles by degenerating motor axons produces the presenting weakness.

evidence.snippet: distal wasting and weakness, minimal sensory disturbance
evidence.explanation: Reports distal wasting alongside the weakness in WARS1-variant patients.

edges/8.description: Chronic denervation produces distal muscle wasting.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, these findings establish WARS as a gene whose mutations may cause distal hereditary motor neuropathy and alter canonical and non-canonical functions of TrpRS.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease assertion, in the study's own words.

evidence.snippet: Variants in tryptophanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (WARS1) cause autosomal dominantly inherited distal hereditary motor neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
evidence.explanation: Independent restatement of the dominant WARS1-dHMN relationship by a group studying the recessive disorder.

genes/0.notes: A third allele, p.Phe138Tyr (c.413T>A), is reported in a further Chinese family in the letter-and-reply pair PMID:31321409 / PMID:31321406. It is named here without an evidence item because both references cache with no abstract text, so there is no quotable finding - see the entry-level notes. Recorded so a curator with full-text access knows the allelic series is larger than the two variants evidenced above.

open_questions/0.rationale: The discovery study demonstrated both effects of p.His257Arg and reported the neurite phenotype, but did not separate the two. This matters beyond bookkeeping: the two arms imply different therapeutic targets, and they imply different explanations for the cell-type specificity. A pure charging-capacity defect has to explain why only the longest motor axons fail when every cell needs tryptophanyl-tRNA; the angiostatic arm offers an alternative in which the relevant target is not the ribosome at all. The same unresolved question runs through the wider ARS-neuropathy field, where for GARS1 the dominant view has moved away from simple charging loss.

open_questions/1.rationale: Every cellular result curated for this entry comes from transfected cell lines or rat motor neurons; no human neuronal model, patient-derived iPSC line, or animal model of dHMN9 has been reported. The mismatch is mechanistically pointed rather than generic, because the disease's defining feature is length dependence: a cultured rat motor neuron extends neurites orders of magnitude shorter than the human axons that actually fail, so the assay cannot in principle test the property that defines the phenotype. Over-expression of the mutant subunit in transfection also sets a stoichiometry between mutant and wild-type TrpRS that need not match the heterozygous state.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the genes encoding the endothelin type-B receptor (EDNRB) and its physiological ligand endothelin 3 (EDN3) are now known to account for the majority of HSCR II patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the ligand-receptor gene pair as the endothelin-axis cause of WS4/HSCR II phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: EDN3 thus becomes the third known gene (after RET and EDNRB) predisposing to HSCR, supporting the view that the endothelin-signaling pathways play a major role in the development of neural crests.
evidence.explanation: Links EDN3 to the same neural crest endothelin pathway as EDNRB.

steps/2.description: Pathogenic variants reduce endothelin-3 ligand availability, endothelin receptor type B function, or receptor-mediated signaling in neural crest-derived melanoblast and enteric precursor populations.

evidence.snippet: EDNRB signaling is exclusively required between E10.5 and E12.5 during the migratory phase of melanoblast and enteric neuroblast development.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistically localizes EDNRB signaling to the migration phase of the affected neural crest-derived precursors.

steps/3.description: EDNRB-mediated signaling is required during a critical embryonic window for terminal migration of melanoblast and enteric neuron precursors, rather than for their initial specification from the neural crest.

evidence.snippet: double mutants present with a severe increase in white spotting, absence of melanocytes within the inner ear, and in the stria vascularis in particular, and more severe ENS defects.
evidence.explanation: Supports combined SOX10/endothelin-axis effects on pigmentation, cochlear melanocytes, and ENS development.

steps/4.description: Melanocyte deficiency in the epidermis, hair, iris, and cochlear stria vascularis produces the pigmentary and sensorineural hearing components of Waardenburg-Shah syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Hirschsprung's disease (HSCR) is characterized by an absence of enteric ganglia
evidence.explanation: Defines the enteric ganglion deficiency phenotype connected to EDNRB in the same report.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe a mutation of the human gene for endothelin 3 (EDN3), homozygously present in a patient with a combined Waardenburg syndrome type 2 (WS2) and HSCR phenotype (Shah-Waardenburg syndrome).
evidence.explanation: Establishes EDN3 mutation in combined Waardenburg and Hirschsprung disease.

steps/5.description: Reduced enteric neural crest colonization leaves distal bowel regions aganglionic, producing Hirschsprung disease.

evidence.snippet: molecular segregation investigations unraveled a dominant mode of inheritance with incomplete penetrance.
evidence.explanation: Supports incompletely penetrant heterozygous EDNRB disease contribution.

evidence.snippet: We now estimate EDNRB mutations to be responsible for 5%-6% of WS2.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the reported contribution of heterozygous EDNRB variants to WS2 in this cohort study.

steps/6.description: Heterozygous EDNRB variants can cause or contribute to WS2-like or WS4-like phenotypes with incomplete penetrance. This arm is modeled as a limited, dosage-sensitive susceptibility mechanism rather than the canonical AR WS4A mechanism.

evidence.snippet: WS type 4 (WS4), or Shah-Waardenburg syndrome, is also known as Hirschsprung disease Type II (HSCR II) and is characterized by an absence of epidermal melanocytes and enteric ganglia.
evidence.explanation: Defines WS4 as combined melanocyte and enteric ganglion deficiency.

steps/7.description: Hirschsprung disease results from failed enteric neural crest development and is the defining enteric component of Waardenburg-Shah syndrome.

evidence.snippet: This condition is associated with sensorineural hearing loss; atypical pigmentation of the hair, skin, and eyes; and Hirschsprung’s disease (aganglionic megacolon).
evidence.explanation: ClinGen summarizes sensorineural hearing loss as part of the EDNRB WS4A phenotype.

steps/8.description: Sensorineural hearing loss is part of the Waardenburg component of the EDN3/EDNRB axis phenotype.

evidence.snippet: characterized by an absence of epidermal melanocytes and enteric ganglia.
evidence.explanation: Links EDN3/EDNRB-associated WS4 to epidermal melanocyte deficiency.

steps/9.description: Hypopigmented skin or hair patches and ocular pigmentary findings reflect melanoblast and melanocyte developmental failure.

edges/3.description: Loss of endothelin signaling impairs terminal migration of melanoblast and enteric neural crest precursors.

edges/4.description: Failed melanoblast migration reduces melanocytes in pigmentary and auditory tissues.

edges/5.description: Failed enteric precursor migration produces aganglionosis.

edges/6.description: Stria vascularis melanocyte deficiency disrupts cochlear function and produces sensorineural hearing impairment.

edges/7.description: Cutaneous and ocular melanocyte deficiency produces the pigmentary abnormalities of Waardenburg-Shah syndrome.

edges/8.description: Enteric ganglion cell deficiency causes aganglionic megacolon.

evidence.snippet: We recently mapped a recessive susceptibility locus (HSCR2) to human chromosome 13q22, which we now demonstrate to be the endothelin-B receptor gene (EDNRB).
evidence.explanation: Original EDNRB human disease mapping in Hirschsprung disease.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report a homozygous substitution/deletion mutation of the EDN3 gene in a WS-HSCR patient.
evidence.explanation: Establishes homozygous EDN3 mutation in Waardenburg-Hirschsprung disease.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies showed that all hypercalcemia-associated missense variants impaired heterologous expression, plasma membrane targeting, and/or signaling
evidence.explanation: Direct functional demonstration that the FHH1-associated alleles are loss of function, and that the impairment can act at expression, trafficking or signalling.

evidence.snippet: The expressed wild-type receptor elicited large inward currents in response to perfused polyvalent cations; a markedly attenuated response was observed with the mutated protein.
evidence.explanation: The original oocyte expression experiment showing an FHH allele signals poorly compared with wild type.

steps/1.description: An inactivating variant, most often missense and frequently in the large extracellular calcium-binding domain, that raises the calcium concentration required to activate the receptor. Nonsense and frameshift alleles occur as well. Functional work on hypercalcaemia-associated missense alleles shows the defect is not confined to one step: expression, plasma-membrane targeting and signalling can each be impaired.

evidence.snippet: LOF of CaSR (in FHH1) or its downstream partner signaling proteins (in FHH2 and FHH3) result in an elevation of the body's calcium set point, defined as the serum calcium concentration at which PTH secretion is half-maximal.
evidence.explanation: Defines the set point and states that CASR loss of function raises it, which is exactly this node.

steps/2.description: The set point is the serum calcium concentration at which PTH secretion is half-maximal. Shifting it upward is the single mechanistic statement from which the rest of the disease follows: nothing downstream is broken, but every calcium-sensing tissue is now regulating toward a higher target.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies demonstrate that hypercalcemia-induced increases in urinary calcium excretion depend on renal CASR signaling, primarily through reduced paracellular calcium permeability in the TAL. Loss of the renal Casr in mice impairs urinary calcium excretion in conditions of hypercalcemia.
evidence.explanation: Shows in mice that the calciuric response to hypercalcaemia requires renal CASR, which is the mechanism whose loss produces hypocalciuria here.

evidence.snippet: CASR activation upregulates claudin-14 (CLDN14), a tight junction protein that selectively blocks paracellular divalent cation reabsorption.
evidence.explanation: Names the molecular effector through which the receptor restrains paracellular calcium reabsorption.

steps/3.description: In the thick ascending limb the receptor normally responds to a rise in blood calcium by reducing paracellular calcium permeability, acting through the tight-junction protein claudin-14. A blunted receptor does not apply that brake, so calcium continues to be reabsorbed at concentrations where it should be shed. This is the limb that converts what would otherwise be ordinary hypercalcaemia into the hypocalciuric form.

evidence.snippet: In the kidney, this defect leads to an increase in tubular calcium and magnesium reabsorption resulting in hypercalcemia, hypercalcaemia, and frequently high normal levels of serum magnesium
evidence.explanation: States that the same renal reabsorptive defect retains magnesium alongside calcium, which is the claim this node makes.

steps/4.description: Magnesium shares the claudin-gated paracellular route that the receptor regulates, so a blunted receptor retains magnesium alongside calcium. The resulting serum magnesium is typically high-normal to mildly raised rather than overtly abnormal.

evidence.snippet: 80% of FHH-affected individuals are hypocalciuric (Ca creatinine clearance ratio [CCCR] < 0.01) versus <20% of PHPT individuals with CCCR < 0.01
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how far hypocalciuria separates FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism, and by omission how often it does not.

steps/5.description: Urinary calcium that is low in absolute terms or, more informatively, low relative to the prevailing serum calcium. It is simultaneously the diagnostic signature of the disease and the reason for its benign course, since the renal complications of chronic hypercalcaemia require calcium to be passing through the kidney.

evidence.snippet: Clinically, FHH is a benign, typically asymptomatic disease and usually presents with the biochemical triad: life-long, non-progressive hypercalcemia, normal or slightly increased serum PTH levels and hypocalciuria
evidence.explanation: States the hypercalcaemia and that it is lifelong and non-progressive, which is what the STABLE clinical course records.

steps/6.description: Lifelong, non-progressive and usually mild. Most often found incidentally on a routine calcium measurement rather than through symptoms.

evidence.snippet: FHH1 accounts for ∼65% of cases, and is an autosomal-dominant condition characterized by lifelong elevations of serum calcium concentrations and normal or elevated serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentrations.
evidence.explanation: States that PTH is normal or elevated rather than suppressed, which is the finding this phenotype records.

steps/7.description: PTH that is not suppressed in the face of hypercalcaemia. It may sit within the reference interval - which is itself abnormal at this calcium level - or be frankly raised. This is the finding that puts primary hyperparathyroidism on the differential and cannot be used to exclude it.

evidence.snippet: The resulting disorders share a constellation of inappropriately high PTH concentrations despite elevated serum calcium levels
evidence.explanation: States the defining parathyroid abnormality - PTH that is inappropriate for the prevailing calcium rather than absolutely raised.

steps/8.description: Parathyroid chief cells continue to secrete PTH at calcium concentrations that should silence them. The cells are not autonomous and the glands are not neoplastic, which is why removing them does not address the lesion - they are obeying a receptor that is under-reporting the calcium level.

evidence.snippet: Clinically, FHH is a benign, typically asymptomatic disease and usually presents with the biochemical triad: life-long, non-progressive hypercalcemia, normal or slightly increased serum PTH levels and hypocalciuria
evidence.explanation: The biochemical triad this node names, together with the benign, non-progressive course.

steps/9.description: The biochemical core of the disease and the source of its entire clinical problem, which is that it looks like mild primary hyperparathyroidism. The hypercalcaemia is lifelong, non-progressive and usually mild, and the PTH accompanying it is normal or slightly raised rather than suppressed as it would be if the hypercalcaemia had a non-parathyroid cause.

evidence.snippet: Familiar hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is associated with increased PTH and AP compared to normal controls, but not with bone loss irrespective of the severity of the CASR mutations.
evidence.explanation: Directly states the dissociation between chronically raised PTH and bone loss, and that it holds across variant severity.

evidence.snippet: They had higher Z-scores in the hip and in the forearm.
evidence.explanation: The densitometric comparison against primary hyperparathyroidism underlying this node.

steps/10.description: A deliberately negative node. Patients carry raised PTH and alkaline phosphatase for decades without losing bone, and bone density does not track the severity of the CASR variant. This is a real dissociation rather than an absence of data, and it belongs in the pathograph because it is one of the things that makes FHH1 mechanistically unlike primary hyperparathyroidism despite the shared biochemistry.

evidence.snippet: and mild hypermagnesemia may be present
evidence.explanation: The review states mild hypermagnesaemia as an expected accompanying finding, which is the strength of claim this phenotype records.

steps/11.description: Mildly raised serum magnesium, reflecting the same paracellular transport defect that retains calcium. Supportive rather than diagnostic, and mild enough that it is often reported as high-normal rather than frankly raised.

evidence.snippet: Serum phosphate levels are often reduced, intact PTH levels are typically inappropriately normal in 80% of patients and mildly elevated in the remainder, and mild hypermagnesaemia may be present
evidence.explanation: Names mild hypermagnesaemia as part of the expected FHH biochemistry, alongside the phosphate and PTH findings curated elsewhere in this entry.

steps/12.description: Mildly raised serum magnesium, a supportive rather than a diagnostic finding. It is worth recording because it is a point of difference from primary hyperparathyroidism, where magnesium is typically normal or low.

evidence.snippet: Although typically asymptomatic, some patients with moderate-to-severe hypercalcemia may present with classical hypercalcemic symptoms (i.e., polyuria- polydipsia, fatigue, acute and chronic pancreatitis, gallstones and chondrocalcinosis, acute pancreatitis, chondrocalcinosis, and nephrolithiasis)
evidence.explanation: Names chondrocalcinosis among the classical hypercalcaemic presentations and scopes them to the moderate-to-severe end of the range rather than to FHH1 as a whole.

steps/13.description: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition in cartilage, one of the few complications attributable to the chronic hypercalcaemia itself. Like the other symptomatic presentations of FHH1 it is reported in the moderate-to-severe end of the hypercalcaemic range rather than across carriers generally.

evidence.snippet: Although typically asymptomatic, some patients with moderate-to-severe hypercalcemia may present with classical hypercalcemic symptoms (i.e., polyuria- polydipsia, fatigue, acute and chronic pancreatitis, gallstones and chondrocalcinosis, acute pancreatitis, chondrocalcinosis, and nephrolithiasis)
evidence.explanation: Names acute and chronic pancreatitis among the classical hypercalcaemic presentations and scopes them to the moderate-to-severe end of the range rather than to FHH1 as a whole.

steps/14.description: An uncommon association, and reported in the subset with moderate-to-severe hypercalcaemia rather than across FHH1 generally. Its causal attribution to FHH1 is contested rather than settled, and it should not be assumed in an individual patient without excluding the usual causes.

edges/1.description: A receptor that requires more calcium to activate is, at the level of the whole homeostatic loop, a receptor with a higher set point.

edges/2.description: The parathyroid limb of the shifted set point.

edges/3.description: The renal limb. It is a separate edge rather than a consequence of the parathyroid limb, because the receptor acts on the tubule directly.

edges/4.description: Continued PTH secretion sustains bone resorption and renal calcium retention, holding serum calcium above the normal range.

edges/5.description: Reabsorbed calcium is calcium that does not appear in the urine.

edges/6.description: Renal retention contributes to the circulating excess independently of the parathyroid limb.

edges/7.description: The same paracellular pathway carries magnesium, so the transport defect is not selective for calcium.

edges/8.description: Retention raises circulating magnesium.

edges/9.description: Chronic exposure to a modestly raised PTH does not, in this disease, translate into the bone loss the same biochemistry causes in primary hyperparathyroidism.

edges/10.description: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition follows the sustained calcium elevation rather than the receptor defect directly, and is reported at the moderate-to-severe end of the range rather than across carriers.

edges/11.description: Reported among the classical hypercalcaemic presentations at the moderate-to-severe end of the range. The attribution is contested rather than settled, which is why the phenotype records it as VERY_RARE.

edges/12.description: The clinical finding corresponding to the pathophysiology node.

edges/13.description: The circulating readout of the parathyroid limb of the lesion.

edges/14.description: The clinical finding corresponding to the pathophysiology node.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that mutations in the human Ca(2+)-sensing receptor gene cause familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) and neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism (NSHPT), two inherited conditions characterized by altered calcium homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: The founding demonstration that CASR is the causative gene, and that the same gene accounts for the neonatal subtype.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations cause familial (benign) hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) in which the lifelong mild hypercalcemia is generally asymptomatic. Homozygous inactivating mutations give rise to neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism (NSHPT) with extreme hypercalcemia and marked skeletal changes.
evidence.explanation: The dose-dependent allelic series in one passage, which is what the note above is describing.

evidence.snippet: FHH1 accounts for ∼65% of cases
evidence.explanation: Source for the share of FHH attributable to CASR rather than to GNA11 or AP2S1, which is why a negative CASR result does not exclude FHH.

genes/0.notes:
CASR is one of the clearest allelic series in medicine, and FHH1 is best read against the rest of it: heterozygous loss of function gives this disease, biallelic loss of function gives neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism, and heterozygous gain of function gives autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 1, curated separately in this knowledge base. One receptor, dosed in both directions from normal.
Two limits on genetic testing are worth recording. FHH1 accounts for roughly two-thirds of FHH; the remainder is FHH2 (GNA11) and FHH3 (AP2S1), which affect the receptor's downstream partners rather than the receptor itself and are clinically similar, so a negative CASR result does not exclude FHH. And within CASR, variant interpretation carries the usual difficulty that a rare missense change of uncertain significance is not by itself a diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: FHH1 is usually asymptomatic and requires no intervention
evidence.explanation: States directly that the usual management is no intervention.

treatments/0.description: The correct management for the great majority of carriers. The hypercalcaemia is stable, the renal and skeletal complications that would justify treating it do not develop, and there is no evidence that lowering the calcium improves any outcome. Recording this as a treatment rather than as an absence of one is deliberate: the intervention that matters in FHH1 is the decision not to operate.

evidence.snippet: In children, adolescents and young adults with FHH the main challenge is to distinguish the condition from primary hyperparathyroidism and thereby to avoid unnecessary treatments including parathyroidectomy.
evidence.explanation: States avoidance of parathyroidectomy as the object of the diagnostic effort, which is what this entry records as a treatment decision.

evidence.snippet: In NSHPT, total parathyroidectomy is generally considered the definitive treatment.
evidence.explanation: The neonatal exception noted here, where the same operation is indicated rather than avoided.

treatments/1.description: The single most consequential management decision in the disease, and the reason the diagnosis matters. Parathyroidectomy is the treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism and is inappropriate here, because the glands are responding correctly to a receptor that under-reports calcium; removing them does not reset the set point. The exception is the neonatal biallelic subtype, where parathyroidectomy is the definitive treatment and subtotal resection is reported as ineffective.

evidence.snippet: In FHH, cinacalcet results in a significant reduction of serum calcium levels and improvement of calcium clearance after initiation of cinacalcet therapy
evidence.explanation: Reports the biochemical effect of cinacalcet in FHH, which is the basis for its selective use here.

evidence.snippet: Calcimimetic drugs, such as cinacalcet, are allosteric agonists at the CaSR
evidence.explanation: Establishes the pharmacological class and mode of action that the target_mechanisms link asserts.

treatments/2.description: A calcimimetic - a positive allosteric modulator that lowers the calcium concentration needed to activate the receptor - and therefore a drug aimed at the actual lesion rather than at the number. It is reserved for the minority with symptomatic or marked hypercalcaemia, since most carriers need nothing. Reported to lower serum calcium and improve calcium clearance, and used successfully in the neonatal forms as well.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Allosteric sensitisation of the mutant receptor partially offsets the rightward shift, which is why the drug acts on the mechanism and not merely on the calcium level.

open_questions/0.rationale: A rare-variant burden test in the DiscovEHR exomes associated aggregated CASR loss-of-function variants with cardiovascular, neurological and other diagnoses. That is a real signal against the long-standing description of FHH1 as entirely benign, and this entry deliberately does not fold it into the pathograph, because the study design cannot separate a mechanistic consequence of impaired calcium sensing from confounding in a healthcare-derived cohort. CASR is expressed well beyond parathyroid and kidney, so a genuine extra-calcitropic effect is biologically plausible rather than implausible - which is exactly why the question is worth recording rather than dismissing.

evidence.snippet: Approximately 85% of FL cases harbor the t(14;18)(q32;q21)/IGH::BCL2 which leads to the overexpression of BCL2.
evidence.explanation: Abstract identifies the hallmark IGH::BCL2 rearrangement and resulting BCL2 overexpression in classic FL.

steps/1.description: In most cases, the hallmark t(14;18)(q32;q21)/IGH::BCL2 rearrangement places BCL2 under immunoglobulin enhancer control, driving constitutive BCL2 overexpression in germinal center B cells.

evidence.snippet: These neoplasms often exhibit hallmark epigenetic deregulation due to recurrent mutations in genes such as KMT2D, CREBBP, and EZH2
evidence.explanation: Abstract directly links FL to recurrent mutations in major chromatin-modifying genes.

evidence.snippet: abnormalities in epigenetic modifier genes lead to desynchronization of gene expression changes in germinal center B cells.
evidence.explanation: Abstract supports disruption of the normal germinal center transcriptional program by epigenetic lesions.

steps/2.description: FL commonly carries recurrent mutations in chromatin-modifying genes including KMT2D, CREBBP, and EZH2. These lesions distort transcriptional programs required for normal germinal center exit and differentiation, reinforcing the malignant state.

evidence.snippet: Follicular lymphoma (FL), the most frequent indolent non-Hodgkin's B cell lymphoma, is considered as a prototypical centrocyte-derived lymphoma, dependent on a specific microenvironment mimicking the normal germinal center (GC).
evidence.explanation: Abstract states that FL biology depends on a supportive microenvironment resembling the normal germinal center.

steps/3.description: FL cells remain highly dependent on the lymph node microenvironment. Reciprocal signaling with follicular helper T cells, stromal cells, and other immune cells provides survival, adhesion, and immune-evasive signals that preserve tumor fitness.

evidence.snippet: BCL2 overexpression by t(14;18) confers a survival advantage to B cells during the germinal center reaction
evidence.explanation: Review abstract states that t(14;18)-driven BCL2 expression provides a survival advantage during the germinal center reaction.

steps/4.description: Constitutive BCL2 expression blocks the mitochondrial apoptosis program, allowing germinal center B cells that would normally be deleted during the germinal center reaction to survive as lymphoma precursors.

evidence.snippet: FL cells frequently carry N-linked glycosylation motifs within the immunoglobulin gene, leading to chronic activation of the B-cell receptor (BCR). Recent evidence suggests that this chronic BCR signaling drives FL polarization toward a dark-zone phenotype and promotes clonal evolution.
evidence.explanation: Review abstract directly links chronic BCR signaling to clonal evolution in FL.

steps/5.description: FL immunoglobulins often acquire N-linked glycosylation motifs that support chronic B-cell receptor signaling. This persistent signaling promotes dark-zone polarization and ongoing clonal evolution.

steps/6.description: The combination of anti-apoptotic signaling, epigenetic deregulation, and microenvironmental support, and chronic BCR signaling allows FL clones to survive for years, relapse after therapy, and occasionally transform into aggressive large B-cell lymphoma.

edges/1.description: BCL2 overexpression prevents deletion of germinal center B cells

evidence.snippet: Studies in mouse models have shown that BCL2 overexpression and epigenetic deregulation in B cells cooperatively promote lymphomagenesis.
evidence.explanation: Mouse-model evidence that BCL2 overexpression cooperates with epigenetic deregulation to drive clonal lymphomagenesis.

edges/2.description: Oncogenic BCL2 expression helps establish long-lived precursor clones

edges/3.description: Anti-apoptotic signaling allows precursor and tumor B cells to persist long enough to accumulate additional lesions

edges/4.description: Distorted chromatin programs stabilize malignant identity and support ongoing clonal diversification

edges/5.description: Sustained trophic signaling from the niche promotes relapse-prone survival and immune escape

edges/6.description: Persistent BCR signaling supports ongoing adaptation and outgrowth of FL clones

evidence.snippet: Approximately 85% of FL cases harbor the t(14;18)(q32;q21)/IGH::BCL2 which leads to the overexpression of BCL2.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the defining t(14;18)/IGH::BCL2 lesion in ~85% of FL and links it to BCL2 overexpression.

genes/0.notes: The hallmark t(14;18)(q32;q21)/IGH::BCL2 rearrangement is present in most classic FL cases and promotes lymphoma cell survival through BCL2 overexpression.

evidence.snippet: with KMT2D and CREBBP considered founding events in FL lymphomagenesis
evidence.explanation: Identifies KMT2D as a founding genetic event in FL lymphomagenesis.

genes/1.notes: KMT2D loss-of-function mutations are among the most frequent early lesions in FL and contribute to aberrant enhancer regulation and germinal center reprogramming.

evidence.snippet: with KMT2D and CREBBP considered founding events in FL lymphomagenesis
evidence.explanation: Identifies CREBBP as a founding genetic event in FL lymphomagenesis.

genes/2.notes: CREBBP mutations impair acetylation-dependent transcriptional control, affecting antigen presentation and germinal center exit programs.

evidence.snippet: These neoplasms often exhibit hallmark epigenetic deregulation due to recurrent mutations in genes such as KMT2D, CREBBP, and EZH2
evidence.explanation: Lists EZH2 among the recurrent epigenetic-modifier mutations characteristic of FL.

genes/3.notes: Gain-of-function EZH2 mutations alter histone methylation, reinforce the germinal center phenotype, and provide a targetable vulnerability in a subset of relapsed FL.

treatments/0.description: Standard therapy for symptomatic advanced FL combines an anti-CD20 antibody such as rituximab or obinutuzumab with chemotherapy backbones such as bendamustine, CHOP, or CVP, depending on patient fitness and disease burden.

treatments/1.description: The chemo-free lenalidomide plus rituximab regimen is an established option for selected patients in frontline or relapsed settings.

treatments/2.description: Oral EZH2 inhibition with tazemetostat is used in relapsed or refractory FL, especially in tumors with EZH2 mutation, and offers a targeted option with relatively favorable tolerability.

evidence.snippet: A recent pivotal phase I/II clinical trial (GO29781) demonstrated that mosunetuzumab induced an overall response rate of 80%, complete response rate of 60%, and a median progression-free survival of 17.9 months in patients with relapsed/refractory (r/r) follicular lymphoma (FL) following at least two prior lines of systemic therapy, including alkylator and anti-CD20 antibody-based therapy.
evidence.explanation: Phase I/II clinical trial data support mosunetuzumab as an active therapy for relapsed or refractory FL after multiple prior lines.

treatments/3.description: CD20xCD3 bispecific antibody immunotherapy for relapsed or refractory FL after at least two prior systemic therapy lines, supported by the GO29781 phase I/II program.

evidence.snippet: Axicabtagene ciloleucel showed high rates of durable responses
evidence.explanation: ZUMA-5 provides phase II clinical evidence for axicabtagene ciloleucel in relapsed or refractory indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma including FL.

treatments/4.description: Autologous anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy used for relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after prior anti-CD20 antibody and alkylator-based therapy, supported by the ZUMA-5 phase II trial.

evidence.snippet: Tisagenlecleucel is safe and effective in extensively pretreated r/r FL, including in high-risk patients.
evidence.explanation: The ELARA phase 2 trial's conclusion directly supports tisagenlecleucel as an effective therapy for extensively pretreated relapsed or refractory FL.

treatments/5.description: Autologous anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy for adults with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after multiple prior treatment lines, supported by the ELARA phase II trial.

evidence.snippet: Observation continues to be appropriate for asymptomatic patients with low bulk disease and no cytopenias. There is no overall survival (OS) advantage for early treatment
evidence.explanation: Establishes active surveillance as appropriate for asymptomatic low-burden FL, with no survival benefit from early treatment.

treatments/6.description: For asymptomatic patients with low tumor burden and no cytopenias, observation without immediate therapy is standard, as early treatment confers no overall-survival advantage. Treatment is initiated at symptomatic, bulky/progressive disease or cytopenias.

evidence.snippet: about 15% of FL cases are negative for the t(14;18), which could present diagnostic challenges
evidence.explanation: Defines the t(14;18)-negative subset whose biology and classification remain incompletely resolved.

open_questions/0.rationale: The BCL2-overexpression model explains classic t(14;18)-positive FL, but a substantial minority lack the translocation, may use alternative drivers, and present diagnostic and nosologic challenges (e.g., the provisional t(14;18)-negative CD23+ follicle center lymphoma entity).

evidence.snippet: time to relapse of less than 2 years from chemoimmunotherapy and specific gene mutations may also be useful for prognosis
evidence.explanation: Early relapse (POD24) is prognostically important but is identified only after it occurs.

open_questions/1.rationale: Early relapse after chemoimmunotherapy is a powerful adverse prognostic marker, but it is currently recognized only retrospectively; a validated upfront predictor of POD24 would enable risk-adapted treatment.

evidence.snippet: patients with t-FL continue to have an inferior survival in the modern era and should be prioritized for enrollment in clinical trials
evidence.explanation: Transformed FL retains inferior survival, underscoring the unmet need to understand and predict transformation.

open_questions/2.rationale: Transformation is the major driver of FL mortality and carries survival inferior even to de novo DLBCL, yet the triggering molecular events and a means to predict or prevent it remain incompletely defined.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous PRNP coding variant is present from conception in every cell. It does not break the gene; it renders the encoded protein conformationally unfaithful, a gain-of-toxic-function rather than a loss-of-function lesion.

evidence.snippet: The stability properties of the P102L variant were indistinguishable from those of wild-type PrP
evidence.explanation: Establishes the actual observed biophysical property of the P102L variant used to replace the refuted destabilization claim: recovered soluble, with stability indistinguishable from wild-type, rather than an intrinsically destabilized fold.

steps/2.description: The substitution renders PrP-C susceptible to a stochastic conformational conversion into the PrP-Sc-templating fold, eventually making a misfolding event possible over years to decades. For the classic P102L GSS variant this is not explained by loss of native-state thermodynamic stability: recombinant human PrP(90-231) carrying P102L is recovered soluble, with secondary structure and guanidine/thermal unfolding stability indistinguishable from wild-type. (For A117V, an alternative upstream trigger is aberrant C-terminal-transmembrane PrP topogenesis rather than a globular-domain conformational change.)

evidence.snippet: It can also be horizontally transmitted to non-human primates and rodents through intracerebral inoculation of brain homogenates from patients with the disease.
evidence.explanation: Experimental transmission into non-human primates and rodents demonstrates the self-propagating, transmissible nature of the misfolded conformer.

steps/3.description: The autocatalytic core of the disease: a nucleated conformational conversion in which a misfolded PrP molecule recruits and refolds native PrP-C. This is the step that makes the disease self-propagating and experimentally transmissible.

evidence.snippet: showed two major protease-resistant PrP fragments (PrP-res) with molecular masses of approximately 21 and 8 kDa
evidence.explanation: Identifies the two protease-resistant fragment species characteristic of GSS.

evidence.snippet: the formation of PrP-res fragments of 7-8 kDa with ragged N and C termini is not a feature of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease or fatal familial insomnia
evidence.explanation: The ~8 kDa ragged fragment is a molecular marker distinguishing GSS from CJD/FFI.

steps/4.description: GSS brains carry two major protease-resistant PrP fragments: an ~8 kDa unglycosylated fragment with ragged N- and C-termini (derived from the center of PrP), which is the GSS-defining species and tracks with multicentric amyloid, and a 21 kDa (type-1-like) fragment present in the CJD-like variant. Which fragment forms in vivo determines the neuropathology.

evidence.snippet: the 8-kDa fragment, similar to those described in other variants of GSS, was found in all subjects in brain regions showing PrP-positive multicentric amyloid deposits
evidence.explanation: Links the 8 kDa fragment to the multicentric amyloid plaques.

steps/5.description: The 8 kDa fragment drives the pathognomonic lesion: multicentric PrP amyloid plaques (a dense core with satellite deposits) concentrated in the cerebellar molecular layer and cerebral cortex.

evidence.snippet: correlated with the presence of spongiform degeneration and
evidence.explanation: The 21 kDa fragment correlates with spongiform degeneration and a synaptic PrP-deposition pattern.

steps/6.description: The 21 kDa fragment drives a parallel, strain-dependent lesion of spongiform degeneration with a synaptic pattern of PrP deposition. It is present in the CJD-like variant and absent in some GSS variants (e.g. D202N without spongiform change), explaining much of the intra-mutation phenotypic variability.

steps/7.description: Both deposition routes converge on synaptotoxicity and neuronal apoptosis, the proximate cause of the clinical decline.

steps/8.description: Reactive astrogliosis and microglial activation track the PrP deposits, a purely innate neuroinflammatory response (PrP-Sc is a self-protein in a different fold and is not immunogenic, so no adaptive immune response occurs).

evidence.snippet: Patients initially suffer from ataxia or dementia and deteriorate until they die, in one to ten years.
evidence.explanation: The clinical syndrome and its slowly progressive fatal course.

steps/9.description: Regionally selective neuronal loss maps to the clinical syndrome: cerebellar Purkinje/granule loss produces ataxia, cortical involvement produces dementia, substantia nigra loss produces parkinsonism, and caudal spinal cord pathology produces areflexia and painful dysaesthesiae.

evidence.snippet: neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) with paired helical filaments (PHF) are numerous, widespread and consistently present in the cerebral cortex and several subcortical nuclei
evidence.explanation: The Indiana F198S kindred shows abundant Alzheimer-type neurofibrillary tangles co-occurring with the prion pathology.

steps/10.description: In the F198S (and Q217R) variants, neurofibrillary tangles indistinguishable from those of Alzheimer disease arise around PrP plaques. Bank-vole transmission shows the PrP amyloid and tau tangles are independent parallel pathologies rather than one driving the other, so this node is modeled parallel to the amyloid arm without a driving causal edge from it.

evidence.snippet: PrP is implicated in the pathogenesis and transmission of the condition
evidence.explanation: Prion protein is implicated in GSS pathogenesis.

genes/0.notes: Causal gene. The most common GSS allele is P102L (c.305C>T); A117V (in the transmembrane-determining region) is second-most-common; F198S defines the Indiana kindred with co-occurring neurofibrillary tangles. Many further reported variants have uncertain pathogenicity/penetrance.

evidence.snippet: the earliest eight clinical onsets were all MM homozygotes and overall age at onset was 7 years earlier for MM compared with MV heterozygotes
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the PRNP codon-129 modifier effect on age at onset in P102L GSS.

evidence.snippet: apolipoprotein E4 carriers have a delayed age of onset by 10 years
evidence.explanation: Documents the paradoxical APOE4-delays-onset modifier effect in P102L GSS.

genes/1.notes: The common PRNP codon-129 polymorphism (M129V), including its cis/trans phase relative to the mutation, is the best-characterized modifier of age at onset and phenotype; APOE genotype has also been examined as a modifier. Mechanisms remain incompletely explained.

evidence.snippet: No treatment of the underlying cause of genetic prion disease is available.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms only supportive management is available.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying treatment exists; management is supportive and symptomatic, with a multidisciplinary team, physical/occupational therapy, and advance care planning given the progressive cognitive trajectory.

evidence.snippet: 50% chance of inheriting the variant
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states each child of an affected individual has a 50% chance of inheriting the PRNP variant.

treatments/1.description: Autosomal dominant risk counseling, predictive testing protocols for at-risk relatives, and reproductive options; the psychological burden on 50%-at-risk relatives is a distinctive management dimension.

evidence.snippet: PRN100 was well tolerated and reached the target CSF drug concentration (50 nM)
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates target engagement of the anti-PrP antibody, though clinical decline continued.

treatments/2.description: First-in-human anti-PrP monoclonal antibody; in six CJD patients it was well tolerated and reached target CSF concentration, but all patients still declined, consistent with the difficulty of reversing established neurodegeneration. Experimental.

evidence.snippet: some hereditary forms of prion disease cannot be rationalized using the concept of mutation-induced thermodynamic destabilization of the cellular prion protein
evidence.explanation: Direct test of the P102L GSS variant itself; its stability was indistinguishable from wild-type, so the destabilization model cannot explain this variant.

evidence.snippet: These data suggest that destabilization of PrPC is neither a general mechanism underlying the formation of PrPSc nor the basis of disease phenotypes in inherited human TSEs.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication across all eight C-terminal familial PRNP substitutions: measured thermodynamic stabilities do not correlate with disease phenotype.

hypotheses/0.description: Familial PRNP substitutions cause disease by lowering the thermodynamic and/or kinetic barrier separating the native alpha-helical PrP-C fold from beta-sheet-rich conformers, so that a stochastic misfolding event becomes possible.

evidence.snippet: other variants have genuine effects on disease susceptibility but confer lifetime risks ranging from
evidence.explanation: Population-scale analysis showing PRNP variant penetrance is variant-specific, spanning a wide range of lifetime risks.

open_questions/0.rationale: Large population control cohorts show that PRNP variants previously reported as pathogenic are far more common than expected and confer a wide range of lifetime risks, so penetrance is variant-specific rather than uniformly high. The codon-129 genotype (and its cis/trans phase) and APOE genotype modify onset by incompletely understood mechanisms, and the reported APOE4-delays-onset effect is the opposite of its effect in Alzheimer disease. Resolving these would sharpen predictive counseling and the timing of any presymptomatic PrP-lowering therapy.

evidence.snippet: depleting PrP in the brain is an established strategy to prevent or stall templated misfolding of PrP
evidence.explanation: Base-editing proof-of-concept for PrP lowering in a humanized prion mouse model.

open_questions/1.rationale: Because the mutant allele actively templates misfolding and heterozygous PRNP loss-of-function is tolerated, lowering PrP is a mechanistically rational target. In vivo base editing lowered brain PrP and extended lifespan in a humanized prion mouse model, and the ION717 antisense oligonucleotide is in a first-in-human intrathecal trial. Whether these translate to clinical benefit - and how early they must start - is the central open therapeutic question.

evidence.snippet: G6PD deficiency, one of the commonest inherited enzyme abnormalities in humans, arises through one of many possible mutations, most of which reduce the stability of the enzyme and its level as red cells age.
evidence.explanation: This review supports reduced enzyme stability as a common molecular consequence of G6PD variants.

evidence.snippet: Infants with this novel variant showed decreased activity of G6PD, severe anemia, and pathological jaundice
evidence.explanation: Human variant data directly links G6PD variants to decreased enzyme activity.

steps/1.description: Pathogenic variants in G6PD reduce enzyme stability or activity in erythrocytes, limiting the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway.

evidence.snippet: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) plays a key role in the generation of NADPH which is essential for maintaining glutathione in the reduce state
evidence.explanation: This review connects G6PD activity to NADPH generation and glutathione reduction.

evidence.snippet: The generation of reducing equivalent NADPH via glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is critical for the maintenance of redox homeostasis and reductive biosynthesis in cells.
evidence.explanation: This review supports G6PD-dependent NADPH generation as a redox-homeostasis mechanism.

steps/2.description: Reduced G6PD activity lowers NADPH availability and compromises glutathione-dependent antioxidant buffering.

evidence.snippet: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway, is indispensable to maintenance of the cytosolic pool of NADPH and thus the cellular redox balance.
evidence.explanation: This review supports the link between G6PD, NADPH, and cellular redox balance.

evidence.snippet: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is an erythrocyte enzyme defect that amplifies the susceptibility of erythrocytes to oxidative stress due to excessive levels of reactive oxygen species. Consequently, erythrocyte destruction and hemolysis occur.
evidence.explanation: This review directly connects G6PD deficiency to erythrocyte oxidative stress and hemolysis.

steps/3.description: NADPH and glutathione insufficiency leave G6PD-deficient erythrocytes susceptible to oxidant injury from drugs, infections, foods, or chemicals.

evidence.snippet: The presence of unopposed oxidizing agents leading to oxidation of the sulfhydryl bridges between parts of the haemoglobin molecule decrease the solubility of haemoglobin, leading to precipitations called Heinz bodies.
evidence.explanation: The abstract describes the oxidative hemoglobin damage that yields Heinz bodies.

steps/4.description: Unopposed oxidants damage hemoglobin sulfhydryl groups, reduce hemoglobin solubility, and form Heinz body precipitates.

evidence.snippet: The G6PD enzyme is critical to protecting erythrocytes against oxidative stress, and deficiency may lead to hemolysis in the presence of certain environmental factors such as infection and some medications and foods.
evidence.explanation: The abstract supports triggered hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Although most individuals are asymptomatic, exposure to certain food, drugs, or infections can trigger acute hemolytic anemia.
evidence.explanation: This review supports episodic acute hemolytic anemia after triggers.

steps/5.description: Oxidative stressors trigger episodic erythrocyte destruction and anemia in susceptible G6PD-deficient individuals.

evidence.snippet: People, usually males, with deficient alleles are susceptible to neonatal jaundice, and acute hemolytic anemia, usually during infection, after treatment with certain drugs or after eating fava beans.
evidence.explanation: This review identifies acute hemolytic anemia as a major G6PD-deficiency manifestation.

evidence.snippet: G6PD deficiency anemia presented mainly with pallor, dark red urine and jaundice after exposure to certain diets, drugs and diseases
evidence.explanation: This cohort supports hemolytic anemia presentations after precipitating exposures.

evidence.snippet: Patients presented mainly with pallor (1000 patients; 100%), dark red urine (896 patients; 89.6%) and jaundice (878 patients; 87.8%) after 24-72 hours of exposure to the precipitating factors
evidence.explanation: The cohort directly reports dark red urine during G6PD hemolytic episodes.

evidence.snippet: The classic features of favism, which are pallor, hemoglobinuria, and jaundice, were detected in all cases.
evidence.explanation: Hemoglobinuria supports dark urine during favism.

evidence.snippet: G6PD-deficient persons are mostly asymptomatic, but they can develop severe jaundice during the neonatal period and acute hemolytic anemia when they ingest fava beans or when they are exposed to certain infections or drugs.
evidence.explanation: This review directly supports severe neonatal jaundice.

evidence.snippet: This inherited deficiency causes neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and chronic hemolytic anemia.
evidence.explanation: This systematic review states that G6PD deficiency causes neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.

evidence.snippet: Favism is a hemolytic disease due to the ingestion of fava beans in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
evidence.explanation: This review defines favism as fava-bean-triggered hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

evidence.snippet: any of them may develop acute and sometimes very severe hemolytic anemia when triggered by ingestion of fava beans
evidence.explanation: This review supports fava-bean-triggered acute hemolytic anemia.
