steps/42.description: Deprivation or refractive amblyopia affecting the better or fellow eye in unilateral and asymmetric disease; the principal preventable cause of additional visual loss and the reason for early refraction and fellow-eye protection.

evidence.snippet: 34% had systemic involvement, most

steps/43.description: Psychomotor delay is the commonest extraocular feature of SOX2-related A/M and occurs across the wider spectrum. Its presence formally reclassifies a case as non-isolated, which is precisely why it must be actively sought in apparently isolated disease.

evidence.snippet: Neuroimaging demonstrated pathology in 14/20 cases with corpus callosum dysgenesis (6/20) being the most common.
evidence.explanation: Documents corpus callosum dysgenesis as the commonest neuroimaging finding in a paediatric A/M cohort (6/20); the conservative OCCASIONAL band is used.

steps/44.description: Midline forebrain malformation, the commonest neuroimaging abnormality in paediatric A/M cohorts (6 of 20 scanned children), reflecting the forebrain role of the same transcription factors.

evidence.snippet: Two chromosomal deletions and six haploinsufficient mutations were identified in individuals with eye abnormalities
evidence.explanation: Identifies OTX2 haploinsufficiency in congenital hypopituitarism patients with eye abnormalities.

evidence.explanation: Documents hypopituitarism co-occurring with anophthalmia in a RAX-diagnosed patient.

steps/45.description: Anterior and/or posterior pituitary hormone deficiency. OTX2 is a recognised cause of combined pituitary hormone deficiency with eye involvement, and truncating RAX variants have caused anophthalmia with congenital hypopituitarism and diabetes insipidus.

evidence.snippet: hypogonadism and growth retardation, possibly related to pituitary anomalies, and renal
evidence.explanation: Lists hypogonadism among the common extraocular features of SOX2-related A/M.

steps/46.description: Gonadal-axis dysfunction, reported among the classical extraocular features of SOX2-related disease and attributed to pituitary involvement.

evidence.explanation: Documents oesophageal atresia as a rare extraocular feature of SOX2-related A/M, supporting the VERY_RARE band.

The defining extraocular feature of the anophthalmia-oesophageal-genital (AEG) syndrome, OMIM:206900 / MCOPS3, caused by the same SOX2 variants that cause apparently isolated A/M in other individuals.

edges/14.description: Loss of eye-field specification prevents the eye-forming region from evaginating into paired optic vesicles.

edges/15.description: Partial dosage loss permits vesicle formation but impairs subsequent invagination and growth.

edges/16.description: Reduced dosage of the same network perturbs ventral optic-cup patterning required for fissure fusion.

edges/17.description: Loss of VSX2, itself a member of this eye-field network, removes the neural-retina specification and RPE-repression node.

edges/18.description: The same dosage lesion acts in the non-ocular expression domains of SOX2, OTX2 and RAX, producing extraocular disease.

edges/19.description: Failure of the earliest evagination step aborts globe formation, producing anophthalmia.

edges/20.description: Impaired invagination and growth of the optic cup produce a small globe.

edges/21.description: Disrupted optic-cup morphogenesis is executed cellularly as excess apoptosis with reduced progenitor proliferation.

edges/22.description: Failure of lens induction and early retinal differentiation produces associated segment anomalies.

edges/23.description: Failure of nasal-temporal fissure fusion leaves a persistent ventral tissue defect.

edges/24.description: A persistent fissure defect disrupts normal iris, retinal, choroidal and optic-nerve architecture.

edges/25.description: Retinoic acid depletion impairs ventral optic-cup morphogenesis and growth.

edges/26.description: Retinoic acid receptor signalling is required in both the ventral optic cup and the periocular mesenchyme for fissure closure.

edges/27.description: Loss of the retinal progenitor pool prevents the optic cup from expanding to normal size.

edges/28.description: Excess apoptosis with reduced proliferation depletes the cell mass available to build a normal-sized globe.

edges/29.description: First-trimester teratogenic or infectious insult perturbs optic-cup morphogenesis during the critical window.

edges/30.description: Maternal vitamin A deficiency and retinoid teratogens perturb embryonic retinoic acid availability directly.

edges/31.description: Complete failure of globe formation presents clinically as anophthalmia.

edges/32.description: Partial failure of globe growth presents clinically as microphthalmia.

edges/33.description: Reduced globe size is accompanied by a reduced corneal diameter.

edges/34.description: The absent or small globe fails to provide the mechanical stimulus that drives orbital expansion.

edges/35.description: Absent or malformed ocular tissue prevents formation of a functional visual pathway.

edges/41.description: Extraocular action of the same transcription factors impairs neurodevelopment.

edges/42.description: OTX2 and RAX act in pituitary and hypothalamic development.

edges/43.description: Pituitary and gonadal-axis involvement follows from the same dosage lesion.

edges/44.description: SOX2 loss disrupts foregut separation, the AEG/MCOPS3 association.

edges/45.description: SOX2 loss produces midline forebrain malformation.

edges/46.description: Loss of ocular tissue directly reduces visual function.

edges/47.description: Bilateral severe disease abolishes form vision.

edges/48.description: In unilateral disease the fellow eye is at risk of deprivation and refractive amblyopia.

evidence.explanation: Ranks gestational infection as the best-evidenced environmental cause, ahead of the other three exposures this entry records. Quoted as the whole sentence, since it is the comparison between the exposures that does the work.

evidence.explanation: Quantifies microphthalmia in 2.7% of postnatally examined congenital Zika cases, giving one infection a measured rate rather than a listing.

edges/49.description: This node was written to hold the non-genetic minority of cases, and it names gestational infection as the strongest environmental evidence in its own text. Recorded as direct because infection disrupts ocular tissue during the developmental window itself, which is the node's own event rather than something upstream of it. Graded above the other three exposures pointing here, on the source's own ranking rather than a curatorial preference.

evidence.snippet: The strongest evidence appears to be with gestational-acquired infections, but may also include maternal vitamin A deficiency, exposure to X-rays, solvent misuse and thalidomide exposure
evidence.explanation: Names maternal vitamin A deficiency among the environmental contributors, under a hedge the sentence does not apply to gestational infection.

evidence.explanation: Sixteen percent of mothers in a coloboma series reported night blindness during the affected pregnancy. Maternal history rather than any measurement of embryonic signalling.

edges/50.description: Graded below the infection link into this same node, because the sentence that names both exposures ranks infection first and attaches maternal vitamin A deficiency to a hedged may also include. The mechanistically specific edge for this exposure is the separate one into the retinoic acid node.

evidence.snippet: Eleven (16%) mothers had a history of night blindness while pregnant with the affected child
evidence.explanation: Maternal night blindness during the affected pregnancy is a clinical marker of the vitamin A deficiency that would limit retinoid substrate at this node.

edges/51.description: The substrate-supply edge, and the reason this exposure is graded differently from the other three: maternal retinol is the source of the embryonic retinoic acid this node is built around, so the intervening step is a known one rather than an unknown. Night blindness in the mother is a clinical marker of the deficiency and not a measurement of embryonic signalling, which is what keeps the evidence partial while the link itself is specific.

evidence.snippet: The strongest evidence appears to be with gestational-acquired infections, but may also include maternal vitamin A deficiency, exposure to X-rays, solvent misuse and thalidomide exposure
evidence.explanation: Names thalidomide exposure among the environmental contributors, under the same hedge as vitamin A deficiency.

evidence.explanation: Eight percent of mothers took medication in the first trimester. The agents are not all identified, so this supports an exposure class rather than a drug.

Not also pointed at the retinoic acid node, although this entry's own description makes that argument for systemic retinoids: no cited sentence names a retinoid, so the edge would rest on the description rather than on evidence.

edges/53.description: X-rays and solvent misuse are listed in the same hedged clause as the other two non-infectious exposures and are graded identically to them. The supporting case-series figure is about agricultural chemicals rather than about either named exposure, which is a further reason this stays partial.

evidence.snippet: SOX2 pathogenic variants, including whole gene deletions, are present in 10-15% of all A/M patients
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the SOX2 contribution to A/M.

evidence.explanation: Quantifies the much higher SOX2 yield specifically in bilateral A/M.

genes/0.notes: Autosomal dominant. The single commonest genetic cause of A/M. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants, including whole-gene deletions (which account for 25-50% of pathogenic SOX2 alleles), reduce dosage of this pluripotency and eye-field transcription factor. The ocular phenotype is classically bilateral and severe, with anophthalmia in the majority. Most variants are de novo but germline mosaicism is documented. OMIM classifies SOX2 A/M in the SYNDROMIC MCOPS3 series (anophthalmia/microphthalmia-oesophageal atresia syndrome, OMIM:206900), not the isolated MCOP series — a direct reflection of its frequent extraocular involvement.

evidence.snippet: The ocular phenotype of patients with pathogenic OTX2 variants is highly variable even within the
evidence.explanation: Documents the marked variability of OTX2 ocular expressivity.

evidence.snippet: OTX2 mutations are rarely associated with hypopituitarism in isolation without eye abnormalities, and may be variably penetrant, even within the same pedigree.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the coupled pituitary-eye phenotype and the variable penetrance of OTX2 disease.

genes/1.notes: Autosomal dominant. The second commonest dominant cause. Truncating, missense and whole-gene deletion alleles (deletions being 30-40% of variants) reduce dosage of this homeobox transcription factor. The ocular phenotype ranges from bilateral anophthalmia through Leber congenital amaurosis to no ocular malformation even within one family, making counselling difficult. OTX2 is expressed in the posterior pituitary, retina, ear, thalamus and choroid plexus during human embryogenesis, which underlies the characteristic pituitary-plus-eye phenotype; OMIM assigns it to the syndromic MCOPS5 series (OMIM:610125).

evidence.snippet: In humans, homozygous or compound heterozygous RAX mutations have been reported to cause bilateral microphthalmia or anophthalmia without consistent associated features.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the recessive RAX mechanism and its ocular phenotype.

genes/2.notes: Autosomal recessive. Biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) variants in this paired-type homeobox gene cause bilateral microphthalmia or anophthalmia, often with sclerocornea. RAX patterns the ventral forebrain and hypothalamus as well as the eye; truncating alleles have produced anophthalmia together with congenital hypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus and cleft palate, so a RAX diagnosis should not be assumed to be ocularly isolated. Corresponds to MCOP3 (MONDO:0012604, OMIM:611038).

evidence.snippet: Homozygous mutations in VSX2 were identified in two out of five
evidence.explanation: Directly documents biallelic VSX2 variants in consanguineous families with isolated microphthalmia.

genes/3.notes: Autosomal recessive. Biallelic VSX2 (CHX10) variants cause bilateral microphthalmia, particularly in consanguineous pedigrees. Reported alleles disrupt the homeodomain or the conserved CVC motif required for DNA binding and transcriptional repression, impairing retinal-progenitor specification and de-repressing the RPE programme. Corresponds to MCOP2 (MONDO:0012409) and MCOPCB3 (MONDO:0012408).

evidence.snippet: All affected individuals had bilateral anophthalmia/microphthalmia (A/M), three with additional intellectual or developmental delay, one with autism and seizures and three with facial dysmorphic features.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the fully penetrant ocular phenotype and the variable neurodevelopmental extension.

evidence.snippet: we identified a novel homozygous missense mutation in ALDH1A3 using exome sequencing
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of the recessive ALDH1A3 mechanism.

genes/4.notes: Autosomal recessive. Biallelic variants in retinaldehyde dehydrogenase 3 block the final step of retinoic acid synthesis. Every affected individual across seven reported families had bilateral A/M, with variably present intellectual disability, developmental delay, autism, seizures and facial dysmorphism — again illustrating that the "isolated" designation is provisional. Corresponds to MCOP8 (MONDO:0014050, OMIM:615113).

evidence.snippet: This review demonstrates that correlations exist between the mutation type, mode of
evidence.explanation: Establishes the dual dominant/recessive FOXE3 mechanism and its genotype-phenotype structure.

genes/5.notes: Both dominant and recessive. A forkhead transcription factor of the lens placode. Monoallelic variants were first described in dominant anterior-segment dysgenesis; biallelic variants cause recessive primary aphakia, sclerocornea and microphthalmia. Genotype-phenotype correlations exist between mutation type, mode of inheritance and severity.

evidence.snippet: A novel heterozygous likely pathogenic variant in PAX6, c.767T>C,
evidence.explanation: Documents a pathogenic PAX6 variant in probands with bilateral microphthalmia and coloboma.

genes/6.notes: Autosomal dominant. The master eye-field regulator, best known for aniridia but also a recognised lower-frequency cause of A/M and coloboma. A heterozygous homeodomain variant was identified in two brothers with bilateral microphthalmia, coloboma, primary aphakia, iris hypoplasia, sclerocornea and congenital glaucoma, with an apparently mosaic unaffected carrier mother — illustrating both the phenotypic breadth and the mosaicism that complicates counselling across this spectrum.

evidence.snippet: New phenotypic associations were found for FOXE3 (bilateral sensorineural hearing loss) and MAB21L2 (unilateral microphthalmia).
evidence.explanation: Documents MAB21L2 as a causal MAC gene with a newly described unilateral microphthalmia association.

genes/7.notes: Both dominant and recessive disease occur. Heterozygous substitutions at p.Arg51 cause severe bilateral disease and are proposed to act through a dominant-negative mechanism, whereas a homozygous p.Arg247Gln produced a milder phenotype in a consanguineous family. Identified among the causal genes in a prospective real-world MAC cohort, with a novel association with unilateral microphthalmia.

evidence.snippet: Variants in these genes account for 1.7% and 1% of A/M and coloboma patients screened for GDF3 or GDF6 mutations, respectively

steps/7.description: The initiating lesion is a missense point mutation in a gene encoding a core subunit of respiratory-chain complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase). The large majority of molecularly resolved classical cases carry one of three usually homoplasmic mtDNA variants — m.11778G>A in MT-ND4, m.3460G>A in MT-ND1, or m.14484T>C in MT-ND6, which together are responsible for the majority of LHON cases worldwide. In arLHON the equivalent lesion is biallelic disruption of a nuclear complex I subunit or assembly/maintenance factor (DNAJC30, NDUFS2, MCAT, NDUFA12). Because mtDNA is present in every cell, the mutation itself is systemic; the disease phenotype is not.

steps/8.description: Mutant complex I transfers electrons from NADH to ubiquinone inefficiently. Proton pumping across the inner membrane falls, the NADH/NAD+ redox couple shifts, and the coupled ATP-generating capacity of oxidative phosphorylation is reduced. The severity of the biochemical lesion is not uniform across the three primary variants: transmitochondrial cybrid work cited here shows a frank assembly and catalytic-activity defect for m.3460G>A, whereas m.11778G>A and m.14484T>C are generally reported to impair coupling efficiency and raise ROS with comparatively better preserved catalytic activity — that second half is the wider literature's consensus and is not curated here against a cited source. The node should therefore be read as a shared functional endpoint rather than an identical molecular block. Idebenone's therapeutic rationale is to accept electrons via NQO1 and deliver them downstream to complex III, partly bypassing this block.

steps/9.description: The combination of a bioenergetic shortfall and increased electron leak creates chronic oxidative stress. Cybrid experiments show directly that the primary mutations raise mitochondrial ROS production while lowering ATP output and membrane potential, and that this is coupled to apoptotic activation (cytochrome c release, BAK/BAX, cleaved caspases) and impaired PINK1/parkin mitophagy. Why the resulting injury is confined to retinal ganglion cells remains unsettled. One proposed explanation is that RGCs regulate superoxide unusually tightly and that LHON mutations subvert that regulation — but the supporting measurement was made in the RGC-5 cell line, which the later cell-line-authentication literature (not cited in this entry) reports not to be of retinal ganglion cell origin, so this should be treated as an unconfirmed hypothesis. The better-supported account of selective vulnerability is the anatomical one given in the downstream node: the long, partly unmyelinated intraretinal axon segment imposes an exceptionally high and spatially distributed ATP demand.

steps/10.description: LHON is not a deterministic monogenic disease. Most carriers of a primary mtDNA variant never lose vision; conversion is gated by additional factors that act on the bioenergetic threshold of the retinal ganglion cell. Three modifier classes are established. (1) mtDNA haplogroup background: risk of visual failure is higher for m.11778G>A on haplogroup J2 and for m.14484T>C on haplogroup J1, higher for m.3460G>A on haplogroup K, and significantly lower for m.11778G>A on haplogroup H, with MT-CYB substitutions offering a mechanistic explanation. (2) Sex: males are affected several times more often than females, an asymmetry not explicable by maternal transmission alone. The size of that excess is contested: GeneReviews gives four to five times, whereas the Australian registry figures below imply a ratio closer to three. (3) Environmental exposure: smoking is strongly and consistently associated with visual loss independent of sex and alcohol, with clinical penetrance reaching 93% in men who smoked; heavy alcohol intake shows a weaker trend. This node is the mechanistic bridge between genotype and the observed low penetrance (17.5% of males and 5.4% of females in a contemporary Australian registry cohort). Those two penetrance figures are not in conflict and must not be compared directly: the 93% figure is conditional on smoking and comes from LHON-affected pedigrees ascertained through probands, whereas the 17.5%/5.4% figures are unconditional lifetime risks from a registry that includes 4,948 largely asymptomatic carriers. The registry authors state explicitly that historically higher male rates are not supported by their data. The same ascertainment caveat separates the clinical carrier prevalence recorded under `prevalence` (11.82 per 100,000) from the population-genomic susceptibility estimate of roughly 1 in 1,000.

steps/11.description: Retinal ganglion cells are the selectively vulnerable cell type in LHON and in mitochondrial optic neuropathies generally. Their long, partly unmyelinated intraretinal axons impose a high and spatially distributed energy demand that a complex-I-deficient mitochondrial population cannot sustain, and the cells die by apoptosis. Ganglion cell layer thinning on OCT can precede overt optic atrophy.

steps/12.description: Ultrastructural morphometry of LHON optic nerves shows 95-99% depletion of the nerve fiber population, with surviving fibers confined to the periphery and a marked loss of axons below 1 micron in diameter — the P-cell population that forms the papillomacular bundle. This anatomical selectivity is what converts a generalized bioenergetic defect into the characteristic clinical picture of dense central/centrocecal scotoma and dyschromatopsia with relative sparing of peripheral fields and pupillary responses.

steps/13.description: The clinical endpoint: bilateral, painless, subacute central visual failure with dense central or centrocecal scotoma, severe dyschromatopsia, and optic atrophy. Visual acuity commonly deteriorates to the level of legal blindness and then plateaus, and the loss is generally irreversible. Spontaneous recovery does occur and is genotype-dependent, being most frequent with m.14484T>C and least with m.11778G>A; the quoted recovery percentages vary widely between series and are not curated here (see `notes`).

treatments/0.description: Idebenone is a short-chain benzoquinone/coenzyme Q10 analogue that, after NQO1-mediated reduction, can accept electrons and deliver them to complex III, partly bypassing the defective complex I while also limiting oxidative injury. It is the only disease-specific drug authorised for LHON (European Medicines Agency, under exceptional circumstances), given at 900 mg/day (300 mg three times daily). The pivotal RHODOS randomised placebo-controlled trial did not meet its primary endpoint but favoured idebenone in secondary analyses, particularly in patients with discordant visual acuities at baseline; the later externally controlled LEROS study met its primary endpoint and confirmed long-term efficacy in the subacute/dynamic and chronic phases, with effect size varying by disease phase and causative variant. Benefit is greatest when treatment begins within the first year of visual loss.

treatments/1.description: Lenadogene nolparvovec (GS010, rAAV2/2-ND4) is a single intravitreal AAV2 vector delivering a nuclear-encoded, mitochondrially targeted wild-type ND4 (allotopic expression) for m.11778G>A/MT-ND4 LHON. Interpretation is materially confounded: sham-injected fellow eyes improved to essentially the same degree as treated eyes, so the within-patient primary endpoints were not met. A nonhuman-primate study found transfer of viral vector DNA to the contralateral, non-injected eye, which offers a plausible mechanistic explanation for that bilateral effect but also removes the fellow eye as an independent control. Gene therapy is therefore promising but not established routine care.

treatments/5.description: Counselling must explain strict maternal transmission for mtDNA LHON, the inability of affected males to transmit, the sex- and age-dependent incomplete penetrance, and the different (autosomal recessive) risks of arLHON. Because heteroplasmy means a maternal relative may not carry the variant, each maternal family member seeking risk advice should undergo molecular testing rather than being assumed to be a carrier. Once the maternal variant is known, prenatal testing and preimplantation genetic testing are technically possible, but counselling must be explicit that a positive prenatal result is hard to interpret — mutational load in amniocytes and chorionic villi may not reflect other fetal or adult tissues, and the presence of the variant does not predict whether, when, how severely, or how fast visual loss will occur.

open_questions/2.rationale: Idebenone's mechanism requires NQO1-mediated reduction before it can shuttle electrons to complex III, so variants lowering NQO1 protein levels are a mechanistically coherent candidate explanation for non-response — and the unreduced, oxidized drug actively inhibits complex I, so the stakes are higher than simple inefficacy. evidence.snippet: We report germline loss-of-function mutations in SPRED1 in a newly identified autosomal dominant human disorder. SPRED1 is a member of the SPROUTY/SPRED family of proteins that act as negative regulators of RAS->RAF interaction and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling.
evidence.explanation: The founding report establishing germline SPRED1 loss of function as the cause of the disorder and its role as a RAS-MAPK negative regulator.

evidence.snippet: Like Sprouty, Spred inhibited growth-factor-mediated activation of MAP kinase.
evidence.explanation: Original functional characterization of Spred proteins as suppressors of growth-factor-driven MAPK activation, the activity lost in Legius syndrome.

steps/1.description: Legius syndrome is caused by heterozygous germline loss-of-function variants in SPRED1, a member of the SPROUTY/SPRED family of proteins that act as negative regulators of the RAS-RAF interaction and downstream MAPK signaling. This was the first human disease attributed to the SPRY/SPRED gene family and placed the disorder within the RASopathy group of RAS-MAPK pathway disorders.

evidence.snippet: We show that Spred1 binding induces the plasma membrane localization of NF1, which subsequently down-regulates Ras-GTP levels.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration that SPRED1 acts as a membrane-targeting adaptor for neurofibromin, which is the claim this node makes; the EVH1-GRD interaction and structural papers establish the binding interface but not the membrane localization itself.

evidence.snippet: This novel mechanism for the regulation of neurofibromin provides a molecular bridge for understanding the overlapping pathophysiology of NF1 and Legius syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Establishes this node as the shared molecular step that explains why SPRED1 loss and NF1 loss produce overlapping pathophysiology.

evidence.snippet: we found that the SPRED1 EVH1 domain interacts with the N-terminal 16 amino acids and the C-terminal 20 amino acids of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP)-related domain (GRD) of neurofibromin
evidence.explanation: Maps the SPRED1-neurofibromin interface whose disruption underlies Legius syndrome.

evidence.snippet: pathogenic missense mutations in the EVH1 domain of SPRED1 in Legius syndrome reduced the binding affinity between the EVH1 domain and the GRD
evidence.explanation: Shows that Legius-associated EVH1 missense variants act by weakening neurofibromin binding.

evidence.snippet: The structure provides insight into how the membrane targeting of neurofibromin by SPRED1 allows simultaneous interaction with activated KRAS.
evidence.explanation: Structural confirmation that SPRED1 positions neurofibromin at the membrane to act on active RAS.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of the neurofibromin-SPRED1 interface provides a rationale for mutations observed in Legius syndrome and suggests why SPRED1 can bind to neurofibromin but no other RasGAPs.
evidence.explanation: Explains both the pathogenicity of interface variants and the selectivity of SPRED1 for neurofibromin rather than other RasGAPs.

steps/2.description: SPRED1 suppresses RAS-ERK signaling not by acting on RAS directly but by serving as a membrane-targeting adaptor for neurofibromin, the RAS-GAP encoded by NF1. The SPRED1 EVH1 domain binds short N- and C-terminal helical extensions flanking the GAP-related domain (GRD) of neurofibromin — regions dispensable for GAP catalysis and absent from p120GAP, which explains the selectivity of SPRED1 for neurofibromin among RasGAPs. Pathogenic EVH1-domain missense variants found in Legius syndrome reduce GRD binding affinity and correspondingly abolish the ERK-suppressing activity of SPRED1, providing a direct molecular link between genotype and pathway dysregulation. Structural work confirms that SPRED1-mediated membrane targeting allows neurofibromin to engage activated KRAS simultaneously.

evidence.snippet: This disorder is yet another member of the recently characterized group of phenotypically overlapping syndromes caused by mutations in the genes encoding key components of the RAS-MAPK pathway.
evidence.explanation: Places Legius syndrome within the RAS-MAPK (RASopathy) group sharing this final common mechanism.

steps/3.description: Like the other RASopathies, Legius syndrome results from germline dysregulation of the RAS-MAPK (RAS/ERK) signal transduction cascade. The shared pathway lesion places the disorder in the same phenotypically overlapping family as neurofibromatosis type 1, Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome, and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, and accounts for the macrocephaly, pigmentary, and neurocognitive features shared across the group. In Legius syndrome the dysregulation is comparatively mild and does not reach the threshold required for neurofibroma or other NF1 tumor formation.

evidence.snippet: indicating that complete SPRED1 inactivation is needed to generate a café-au-lait spot in this syndrome
evidence.explanation: States the biallelic-inactivation requirement for the pigmentary lesion.

steps/4.description: Melanocytes isolated from a café-au-lait macule of an affected individual carried, in addition to the germline SPRED1 variant, an acquired somatic mutation in the wild-type SPRED1 allele. Café-au-lait macule formation in Legius syndrome therefore follows a two-hit, mosaic-somatic logic in the melanocyte lineage, mirroring the second-hit requirement described for NF1 pigmentary lesions, rather than arising from germline haploinsufficiency alone.

evidence.snippet: Electrophysiological recordings on brain slices from these animals identified defects in short- and long-term synaptic hippocampal plasticity, including a disequilibrium between long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression in CA1 region.
evidence.explanation: Documents the hippocampal plasticity defect in the Spred1-null mouse model.

evidence.snippet: Spred1(-/-) mice show decreased learning and memory performance in the Morris water maze and visual-discrimination T-maze, but normal basic neuromotor and sensory abilities.
evidence.explanation: Shows a selective learning and memory deficit rather than a general sensorimotor impairment in the model.

steps/5.description: Spred1-null mice show impaired performance in the Morris water maze and visual-discrimination T-maze with normal basic neuromotor and sensory abilities, together with defects in short- and long-term hippocampal synaptic plasticity including a disequilibrium between long-term potentiation and long-term depression in CA1. Increased ERK phosphorylation is measurable in Spred1-null slices after LTP induction, linking the plasticity defect to Ras/ERK hyperactivation. This is the candidate substrate for the learning disability, ADHD, and developmental delay reported in affected individuals, but the translational step from mouse hippocampal physiology to the human cognitive phenotype has not been directly demonstrated (see the HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH discussion).

evidence.snippet: LGSS, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, is characterized by multiple CALMs similar to NF1 with or without skinfold freckling, caused by heterozygous PVs in SPRED1, located on chromosome 15.
evidence.explanation: Consensus statement describing the defining pigmentary phenotype and its genetic basis.

steps/6.description: The cardinal and often sole objective finding of Legius syndrome: multiple, bilaterally distributed café-au-lait macules, with or without skinfold (axillary or inguinal) freckling, clinically indistinguishable from those of neurofibromatosis type 1. Because the pigmentary phenotype is shared, roughly half of individuals with a SPRED1 variant satisfy the older NIH clinical criteria for NF1 despite having a different natural history — the observation that drove the 2021 consensus revision to make a molecular SPRED1 result a required diagnostic criterion.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SPRED1 (chromosome 15) cause Legius syndrome. The mutational spectrum is broad — 34 distinct SPRED1 variants were identified across 43 probands in the defining anonymous cohort — so there is no single recurrent variant, in contrast to the single recurrent SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly variant of NS/LAH. Pathogenic missense variants cluster in the EVH1 domain and act by weakening the neurofibromin GRD interaction. SPRED1 variants account for approximately 1% of sporadic and 19% of familial cases presenting with pigmentary features of NF1 only.

Once the SPRED1 pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.

evidence.snippet: None of the 42 SPRED1-positive individuals (0%; 95% CI, 0%-7%) had discrete cutaneous or plexiform neurofibromas, typical NF1 osseous lesions, or symptomatic optic pathway gliomas.
evidence.explanation: Supports the absence of NF1 tumor manifestations, but the reported confidence interval bounds the residual risk only loosely at 7%, which is what leaves this question open.

open_questions/0.rationale: The clinical management of Legius syndrome — developmental rather than oncologic surveillance — rests on the claim that SPRED1 loss does not confer the tumor predisposition of NF1. The strongest supporting observation is nonetheless a zero count in a modest cohort: 0 of 42 SPRED1-positive individuals, with a 95% confidence interval extending to 7%. A tumor risk anywhere below that upper bound is statistically compatible with the data, and the cohorts are weighted toward children, so adult-onset risk is especially poorly constrained. Because SPRED1 and NF1 converge on the same RAS-inactivation step, a mechanistic prior for some residual risk is not unreasonable, and resolving this determines whether any oncologic surveillance is warranted.

evidence.snippet: We investigated hippocampus-dependent learning and memory as well as synaptic plasticity in Spred1(-/-) mice, an animal model of this newly discovered human syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The mechanism is established in homozygous null mice, whereas human Legius syndrome results from heterozygous loss of function.

open_questions/1.rationale: The mechanistic account of the neurocognitive phenotype rests entirely on a mouse model, and two gaps separate it from the human disease. First is a dosage mismatch: the electrophysiology and behavioral deficits are reported in homozygous Spred1(-/-) animals, whereas humans with Legius syndrome are heterozygous. Second, no human study has demonstrated a corresponding hippocampal plasticity or ERK-signaling abnormality, so the inference from rodent CA1 physiology to human learning disability remains an extrapolation rather than a demonstrated mechanism. This matters therapeutically, because MEK-inhibitor-based cognitive rescue strategies proposed for RASopathies presuppose that the human deficit is ERK-driven in the same way.
