evidence.snippet: minor head trauma, the second most common trigger for acute decline in VWM
evidence.explanation: Ranks minor head trauma as the second most common provoking factor for episodes of acute decline.

evidence.snippet: For children, wearing a helmet when outside helps minimize the effects of head trauma.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends a preventive measure specific to this exposure, which is the management consequence of treating head trauma as a trigger.

evidence.snippet: Clinical evidence for provoking decline is only present for anesthetics: anesthesia was a provoking factor in 16% of the patients with episodes of acute decline.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies anaesthesia as a documented provoking factor for episodes of acute neurological decline in a VWM patient cohort, which is what makes this exposure a curated environmental factor rather than a theoretical one.

evidence.snippet: We have identified mutations in EIF2B5 and EIF2B2, encoding the epsilon- and beta-subunits of the translation initiation factor eIF2B and located on chromosomes 3q27 and 14q24, respectively, as causing VWM.
evidence.explanation: Identifies mutations in eIF2B subunit genes as the cause of VWM, establishing the primary molecular lesion.

evidence.snippet: "Vanishing white matter" (VWM) is a leukodystrophy caused by autosomal recessive pathogenic variants in the genes encoding the subunits of eukaryotic initiation factor 2B (eIF2B).
evidence.explanation: Confirms the genetic basis in eIF2B subunit genes and autosomal recessive inheritance.

evidence.snippet: Disease severity was correlated with age at onset (p < 0.0001) but not with the type of the mutated subunit nor with the position of the mutation within the protein.
evidence.explanation: Supports modelling the lesion at the level of the eIF2B complex rather than per subunit gene: in this cohort which subunit was mutated did not predict severity.

evidence.snippet: The gene (EIF2B1-5) in which the mutation located, and the number of null alleles were not associated with age of onset in these patients.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication in a larger pooled cohort that the identity of the mutated subunit gene does not stratify the phenotype, which is why all five genes are bound to this single complex-level node.

steps/8.description: Biallelic pathogenic variants in EIF2B1-EIF2B5 partially reduce the guanine nucleotide exchange activity of eIF2B, the five-subunit GEF that recycles inactive eIF2-GDP to active eIF2-GTP to permit translation initiation. eIF2B has an essential housekeeping role in translation and in its regulation during stress, yet the white matter (and ovaries) are selectively vulnerable.

evidence.snippet: eIF2B is a central regulatory factor in the integrated stress response (ISR). Genetic variants decrease eIF2B activity and thereby cause constitutive activation of the ISR downstream of eIF2B. Strikingly, the ISR is specifically activated in astrocytes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes deregulated, constitutive ISR activation as the core mechanism and its astrocyte specificity.

evidence.snippet: In brains of VWM compared to wild-type mice we observed the most prominent changes in translation concerning ISR mRNAs; their expression levels correlated with disease severity.
evidence.explanation: Mouse models show ISR mRNA translational changes that correlate with disease severity, linking ISR deregulation to pathology.

steps/9.description: eIF2B is the central regulatory factor of the integrated stress response (ISR): phosphorylation of eIF2-alpha inhibits eIF2B, reducing global translation while up-regulating ISR effector mRNAs. eIF2B-deficient mutations chronically mimic this state, producing constitutive ISR activation that is specifically pronounced in astrocytes; ISR mRNA expression levels correlate with disease severity.

evidence.snippet: In all mutant strains, impaired maturation of white matter astrocytes preceded onset and paralleled disease severity and progression.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that astrocyte maturation impairment precedes and tracks disease, supporting astrocytes as the central affected cell type.

evidence.snippet: In coculture, VWM astrocytes secreted factors that inhibited oligodendrocyte maturation, whereas WT astrocytes allowed normal maturation of VWM oligodendrocytes.
evidence.explanation: Coculture data show astrocytes drive secondary oligodendrocyte dysfunction, establishing the astrocyte-to-oligodendrocyte axis.

evidence.snippet: that VWM cortical astrocytes exhibit morphological changes and are less complex in structure than control cells. Our findings also suggest that these astrocytes are immature and not reactive.
evidence.explanation: Proteomic and immunohistochemical analysis of human VWM patient cortex confirms astrocytes are morphologically abnormal and immature, extending astrocyte involvement beyond white matter.

steps/10.description: White matter astrocytes are the primary affected cell type in VWM. Impaired astrocyte maturation precedes disease onset and parallels severity; immature, morphologically abnormal astrocytes secrete factors that inhibit oligodendrocyte maturation, while wild-type astrocytes permit normal maturation of mutant oligodendrocytes. Specialized astrocytes such as cerebellar Bergmann glia and retinal Mueller cells are also involved.

evidence.snippet: In eight patients with advanced disease, MRI revealed a diffuse cerebral hemispheric leukoencephalopathy, in which increasing areas of the abnormal white matter had a signal intensity close to that of CSF on all pulse sequences.
evidence.explanation: Original clinical description of progressive white matter signal change toward CSF intensity, the hallmark of VWM.

evidence.snippet: Autopsy in one patient confirmed the presence of extensive cystic degeneration of the cerebral white matter with reactive change and a preserved cortex.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy confirms cystic degeneration of white matter with cortical sparing, the cavitation hallmark.

steps/11.description: Diffuse cerebral white matter progressively acquires a CSF-like signal on MRI and undergoes cystic degeneration (cavitation), so that increasing areas of white matter are replaced by fluid while the cortex is relatively preserved. Long-surviving patients also show secondary cortical thinning.

evidence.snippet: As eIF2B has an essential role in the regulation of translation under different conditions, including stress, this may explain the rapid deterioration of people with VWM under stress.
evidence.explanation: Links the eIF2B/ISR defect mechanistically to the characteristic stress-provoked deterioration.

evidence.snippet: There were episodes of deterioration following infections and minor head traumas, and these could results in unexplained coma.
evidence.explanation: Original clinical observation of stress-provoked episodic deterioration and coma.

steps/12.description: Because eIF2B governs translation during stress, the disease is dominated by chronic progressive decline punctuated by episodes of rapid, major neurological deterioration provoked by febrile infections, minor head trauma, major surgery, or acute and extreme fright, which may precipitate unexplained coma.

evidence.snippet: In eight patients with advanced disease, MRI revealed a diffuse cerebral hemispheric leukoencephalopathy, in which increasing areas of the abnormal white matter had a signal intensity close to that of CSF on all pulse sequences.
evidence.explanation: Documents the diffuse leukoencephalopathy with progression to CSF-like signal intensity.

steps/13.description: Diffuse cerebral white matter abnormality progressing to a CSF-like signal with cystic cavitation is the radiologic hallmark.

evidence.snippet: There were episodes of deterioration following infections and minor head traumas, and these could results in unexplained coma.
evidence.explanation: Stress-provoked episodic deterioration may culminate in unexplained coma.

steps/14.description: Stress (infection, head trauma) can precipitate rapid deterioration and unexplained coma.

edges/5.description: Reduced eIF2B GEF activity lowers the pool of active eIF2-GTP and causes constitutive, deregulated activation of the integrated stress response downstream of eIF2B.

edges/6.description: Constitutive ISR activation impairs maturation and function of white matter astrocytes, the cell type selectively affected in VWM.

edges/7.description: Astrocyte dysfunction and the resulting failure of oligodendrocyte maturation lead to progressive loss and cystic degeneration of central nervous system white matter.

edges/8.description: The vulnerable, rarefying white matter is prone to acute episodic decline when challenged by physiological stress, superimposed on the chronic progressive course.

evidence.snippet: In eight patients with advanced disease, MRI revealed a diffuse cerebral hemispheric leukoencephalopathy, in which increasing areas of the abnormal white matter had a signal intensity close to that of CSF on all pulse sequences.
evidence.explanation: Reports the imaging leukoencephalopathy as the correlate of the progressive white matter change this node describes, with autopsy in the same series confirming cystic degeneration.

edges/9.description: Rarefaction and cystic degeneration of the cerebral white matter are what the diffuse confluent white matter signal abnormality on MRI records; in advanced disease the affected white matter approaches CSF signal on all pulse sequences.

evidence.snippet: There were episodes of deterioration following infections and minor head traumas, and these could results in unexplained coma.
evidence.explanation: States that the stress-provoked deterioration episodes could result in unexplained coma, which is the edge from this node to the Coma phenotype.

edges/10.description: An episode of stress-provoked deterioration may itself progress to unexplained coma, which in the original series followed infections and minor head traumas.

evidence.snippet: Fever activates the ISR, and febrile infections are the most common triggers for acute decline in patients with VWM.
evidence.explanation: States the mechanism of this link directly — fever acts on the ISR, which is the node the exposure is attached to.

edges/11.description: Fever activates the same integrated stress response that the eIF2B defect already deregulates, so the exposure amplifies an ISR that is abnormal at baseline. EXACERBATES rather than TRIGGERS: the genetic defect, not the infection, establishes the deregulated state.

evidence.snippet: Patients can present at any age with chronic neurologic decline and additional subacute episodes of rapid neurologic deterioration provoked by stressors such as febrile infections
evidence.explanation: Attributes the episodic-deterioration node specifically to febrile infection as the provoking stressor.

edges/12.description: The episode of acute decline itself does not occur without a stressor, so the exposure initiates it rather than amplifying it; the intermediate is the ISR node above.

evidence.snippet: Chronic progressive decline can be exacerbated by rapid deterioration during febrile illnesses or following head trauma or major surgical procedures, or by acute and extreme fright.
evidence.explanation: Names head trauma among the stressors that provoke the acute deterioration this node describes.

edges/13.description: Head trauma is one of the physiological stressors that precipitates an episode of rapid neurological deterioration on top of the chronic progressive course.

evidence.snippet: Inhalation anesthetics, such as sevoflurane, which are most commonly used to induce anesthesia in children, are known to activate the ISR and may pose a risk for patients with VWM
evidence.explanation: States the mechanism of the link — the anaesthetic activates the ISR, which is the node this exposure is attached to.

evidence.snippet: It is, therefore, recommended to consider using alternative anesthetic agents, such as propofol, which do not affect the ISR.
evidence.explanation: The recommended substitution is agent-specific and turns on ISR effect, which is the clinical consequence of this exposure acting on the ISR node.

edges/14.description: Inhalation anaesthetics act on the same integrated stress response that the eIF2B defect already deregulates, so the exposure pushes an already-abnormal ISR further and is the proposed route by which anaesthesia provokes acute decline.

evidence.snippet: We found 16 different mutations in EIF2B5 in 29 patients from 23 families.
evidence.explanation: EIF2B5 was the first and most frequently mutated eIF2B gene identified in VWM patients.

evidence.snippet: Patients homozygous for p.Arg113His had a milder disease than patients compound heterozygous for p.Arg113His and patients homozygous for p.Thr91Ala.
evidence.explanation: Shows that the mild and severe ends of the VWM spectrum both occur within EIF2B5, so severity tracks the specific allele pair rather than the subunit gene.

genes/0.notes: EIF2B5 (encoding the catalytic epsilon subunit of eIF2B) is the most commonly mutated of the five eIF2B subunit genes in VWM. Severity varies by allele within EIF2B5 rather than by which subunit gene is mutated: in a cross-sectional study drawn from a database of 184 patients with VWM, homozygotes for p.Arg113His had milder disease than p.Arg113His compound heterozygotes and than p.Thr91Ala homozygotes (PMID:20975056). Allele-level detail belongs on this record rather than in a separate per-gene entry.

evidence.snippet: We also found two distantly related individuals who were homozygous with respect to a missense mutation in EIF2B2, affecting a conserved amino acid.
evidence.explanation: EIF2B2 mutations were identified among VWM patients, confirming locus heterogeneity.

genes/1.notes: EIF2B2 (encoding the beta subunit of eIF2B) is one of the five subunit genes that cause VWM when biallelically mutated.

evidence.snippet: identification of biallelic pathogenic variants in one of five genes (EIF2B1, EIF2B2, EIF2B3, EIF2B4, EIF2B5), which encode the five subunits of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (eIF2B).
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews establishes that biallelic variants in any of the five eIF2B genes, including EIF2B1, cause VWM.

genes/2.notes: EIF2B1 (alpha subunit) is one of the five eIF2B subunit genes; biallelic pathogenic variants in any of EIF2B1-EIF2B5 establish the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: identification of biallelic pathogenic variants in one of five genes (EIF2B1, EIF2B2, EIF2B3, EIF2B4, EIF2B5), which encode the five subunits of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (eIF2B).
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews establishes EIF2B3 as one of the five VWM disease genes.

genes/3.notes: EIF2B3 (gamma subunit) is one of the five eIF2B subunit genes causing VWM.

evidence.snippet: In both patients we found the c.1117C>T (p.Arg373Cys) mutation in homozygosis in the EIF2B4 gen.
evidence.explanation: An EIF2B4 homozygous variant was identified in adult-onset ovarioleukodystrophy, confirming EIF2B4 as a VWM gene.

genes/4.notes: EIF2B4 (delta subunit) is one of the five eIF2B subunit genes causing VWM; a homozygous EIF2B4 p.Arg373Cys variant has been reported in adult-onset ovarioleukodystrophy.

evidence.snippet: Physical therapy and rehabilitation for motor dysfunction (mainly spasticity and ataxia)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management recommends physical therapy and rehabilitation for motor dysfunction.

treatments/0.description: Physical therapy and rehabilitation for motor dysfunction (mainly spasticity and ataxia). VWM has no disease-modifying therapy; care is supportive.

evidence.snippet: Prevention of infections and fever when possible through the use of vaccinations, low-dose maintenance antibiotics during winter, antibiotics for minor infections, and antipyretics for fever.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends infection and fever prevention to reduce stress-provoked deterioration.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Contact sports, head trauma, infections, high body temperature and, if possible, major surgery.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists stressors to avoid because they trigger acute neurological deterioration.

treatments/1.description: Prevention of secondary deterioration through vaccinations, low-dose maintenance antibiotics during winter, antibiotics for minor infections, and antipyretics for fever, because febrile infections provoke rapid decline. Helmets and avoidance of contact sports, head trauma, high body temperature, and (where possible) major surgery are advised.

evidence.snippet: The compound ISRIB (for "ISR inhibitor") was administered to VWM mice to increase eIF2B activity.
evidence.explanation: ISRIB, an eIF2B activator, was tested in VWM mice as an ISR-modulating disease-modifying strategy.

evidence.snippet: Both Bergmann glia pathology and cerebellar myelin pathology improved with Guanabenz treatment in mice, showing that Bergmann glia translocation is a sensitive measurement for improvement.
evidence.explanation: Guanabenz, which modulates eIF2B/eIF2 phosphorylation, improved neuropathology in VWM mice, supporting ISR modulation as a therapeutic target.

evidence.snippet: The 33 patients treated with guanabenz had a significantly lower risk of losing the ability to walk with support than the 66 historical controls (HR 0·33 [95% CI 0·16-0·69]; log-rank p=0·0061).
evidence.explanation: First human efficacy signal for ISR modulation in VWM, against matched untreated historical controls.

evidence.snippet: 63 serious adverse events were reported in 25 (76%) of 33 patients.
evidence.explanation: Records the adverse-event burden that the description reports alongside the efficacy signal, so the treatment is not read as benign.

evidence.snippet: Guanabenz treatment had an acceptable and manageable safety profile and, after the initial phase, was well tolerated in children with vanishing white matter.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own tolerability conclusion, which is what makes the adverse-event rate above compatible with continued treatment.

treatments/2.description: Disease-modifying approaches target the deregulated integrated stress response. The eIF2B activator ISRIB normalized ISR mRNA markers and ameliorated neuropathology in VWM mice, and the FDA-approved alpha2-agonist guanabenz, which modulates eIF2 phosphorylation/eIF2B activity, improved Bergmann glia and cerebellar myelin pathology in VWM mice. Guanabenz has since been taken into humans: a single-arm phase 1/2 trial in 33 children with early-childhood-onset VWM reported a significantly lower risk of losing the ability to walk with support than in 66 matched untreated historical controls, at the cost of a substantial adverse-event burden dominated by transient hallucinations. The comparison was non-randomised and the authors call for confirmation in a long-term extension study, so guanabenz is an investigational therapy with the first human efficacy signal rather than an established one. The direct eIF2B activator fosigotifator (ABBV-CLS-7262) is in an ongoing open-label phase 1b/2 study. See the clinical_trials block.

evidence.snippet: The α2-adrenergic antihypertensive drug guanabenz inhibits this stress response and has shown benefit in a mouse model of the disease.
evidence.explanation: States that guanabenz acts on the integrated stress response itself, which is the node this treatment link points at. Graded MODEL_ORGANISM because the benefit this sentence reports is the mouse result, not the trial's own human outcome.

evidence.snippet: Two promising compounds, that is, guanabenz (EU Clinical Trials Register identifier: EudraCT 2027-001438-25, CTIS 2023-503320-89-00) and ABBV-CLS-7262 (fosigotifator, ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT05757141 and NCT06594016), activating eIF2B indirectly or directly, are currently under clinical investigation.
evidence.explanation: Independent expert-consensus statement that both curated agents act by activating eIF2B, which is what makes them a single treatment link on this node rather than two unrelated drugs.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Both agents act on the node the eIF2B defect deregulates, from opposite ends of the same axis: guanabenz indirectly, by damping eIF2-alpha phosphorylation, and fosigotifator by activating eIF2B directly. This is the mechanism both trials in the clinical_trials block are testing, and it is the same ISR node that ISR-activating anaesthetics push the other way.

evidence.snippet: The hallmark itch-scratch cycle contributes not only to visible skin changes but also to substantial sleep disruption, emotional distress, and functional impairment.
evidence.explanation: The review identifies the itch-scratch cycle as a central driver of chronic disease manifestations.

steps/0.description: Persistent scratching sustains a neuroimmune itch-scratch cycle that drives chronic skin changes.

evidence.snippet: Primary intracranial melanocytoma is an uncommon benign pigmented tumor arising from leptomeningeal melanocytes.
evidence.explanation: This case report and review states the leptomeningeal melanocyte origin of the tumor.

evidence.snippet: Primary melanocytic tumors of the central nervous system (CNS) represent a spectrum of rare tumors.
evidence.explanation: The molecular review supports classifying meningeal melanocytoma within the rare primary CNS melanocytic tumor spectrum.

steps/1.description: Meningeal melanocytoma arises from melanocytes in the leptomeninges and forms a circumscribed primary CNS melanocytic neoplasm. The tumor is usually benign or low-grade, but its anatomic location can produce mass effect and neurologic symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Molecular analysis can detect specific mutations, including GNAQ, GNA11, SF3B1, EIF1AX, BAP1, that are typically found in circumscribed primary meningeal melanocytic tumors and not in other melanocytic lesions, whereas NRAS and BRAF mutations are typical for diffuse primary meningeal melanocytic tumors.
evidence.explanation: The EURACAN review supports GNAQ/GNA11 and related molecular alterations as distinguishing circumscribed primary meningeal melanocytic tumors.

evidence.snippet: Melanocytomas carried GNAQ/11 mutations and presented with CNV involving chromosomes 3 and 6.
evidence.explanation: Human tumor methylome and genomic profiling supports GNAQ/GNA11 alterations in melanocytomas.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of the FAK-regulated transcriptome demonstrated that GNAQ stimulates YAP through FAK.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistic GNAQ-driven melanoma models support Hippo-YAP signaling as a plausible downstream pathway for G-alpha-q-mutant melanocytic tumors, but this evidence is not meningeal melanocytoma-specific.

steps/2.description: Circumscribed primary meningeal melanocytic tumors, including many melanocytomas, commonly carry somatic alterations in GNAQ, GNA11, or related G-alpha-q pathway genes. These alterations distinguish them from many metastatic melanomas and support integrated molecular diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Recently, novel insights in the molecular alterations underlying primary melanocytic tumors of the CNS were obtained, including different oncogenic mutations in tumors in adult patients (especially GNAQ, GNA11) vs. children (especially NRAS).
evidence.explanation: The molecular review supports oncogenic GNAQ/GNA11 alterations in adult primary CNS melanocytic tumors.

steps/3.description: Oncogenic G-alpha-q pathway alterations support proliferation of the circumscribed melanocytic tumor mass.

evidence.snippet: We report a case of a 19-year-old woman presenting with progressively worsening headaches, nausea, emesis, and generalized weakness
evidence.explanation: Intracranial case evidence supports mass-effect symptoms including headache and weakness.

evidence.snippet: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine revealed a mass with thecal sac compression which was hypointense on T2-weighted images and hyperintense on T1-weighted images.
evidence.explanation: Spinal recurrence evidence supports local thecal sac compression as a mechanism for neurologic deficits.

steps/4.description: Intracranial or spinal meningeal melanocytoma can compress adjacent CNS structures, producing headache, seizures, limb weakness or sensory symptoms, and sphincter dysfunction depending on tumor location.

edges/1.description: Adult circumscribed CNS melanocytic tumors often carry GNAQ or GNA11 driver alterations.

edges/2.description: Tumor growth in intracranial or spinal meningeal spaces can produce headaches, seizures, weakness, or other neurologic deficits.

edges/3.description: G-alpha-q pathway activation contributes to melanocytic neoplasm growth.

edges/4.description: Tumor cell proliferation expands the meningeal mass and can compress adjacent brain, spinal cord, roots, or thecal sac structures.

evidence.snippet: Recently, novel insights in the molecular alterations underlying primary melanocytic tumors of the CNS were obtained, including different oncogenic mutations in tumors in adult patients (especially GNAQ, GNA11) vs. children (especially NRAS).
evidence.explanation: The review supports GNAQ/GNA11 as major adult primary CNS melanocytic tumor alterations.

evidence.snippet: Melanocytomas carried GNAQ/11 mutations and presented with CNV involving chromosomes 3 and 6.
evidence.explanation: Human tumor profiling supports GNAQ/GNA11 alterations and chromosome 3/6 copy-number variation in melanocytomas.

genes/0.notes: GNA11 is represented in the pathophysiology gene list; this genetic entry summarizes the shared GNAQ/GNA11 pathway axis and reported chromosome 3/6 copy-number changes.

evidence.snippet: Surgery is the preferred therapeutic approach, and total resection is associated with the best outcome.
evidence.explanation: The retrospective meta-analysis supports surgery and total resection as preferred treatment.

evidence.snippet: CTR was found to be significantly superior to ITR with regard to both local control and survival.
evidence.explanation: The pooled therapy analysis supports complete resection over incomplete resection for local control and survival.

treatments/0.description: Gross total surgical resection is the preferred local treatment for circumscribed meningeal melanocytoma when safely feasible and is associated with the best recurrence-free outcomes in retrospective data.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Surgical resection removes the circumscribed melanocytic tumor mass.

evidence.snippet: Patients with partial resection or tumor recurrence benefit from adjuvant radiotherapy, whereas chemo- or immunotherapies do not improve the disease course.
evidence.explanation: The meta-analysis supports adjuvant radiotherapy in partial resection or recurrence settings and notes limited systemic therapy benefit.

evidence.snippet: Outcome was significantly improved by RT after ITR.
evidence.explanation: The older pooled therapy analysis supports radiotherapy after incomplete resection.

treatments/1.description: Radiotherapy is considered after incomplete resection, recurrence, or aggressive features; retrospective evidence suggests benefit after incomplete resection but no definitive prospective standard exists.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Adjuvant radiation is used to improve local control when residual or recurrent tumor remains.

evidence.snippet: We used whole-exome sequencing of five patients with MIC-CAP syndrome and identified recessive mutations in STAMBP, a gene encoding the deubiquitinating (DUB) isopeptidase STAMBP (STAM-binding protein, also known as AMSH, associated molecule with the SH3 domain of STAM) that has a key role in cell surface receptor-mediated endocytosis and sorting.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic STAMBP loss of function as the cause and identifies the deubiquitinase as the affected activity.

evidence.snippet: The Zn(2+)-dependent DUBs AMSH and AMSH-LP regulate receptor trafficking by specifically cleaving Lys 63-linked polyubiquitin chains from internalized receptors.
evidence.explanation: Defines the Zn(2+)-dependent, K63-linkage-specific enzymatic activity that is lost.

evidence.snippet: Immunoblot analysis of patient-derived lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) revealed a severe reduction in STAMBP expression, indicating that Ser236Phe induces protein instability.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates protein destabilization as a route to loss of function in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: The MIC-CAP disease mutation, Thr313Ile, yields a substantial loss of catalytic activity without any significant change in the thermodynamic stability of the protein, indicating that its perturbed catalytic activity is the basis of the disease.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the second, catalytic route to loss of function for a specific disease allele.

evidence.snippet: demonstrated that the MIT domain binds tightly to the catalytic domain (CD), resulting in autoinhibition of its activity
evidence.explanation: Explains why MIT-domain missense variants (the majority of reported MIC-CAP missense alleles) are pathogenic despite lying outside the catalytic site.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function STAMBP variants abolish or severely reduce the activity of AMSH, a Zn(2+)-dependent JAMM/MPN+ metalloprotease deubiquitinase with strict specificity for Lys63-linked polyubiquitin chains. Two routes to loss of function are documented: (i) protein destabilization and near-absence of AMSH, the dominant route, seen with truncating alleles and with missense alleles in the SH3-binding motif (e.g. p.Ser236Phe) that block STAM binding and thereby destabilize the protein; and (ii) direct catalytic or substrate-binding impairment, exemplified by the JAMM-domain allele p.Thr313Ile. Enzyme regulation is itself relevant: the N-terminal MIT domain clamps the catalytic domain in an autoinhibited state that STAM1 binding relieves, which explains why MIT-domain and SH3-binding-motif missense variants - not just catalytic-site variants - are pathogenic.

evidence.snippet: AMSH, a deubiquitinating enzyme (DUB) with exquisite specificity for Lys63-linked polyubiquitin chains, is an endosome-associated DUB that regulates sorting of activated cell-surface signaling receptors to the lysosome, a process mediated by the members of the endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) machinery.
evidence.explanation: Defines the normal ESCRT-associated endosomal sorting role whose failure this node represents.

evidence.snippet: The RXXK motif of AMSH interacts with the SH3 domains of the STAM and Grb2 families of adaptor proteins with high affinity.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the ESCRT-0/STAM recruitment interaction that MIC-CAP SH3-binding-motif variants disrupt.

evidence.snippet: AMSH impairment results in missorted ubiquitinated cargoes in vitro and severe neurodegeneration in vivo
evidence.explanation: Links cargo mis-sorting directly to in vivo neurodegeneration.

steps/2.description: AMSH is recruited to the ESCRT-0 complex through the interaction of its SH3-binding motif with the SH3 domain of STAM, and to ESCRT-III through its MIT domain. There it removes K63-linked chains from internalized, ubiquitin-tagged cell-surface receptors as they are handed down the ESCRT chain into intraluminal vesicles of the multivesicular body. Loss of AMSH leaves K63-ubiquitinated cargo mis-sorted: receptors are neither properly committed to lysosomal degradation nor cleanly recycled, and ubiquitin is not recovered. This is the proximal convergence node from which the proteostasis, signaling, progenitor and inflammatory arms of the disease all branch.

evidence.snippet: Patient cell lines showed reduced STAMBP expression associated with accumulation of ubiquitin-conjugated protein aggregates, elevated apoptosis and insensitive activation of the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways.
evidence.explanation: Primary patient-cell evidence for serum-insensitive RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation.

evidence.snippet: The latter cellular phenotype is notable considering the established connection between these pathways and their association with vascular and capillary malformations.
evidence.explanation: The authors' explicit link from these pathways to the capillary-malformation phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Contrary to previously reported STAMBP mutations, the Ser236Phe mutation did not lead to constitutive activation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway in patient-derived LCLs, as indicated by the expression of phosphorylated S6 ribosomal protein, suggesting that it is not the major pathomechanism underlying the disorder in this patient.
evidence.explanation: Allele-specific counter-evidence: this patient had capillary malformations without mTOR pathway activation, so mTOR activation is not necessary for the cutaneous phenotype.

steps/3.description: Because activated receptors are not committed to lysosomal degradation, they persist and continue to signal from the endosomal compartment. Patient lymphoblastoid cell lines show RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway activity that is maintained even under serum starvation - "insensitive" rather than merely elevated - and lentiviral STAMBP restores a normal serum response. This paradoxical growth-signalling activation in a loss-of-function deubiquitinase disorder is the most plausible mechanistic bridge to the cutaneous capillary malformations, since both pathways are established drivers of vascular and capillary malformations. The arm is not settled: one patient homozygous for p.Ser236Phe had multiple capillary malformations *without* constitutive PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation.

evidence.snippet: Patient cell lines showed reduced STAMBP expression associated with accumulation of ubiquitin-conjugated protein aggregates, elevated apoptosis and insensitive activation of the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways.
evidence.explanation: Direct patient-cell evidence for ubiquitin-conjugate aggregation and elevated apoptosis.

evidence.snippet: Here, we demonstrate that AMSH(-/-) mice developed ubiquitinated protein accumulations as early as embryonic day 10 (E10), and that severe deposits were present in the brain at postnatal day 8 (P8) and P18.
evidence.explanation: In vivo timing of the aggregate phenotype, beginning prenatally.

evidence.snippet: Glutamate receptor and p62 accumulations were also found; these molecules colocalized with ubiquitinated aggregates in the brain.
evidence.explanation: Identifies glutamate receptors and p62 among the accumulating substrates.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, TDP-43 was found to accumulate and colocalize with glial marker-positive cells in the brain.
evidence.explanation: Documents TDP-43 accumulation, placing the aggregate phenotype in proteinopathy territory.

steps/4.description: Undegraded K63-ubiquitinated substrates accumulate as cytoplasmic ubiquitin-conjugate aggregates. Patient-derived lymphoblastoid cell lines show elevated conjugated-ubiquitin aggregates with increased autophagosome content, and lentiviral STAMBP re-expression reverses the phenotype. In the Amsh-null mouse the aggregates begin as early as embryonic day 10 and become severe in the postnatal brain, and the co-accumulating species have been identified as TDP-43, p62/SQSTM1 and glutamate receptors. Glutamate-receptor accumulation offers a direct, still-untested route from failed receptor downregulation to the excitation/inhibition imbalance underlying the epilepsy.

evidence.snippet: Cortical organoids with STAMBP knockout (KO) showed significantly lower proliferation of neural stem cells (NSCs), leading to smaller organoids that are characteristic of microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Human organoid evidence that STAMBP loss reduces neural stem cell proliferation and organoid size.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, STAMBP disruption did not affect apoptosis in early cortical organoids.
evidence.explanation: Qualifies the mechanism: in the human organoid system the early defect is proliferative rather than apoptotic, contrasting with the mouse.

evidence.snippet: We identified the anti-apoptotic protein CFLAR is down-regulated in those affected NPCs and ectopic expression of CFLAR rescues NPC defects induced by STAMBP-deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Identifies CFLAR downregulation as the effector of progenitor loss, with a rescue experiment.

steps/5.description: A developmental arm that operates before birth and is distinct from the postnatal degenerative arm. Human STAMBP-knockout cortical organoids show significantly reduced neural stem cell proliferation and are smaller, with no detectable increase in apoptosis at early stages; re-expression of wild-type STAMBP rescues proliferation while the disease alleles p.Gly307Glu and p.Thr313Ile do not. Independently, neural progenitor cells derived from STAMBP-deficient human embryonic stem cells cannot be maintained long term, with downregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein CFLAR as the identified effector and CFLAR re-expression rescuing the defect. Together these explain why the brain is already small at birth.

evidence.snippet: Here we identify the deubiquitinase STAM-binding protein (STAMBP) as a negative regulator of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
evidence.explanation: Establishes STAMBP as a brake on the NLRP3 inflammasome.

evidence.snippet: While STAMBP does not modulate NLRP3 protein abundance, cellular depletion of the deubiquitinase increased NLRP3 K63 chain polyubiquitination resulting in increased NLRP3 inflammasome activation.
evidence.explanation: Shows the mechanism runs through exactly the K63 chemistry that AMSH is specialized for, making derepression plausible in MIC-CAP.

evidence.snippet: accompanied by aggregation of ubiquitinated proteins, and massive neuroinflammation
evidence.explanation: In vivo neuroinflammation in the CNS-specific Stambp knockout, consistent with but not proving the inflammasome route.

steps/6.description: A proposed inflammatory arm. STAMBP is a negative regulator of the NLRP3 inflammasome, restraining it by removing K63-linked (non-degradative) polyubiquitin from NLRP3; STAMBP depletion in monocytes increases NLRP3 K63 polyubiquitination, inflammasome activation and IL-1beta release. The CNS-conditional Stambp knockout mouse shows massive neuroinflammation accompanying neuronal death. No patient-level inflammasome or IL-1beta data exist, so this arm is hypothesized rather than established in human MIC-CAP - but it is the disease's most tractable drug-repurposing hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: Examination of brain sections at P6 demonstrated significant loss of neurons and apoptotic cells in the CA1 subfield of the hippocampus.
evidence.explanation: Establishes apoptotic CA1 neuronal loss in the Amsh-null mouse.

evidence.snippet: AMSH-deficient hippocampal neuronal cells were unable to survive in vitro, even in the presence of several stimulatory cytokines, while AMSH-deficient cerebellar neurons, thymocytes, and embryonic fibroblasts survived normally.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the cell-autonomous, region-selective survival requirement, including cerebellar sparing.

evidence.snippet: In this MIC-CAP syndrome mouse model, early-onset neuronal death occurs specifically in the hippocampus and cortex, accompanied by aggregation of ubiquitinated proteins, and massive neuroinflammation.
evidence.explanation: Independent CNS-conditional knockout confirming the same regional selectivity and linking it to aggregates.

evidence.snippet: implicates ubiquitin-conjugate aggregation and elevated apoptosis as factors potentially influencing the progressive neuronal loss underlying MIC-CAP syndrome
evidence.explanation: The discovery paper's own causal interpretation linking aggregation and apoptosis to progressive neuronal loss.

steps/7.description: Neurons of the hippocampus (particularly the CA1 field) and cerebral cortex die by apoptosis, while cerebellar neurons, thymocytes and fibroblasts are spared - a cell-autonomous, region-restricted survival requirement that is the most distinctive cellular phenotype of AMSH deficiency and matches the human neuropathology of disproportionately small cerebral hemispheres with a relatively preserved cerebellum. This postnatal degenerative arm explains the *progressive* component of the microcephaly and the cortical atrophy, in contrast with the prenatal proliferation arm that sets brain size at birth.

evidence.snippet: generalized cutaneous capillary malformations (a few to hundreds of oval/circular macules or patches varying in size from 1-2 mm to several cm)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews description of the morphology, number and size range of the lesions.

evidence.snippet: multiple small capillary malformations on the skin
evidence.explanation: Confirms the cutaneous phenotype in the molecularly defined discovery cohort.

steps/8.description: Multiple small, pink-to-red, blanchable, roughly oval or circular capillary malformations are distributed generally and randomly over the body - a few to hundreds, ranging from 1-2 mm to several centimetres. They are present at birth, are not segmental or dermatomal (distinguishing them from the V1 trigeminal port-wine stain of Sturge-Weber syndrome), and carry none of the leptomeningeal-angiomatosis or glaucoma risk of that disorder. Skin biopsy confirms their nature histologically - dilated small-caliber vessels in the papillary dermis - but the proposed signaling substrate, capillary endothelium responding to the dysregulated RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR activity described above, has never been assayed in MIC-CAP lesional skin.

evidence.snippet: Microcephaly-capillary malformation (MIC-CAP) syndrome is characterized by severe microcephaly with progressive cortical atrophy, intractable epilepsy, profound developmental delay and multiple small capillary malformations on the skin.
evidence.explanation: Defines the progressive cortical atrophy that this node represents.

evidence.snippet: Brain atrophy developed by P16 and was accompanied by complete loss of the CA1 neurons in the hippocampus and marked atrophy of the cerebral cortex.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism recapitulation of the progressive brain atrophy.

steps/9.description: The organism-level convergence of the prenatal proliferation arm and the postnatal degenerative arm: a brain that is already small at birth and then falls further behind, with progressive cortical atrophy, a simplified gyral pattern, increased extra-axial cerebrospinal fluid space, hippocampal hypoplasia and, in a minority, thin immature white matter. This structural substrate drives the intractable epilepsy, spastic tetraparesis, optic atrophy and profound developmental delay.

edges/1.description: AMSH acts at the endosome as part of the ESCRT machinery; loss of its catalytic activity is the proximal cause of failed cargo deubiquitination during multivesicular-body sorting.

edges/2.description: Mis-sorted K63-ubiquitinated cargo accumulates as ubiquitin-conjugate aggregates.

edges/3.description: Activated receptors that are not committed to lysosomal degradation persist in the endosomal compartment and continue to signal.

edges/4.description: Failed endosomal cargo handling in neural progenitors limits their expansion during corticogenesis.

edges/5.description: NLRP3 is itself a K63-ubiquitination substrate restrained by AMSH; its derepression is a proposed inflammatory branch.

edges/6.description: Ubiquitin-conjugate aggregation and the associated proteostatic stress drive caspase-3-dependent apoptosis of vulnerable neurons.

edges/7.description: Cumulative neuronal loss produces radiographically progressive cerebral atrophy and a falling head circumference.

edges/8.description: A reduced cortical progenitor pool yields a small brain at birth, on which the postnatal degenerative arm is superimposed.

edges/9.description: Dysregulated growth-factor signaling in capillary endothelium is the proposed route to the cutaneous capillary malformations.

edges/10.description: Neuroinflammation is proposed to amplify neuronal death in the STAMBP-null brain.

evidence.snippet: We used whole-exome sequencing of five patients with MIC-CAP syndrome and identified recessive mutations in STAMBP
evidence.explanation: Original gene-disease discovery by exome sequencing of five patients.

evidence.snippet: Microcephaly-capillary malformation syndrome is a congenital and neurodevelopmental disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the STAMBP gene.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of the biallelic STAMBP gene-disease relationship.

evidence.snippet: we uncovered a homozygous missense variant in STAMBP (p.K303R) in the two siblings, inherited from heterozygous carrier parents
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates recessive segregation from asymptomatic heterozygous carrier parents.

genes/0.notes: STAMBP (2p13.1) encodes the 424-residue STAM-binding protein / AMSH, a Zn(2+)-dependent JAMM/MPN+ metalloprotease deubiquitinase specific for Lys63-linked polyubiquitin. Biallelic loss-of-function variants - homozygous or compound heterozygous - are necessary and sufficient for MIC-CAP. The reported allele spectrum is dominated by truncating and splice-disrupting variants, with a minority of missense alleles that cluster in the N-terminal MIT domain and the SH3-binding motif rather than in the catalytic JAMM domain. Recurrent alleles include p.Arg38Cys and p.Arg424*; a deep-intronic leaky splice allele (c.1005+358A>G) is associated with a markedly attenuated phenotype and is invisible to exome sequencing. Heterozygous carriers are asymptomatic; no gain-of-function or dominant-negative mechanism is known.

evidence.snippet: Supportive care by multidisciplinary specialists including a medical geneticist, neurologist, developmental pediatrician, and feeding specialist is recommended.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management recommendation for multidisciplinary supportive care.

evidence.snippet: Regular follow up with a child neurologist for seizure management and a complex care / palliative care team or experienced pediatrician to monitor for complications associated with severe neurologic impairment.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance recommendation including palliative care.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is supportive and is delivered by a multidisciplinary team including medical genetics, neurology, developmental pediatrics and feeding specialists, with regular child-neurology follow-up and involvement of a complex-care or palliative-care team to monitor complications of severe neurologic impairment.

evidence.snippet: Seizures require management by an experienced pediatric neurology team, as multiple anticonvulsant medications are frequently required for adequate seizure control.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews establishes anticonvulsant polytherapy as standard management.

evidence.snippet: The patient was treated successively with levetiracetam (40-50 mg/kg/day), topiramate (6-7 mg/kg/day), valproic acid (30 mg/kg/day) and corticosteroids at the outpatient clinic. The spasms decreased and became myoclonic, but the epilepsy remained refractory.
evidence.explanation: Documents a real drug sequence and its incomplete efficacy.

treatments/1.description: Seizure management by an experienced pediatric neurology team; multiple anticonvulsant medications are usually required and control is often incomplete. Levetiracetam, topiramate, valproic acid and corticosteroids have been used in sequence in reported cases. Note the valproic-acid caution below.

evidence.snippet: After 1 month, the patient received vigabatrin (60 mg/kg/day) and the seizures reduced by 80% a week later.
evidence.explanation: The single reported vigabatrin response in MIC-CAP.

evidence.snippet: Although the patient in the present study responded well to vigabatrin, the long-term efficacy of the drug could not be evaluated due to the early death of the patient.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own caveat limiting the strength of this n=1 observation.

treatments/2.description: Vigabatrin produced an 80% seizure reduction within a week in a single reported patient whose epilepsy had been refractory to levetiracetam, topiramate, valproic acid, corticosteroids and a ketogenic diet. This is a single case with three weeks of follow-up before the patient died, so long-term efficacy is unknown and vigabatrin should not be presented as established MIC-CAP therapy - though it is biologically coherent given the infantile-spasms phenotype for which vigabatrin is generally first line.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Valproic acid may or may not be associated with adverse effects.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews drug-safety statement; the hedged wording is why this is curated as a caution rather than a contraindication.

treatments/3.description: GeneReviews lists valproic acid under agents and circumstances to avoid, with deliberately hedged wording: one affected male died at 12 months of septic shock following acute pancreatitis possibly secondary to valproate, while other patients tolerated the drug. This is best treated as a caution warranting heightened pancreatic monitoring rather than an absolute contraindication.

evidence.snippet: A feeding tube is essential to optimize nutrition and weight gain while reducing the risk of aspiration.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews treats gastrostomy feeding as essential management.

treatments/4.description: Enteral feeding via gastrostomy tube to optimize nutrition and weight gain and to reduce aspiration risk. Aspiration pneumonia is a leading proximate cause of hospitalization and death.

evidence.snippet: Central hypotonia and peripheral hypertonia require attention to proper seating and bracing to maintain posture and prevent contractures.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management recommendation for tone and posture.

treatments/5.description: Attention to proper seating and bracing to maintain posture and prevent contractures, addressing the characteristic mixed pattern of central hypotonia with peripheral hypertonia.

evidence.snippet: During the follow-up, the seizures were still not well controlled, although the ketogenic diet ratio was modified from 2:1 to 4:1
evidence.explanation: Documents failure of the ketogenic diet in the one case where it was tried.

treatments/6.description: A ketogenic diet was trialled in one reported patient and failed to control seizures even after the ratio was escalated from 2:1 to 4:1. Recorded here as a documented negative result rather than a recommended therapy.

evidence.snippet: carrier testing for at-risk family members, prenatal testing for pregnancies at increased risk, and preimplantation genetic testing are possible
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews genetic-counseling options once familial variants are identified.

evidence.snippet: each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier
evidence.explanation: The standard biparental recurrence risk that counseling conveys.

treatments/7.description: Counseling on the 25% sib recurrence risk for biparental inheritance, and on the substantially lower (<1%) risk when the proband's homozygosity arose through uniparental isodisomy. Once the familial variants are known, carrier testing, prenatal testing and preimplantation genetic testing are available.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, neonatal AAV9-mediated gene supplementation of Stambp in the brain could significantly improve neurological defects, sustain growth, and prolong the lifespan of StambpSox1-cKO mice.
evidence.explanation: Preclinical efficacy of postnatal brain-directed gene replacement.

evidence.snippet: provide preclinical evidence that postnatal gene replacement is an effective approach to cure the disease
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing of the translational claim, explicitly preclinical.

treatments/8.description: Neonatal AAV9-mediated brain-directed supplementation of Stambp significantly improved neurological defects, sustained growth and prolonged lifespan in a CNS-specific Stambp knockout mouse. This is the leading translational prospect for MIC-CAP and is unusually favourable on paper: the STAMBP coding sequence is small enough for AAV packaging, the CNS-restricted knockout phenocopies the global null (so brain-directed delivery may suffice), and the intervention worked postnatally. It remains mouse-only - there is no investigational new drug application, no clinical trial and no human data.

evidence.snippet: neonatal AAV9-mediated gene supplementation of Stambp in the brain could significantly improve neurological defects
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that restoring Stambp in the brain corrects the downstream phenotype.

treatments/8/targets/0.description: Gene supplementation restores AMSH deubiquitinase activity in the brain.

evidence.snippet: The latter cellular phenotype is notable considering the established connection between these pathways and their association with vascular and capillary malformations.
evidence.explanation: The original statement of the hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: the Ser236Phe mutation did not lead to constitutive activation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway in patient-derived LCLs
evidence.explanation: The allele-specific counter-observation that makes the hypothesis contested.

hypotheses/0.description: The discovery cohort found serum-insensitive RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation in patient lymphoblastoid cell lines and proposed it as the link to the capillary malformations, by analogy with PIK3CA- and RASA1-related vascular anomalies. A later patient homozygous for p.Ser236Phe had multiple capillary malformations without detectable PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation, so either the capillary-malformation mechanism is mTOR-independent, or the lymphoblastoid readout does not reflect endothelial biology. No endothelial or skin-biopsy signaling study has been published in MIC-CAP.

evidence.snippet: These findings describe a unique mechanism of non-degradative ubiquitination of NLRP3 by STAMBP to limit excessive inflammasome activation and to reduce injurious IL-1beta signaling.
evidence.explanation: Molecular basis of the hypothesis, in a non-neural cell system.

hypotheses/1.description: STAMBP restrains the NLRP3 inflammasome via K63-deubiquitination, and the CNS-conditional Stambp knockout mouse shows massive neuroinflammation. This supports a hypothesized IL-1beta-driven amplification of neuronal death, but the inflammasome work was done in monocytes with no patient data, so the arm is not established in human MIC-CAP.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, STAMBP disruption did not affect apoptosis in early cortical organoids.
evidence.explanation: The human-organoid observation that directly conflicts with the apoptosis-dominant mouse model.

evidence.snippet: The AMSH-deficient mice were morphologically indistinguishable from their littermates at birth, and histopathological examinations revealed normal morphogenesis in all tissues tested.
evidence.explanation: The mouse is normal at birth, so it cannot model the congenital component of human microcephaly.

open_questions/0.rationale: Amsh-null mice are grossly normal at birth and develop apoptotic CA1 and cortical neuronal loss postnatally, whereas human STAMBP-knockout cortical organoids show reduced neural stem cell proliferation with explicitly no early apoptosis. Human infants are microcephalic at birth AND progressively so, which neither model captures alone. The mismatch is mechanistically meaningful because it determines the therapeutic window: a purely postnatal apoptotic mechanism would be tractable to postnatal intervention, while a prenatal proliferative deficit would not.

evidence.snippet: suggesting that it is not the major pathomechanism underlying the disorder in this patient
evidence.explanation: The authors' explicit rejection of mTOR activation as the mechanism in their patient, who nonetheless had capillary malformations.

open_questions/1.rationale: The mTOR/MAPK hypothesis rests entirely on patient lymphoblastoid cell lines, which are not endothelium. A patient homozygous for p.Ser236Phe had multiple capillary malformations without detectable PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation, so either the mechanism is pathway-independent or the lymphoblastoid readout is uninformative about endothelial biology. Lesional skin has been biopsied and described histologically (dilated small-caliber papillary-dermal vessels), but no endothelial signaling study - phospho-S6, phospho-ERK or equivalent - has ever been performed on that tissue, despite the lesions being trivially accessible.

evidence.snippet: STAMBP knockout directly increased release of IL-1beta with TLR ligation
evidence.explanation: Molecular basis for the IL-1 blockade hypothesis, in monocytes rather than neural cells.

open_questions/2.rationale: AMSH restrains NLRP3 by exactly the K63-linked deubiquitination chemistry it is specialized for, and the CNS-conditional Stambp knockout shows massive neuroinflammation. IL-1 blockade with anakinra is already used in other refractory epilepsy syndromes, making this the most tractable repurposing hypothesis in the disease. It is entirely untested: the inflammasome work was done in monocytes with no patient or neural data.

evidence.snippet: Currently, there is little published information about the natural history and long-term outcomes for individuals with MIC-CAP.
evidence.explanation: Explicit statement of the natural-history gap by the group that maintains the GeneReviews chapter.

open_questions/3.rationale: With roughly 25-30 molecularly confirmed individuals reported worldwide there is no registry, no natural-history study, no survival curve, and no validated quality-of-life or caregiver-burden instrument has ever been administered. Life expectancy is described only as "shortened", with the oldest known living individual reported at 12 years. Prognostic counseling is therefore anecdote-based.

evidence.snippet: Western-blot analysis did not detect dGK protein in the liver of affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Absence of the protein in patient liver establishes loss of function.

evidence.snippet: The mechanism of disease is loss of function.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen expert-panel statement of disease mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The N46S/L266R DGUOK showed 14 and 10% residual activity as compared with controls with dG and deoxyadenosine as phosphate acceptors respectively.
evidence.explanation: Missense alleles can leave measurable residual activity, the basis of the milder end of the spectrum.

steps/1.description: Biallelic DGUOK variants abolish or reduce mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase. Truncating, splice and missense alleles are all reported; in the original Druze kindreds no dGK protein was detectable in liver. Missense alleles with residual activity are associated with milder, occasionally reversible hepatic disease.

evidence.snippet: In addition, mtDNA synthesis requires a balanced supply of nucleotides that is achieved by nucleotide recycling inside the mitochondria and import from the cytosol.
evidence.explanation: Review statement of the nucleotide-supply requirement that dGK serves.

steps/2.description: dGK phosphorylates deoxyguanosine and deoxyadenosine to their monophosphates inside mitochondria. Its loss is proposed to leave the mitochondrial dNTP pool short of purines relative to pyrimidines. Direct measurement of mitochondrial dNTP pools in patient tissue is not among the sources cited here; the imbalance is stated as mechanism in the primary discovery paper and the 2024 cohort introduction.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial DNA content was below 10% of controls in liver in all but one case and modestly reduced in blood cells.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the liver-predominant depletion.

evidence.snippet: Molecular genetics studies demonstrated that mtDNA depletion was present in all liver samples analyzed in patients presenting signs/symptoms of hepatic disease whereas muscle samples analysis showed a reduction of mtDNA copy number in only 66% of the cases.
evidence.explanation: Liver depletion is universal in hepatic disease; muscle is inconsistently affected.

evidence.snippet: A decrease of mtDNA copy number occurred in multiple tissues, with the liver being the most severely affected.
evidence.explanation: The knockout mouse reproduces the liver predominance.

steps/3.description: mtDNA copy number is severely reduced in liver, typically below 10-20% of control, in every liver sample analysed from patients with hepatic disease, whereas skeletal muscle is depleted in only about two thirds and blood only modestly. Why the liver is so much more vulnerable than other tissues is not settled.

evidence.snippet: Affected tissues show both decreased activity of the mtDNA-encoded respiratory chain complexes (I, III, IV, V) and mtDNA depletion.
evidence.explanation: Documents the combined deficiency of the mtDNA-dependent complexes in patient tissue.

evidence.snippet: Histopathology showed severe alterations and immunohistochemistry showed signs of both oxidative stress and regeneration in Dguok-/- liver.
evidence.explanation: Model evidence for the oxidative-stress component of the conformed node.

steps/4.description: Reduced activity of complexes I, III, IV and V, the complexes containing mtDNA-encoded subunits, with complex II preserved. Oxidative stress has been shown in the knockout mouse liver; it has not been measured directly in patient tissue in the sources cited here, so the oxidative arm of the conformed module node rests on model data.

evidence.snippet: Mechanically, this ferroptosis is a process mediated by nuclear receptor co-activator 4 (NCOA4)-dependent degradation of ferritin in lysosome and cellular labile iron release.
evidence.explanation: Mechanism of the ferroptosis in the iPSC hepatocyte model.

steps/5.description: Proposed link between the respiratory chain defect, hepatic iron deposition and hepatocyte death. In patient iPSC-derived hepatocytes and liver organoids, iron loading triggers ferroptosis through NCOA4-dependent ferritinophagy and labile iron release, rescued by N-acetylcysteine; corrected isogenic cells are resistant. Not yet shown in patient liver. The paper's introduction states that most patients develop iron overload, whereas siderosis was found in about a quarter of biopsies in the 2024 cohort, so how often this mechanism operates in vivo is unsettled.

evidence.snippet: Liver specimen analyses revealed steatosis in 61/87 (70.1%) patients, cholestasis in 52/87 (59.8%), fibrosis in 49/87 (56.3%), cirrhosis in 29/87 (33.3%), siderosis in 23/87 (26.4%) and necrosis in 16/87 (18.4%).
evidence.explanation: Histological spectrum of the liver injury in 87 biopsied patients.

evidence.snippet: Progressive hepatic disease is the most common cause of death in both forms.
evidence.explanation: Liver failure is the principal cause of death.

steps/6.description: Cholestatic hepatopathy with steatosis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, siderosis and necrosis on biopsy, progressing to synthetic liver failure. Liver failure is the leading cause of death. Hepatic iron deposition and high ferritin can mimic neonatal haemochromatosis, and raised plasma tyrosine can mimic tyrosinaemia type I.

evidence.snippet: Pancreatic islet cell hyperplasia with numerous confluent giant islets was found in both autopsied infants.
evidence.explanation: The autopsy finding behind this node.

steps/7.description: Autopsy of two infants showed islet cell hyperplasia with giant islets, and two later infants presented with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia whose critical samples suggested hyperinsulinism. This is a hypothesis for part of the hypoglycaemia, based on four patients; the mechanism linking DGUOK loss to islet hyperplasia is unknown.

evidence.snippet: mtDNA copy number was measured in DNA extracted from muscle biopsy samples in 30/202. Depletion was found in 20/30 (66.7%)
evidence.explanation: Muscle mtDNA depletion in two thirds of tested patients (all clinical forms).

evidence.snippet: Histochemical analysis of muscle biopsy showed cytochrome c oxidase (COX) deficient muscular fibres in 19/45 (42.2%) patients
evidence.explanation: Respiratory chain deficiency at the fibre level in muscle biopsies.

steps/8.description: Skeletal muscle is affected less consistently than liver: mtDNA is depleted in about two thirds of muscle samples, and COX-deficient and ragged-red fibres are seen in a minority of biopsies. Clinical muscle involvement (weakness, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia) defines the hepatomyocerebral subtype. The adult isolated myopathy with multiple deletions is a separate allelic entity and is not covered by this node.

evidence.snippet: Early central nervous system (CNS) symptoms were manifested in 123/181 (68%) presenting central hypotonia in 87/181 (48.1%), nystagmus in 59/181 (32.6%), psychomotor delay in 43/181 (23.8%) and lethargy in 14/181 (7.7%).
evidence.explanation: Frequency of CNS involvement at onset in the international cohort.

evidence.snippet: Neurological involvement included hypotonia, nystagmus and developmental delay with MRI brain abnormalities in about half of cases.
evidence.explanation: Independent literature collation describing the same neurological picture.

steps/9.description: Hypotonia, nystagmus (classically rotary, evolving into opsoclonus), psychomotor delay and lethargy, with brain MRI abnormalities in about 40-50% of those imaged. Neurological signs are present at onset in about two thirds of patients and can appear or worsen after liver transplantation.

evidence.snippet: Published mutations in deoxyguanosine kinase (DGUOK) cause mitochondrial DNA depletion and a clinical phenotype that consists of neonatal liver failure, nystagmus and hypotonia.
evidence.explanation: Neonatal liver failure is the core feature.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals with the hepatocerebral form of MDS have early progressive liver failure and neurological abnormalities, hypoglycemia and increased lactate in body fluids.
evidence.explanation: Early progressive liver failure in the original kindreds.

evidence.snippet: The liver disease progressed into liver failure in 152/181 (84%)
evidence.explanation: Frequency of liver failure over the course in the whole cohort.

steps/10.description: Progressive liver failure, usually in the first months of life; in the international cohort liver disease progressed to failure in 84% during follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Infantile-onset disease typically presented with cholestatic jaundice and lactic acidosis.
evidence.explanation: Cholestatic jaundice is the typical infantile presentation.

evidence.snippet: Patients also experienced cholestasis (92/160, 57.5%), jaundice (94/160, 58.8%), hepatomegaly (73/160, 45.6%), ascites (26/160, 16.3%) and liver failure (5/160, 3.1%).
evidence.explanation: Cholestasis at onset in 57.5%.

evidence.snippet: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy on day 26 showed an absence of tracer excretion, suggestive of biliary atresia; however, laparoscopic cholangiography and liver biopsy on day 42 ruled out this diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Neonatal cholestasis mimicking biliary atresia.

steps/11.description: Cholestasis, often the first sign; conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with high GGT in a neonate can lead to evaluation for biliary atresia before the diagnosis is made.

evidence.snippet: Patients also experienced cholestasis (92/160, 57.5%), jaundice (94/160, 58.8%), hepatomegaly (73/160, 45.6%), ascites (26/160, 16.3%) and liver failure (5/160, 3.1%).
evidence.explanation: Jaundice at onset in 58.8%.

evidence.snippet: The majority of affected individuals have the multisystem illness with hepatic disease (jaundice, cholestasis, hepatomegaly, and elevated transaminases) and neurologic manifestations (hypotonia, nystagmus, and developmental delay) evident within weeks of birth.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists jaundice among the hepatic manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Patients also experienced cholestasis (92/160, 57.5%), jaundice (94/160, 58.8%), hepatomegaly (73/160, 45.6%), ascites (26/160, 16.3%) and liver failure (5/160, 3.1%).
evidence.explanation: Hepatomegaly at onset in 45.6%.

evidence.snippet: In detail, 141/160 (88.1%) presented liver involvement at onset and the most prominent sign was an increased level of alanine and aspartate transaminases (ALT/AST) described in 116/160 (72.5%)
evidence.explanation: Raised transaminases are the most common sign at onset.

evidence.snippet: Coagulation tests showed dysfunctional blood clotting.
evidence.explanation: Case-level coagulopathy of liver failure; no cohort frequency is available.

evidence.snippet: Liver specimen analyses revealed steatosis in 61/87 (70.1%) patients, cholestasis in 52/87 (59.8%), fibrosis in 49/87 (56.3%), cirrhosis in 29/87 (33.3%), siderosis in 23/87 (26.4%) and necrosis in 16/87 (18.4%).
evidence.explanation: Cirrhosis in a third of biopsied patients.

evidence.snippet: Liver histopathology showed severe hepatic damage ranging from micronodular formation and cirrhosis to the total loss of liver architecture with diffuse fibrosis and neocholangiolar proliferation.
evidence.explanation: Cirrhosis in infants who died by 18 months.

steps/16.description: Cirrhosis, sometimes micronodular, on biopsy or at autopsy, already present in infancy.

evidence.snippet: One patient was diagnosed with hepatocellular carcinoma aged 6 months, supporting a link between mitochondrial DNA depletion and tumorigenesis; liver transplantation proved beneficial with regard to both tumor treatment and psychomotor development.
evidence.explanation: HCC at six months of age.

evidence.snippet: One of our patients underwent liver transplantation; pathologic findings revealed (in addition to diffuse hepatopathy) a hepatocellular carcinoma, implying a possible link between mtDNA depletion syndrome and tumorigenesis.
evidence.explanation: HCC found in a liver explant.

evidence.snippet: Liver ultrasound showed abnormalities in 40/50 patients: hepatomegaly in 15/40 (37.5%), hyperechogenicity in 10/40 (25%), ascites in 7/40 (17.5%), liver steatosis in 4/40 (10%), solid tumour in 4/40 (10%)
evidence.explanation: Solid liver tumours on cohort imaging; histological type not stated in this sentence.

steps/17.description: Hepatocellular carcinoma in infancy, found at transplantation or on imaging (reported at six months). A solid liver tumour was seen in 4 of 40 abnormal liver ultrasounds in the international cohort, not all histologically typed. This is a hepatic neoplasm arising in the germline disorder, not a separate somatic-cancer entry.

evidence.snippet: Elevated transferrin saturation, high ferritin, and alpha-fetoprotein levels resembled, in two cases, a neonatal hemochromatosis.
evidence.explanation: Raised AFP with iron-overload markers.

steps/18.description: Very high alpha-fetoprotein, which together with raised ferritin and transferrin saturation can suggest neonatal haemochromatosis.

evidence.snippet: Infantile-onset disease typically presented with cholestatic jaundice and lactic acidosis.
evidence.explanation: Lactic acidosis is part of the typical presentation.

evidence.snippet: This case highlights that hyperlactatemia may be absent or only mild in the early stages of MTDPS, making timely diagnosis challenging.
evidence.explanation: Lactate can be normal early, a diagnostic pitfall.

steps/19.description: Lactic acidosis is typical but may be absent or only mild early, so a normal lactate does not exclude the diagnosis in a cholestatic neonate.

evidence.snippet: Metabolic laboratory tests confirmed metabolic acidosis in 106/202 (52.5%) and hypoglycemia in 100/202 (49.5%) cases.
evidence.explanation: Hypoglycaemia in about half the whole cohort, including adult-onset cases.

evidence.snippet: Hypoglycemia (hypoketotic) and lactic acidosis were the constant laboratory findings.
evidence.explanation: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia in every infant of a four-patient series.

steps/20.description: Hypoglycaemia, typically hypoketotic, from the neonatal period; in some infants the biochemistry suggests hyperinsulinism.

evidence.snippet: In both patients, critical samples demonstrated hypoketotic hypoglycemia and a partial glycemic response to glucagon stimulation, thereby suggesting hyperinsulinism (HI).
evidence.explanation: Two case reports; frequency unknown.

evidence.snippet: Specifically, plasma tyrosine level was increased in 48/75 (64%), alanine in 21/75 (28%), methionine in 14/75 (18.7%), phenylalanine in 4/75 (5.3%) and glutamine in 3/75 (4%).

evidence.snippet: Five subjects were detected by newborn screening, with elevated tyrosine or phenylalanine.
evidence.explanation: Detection on newborn screening.

steps/22.description: Raised plasma tyrosine (and sometimes phenylalanine or methionine), detectable on newborn screening and a source of confusion with tyrosinaemia type I.

evidence.snippet: Early central nervous system (CNS) symptoms were manifested in 123/181 (68%) presenting central hypotonia in 87/181 (48.1%), nystagmus in 59/181 (32.6%), psychomotor delay in 43/181 (23.8%) and lethargy in 14/181 (7.7%).

The classic description is rotary nystagmus evolving into opsoclonus (Orphanet), but the cohort does not report how often it is rotary, so the binding is the general term. In the 2024 cohort nystagmus was the only neurological sign associated with worse survival after liver transplantation.

evidence.snippet: rotary nystagmus that develops into opsoclonus

evidence.snippet: The common clinical features of hepatocerebral MDS include hepatic dysfunction, psychomotor delay, hypotonia, rotary nystagmus developing into opsoclonus, lactic acidosis, and hypoglycemia
evidence.explanation: Literature summary restated in a case report's introduction, not the case's own finding.

evidence.snippet: An increased number of patients presented psychomotor delay (61/181, 33.7%) and nystagmus (74/181, 40.9%).

evidence.snippet: Patients also experienced cholestasis (92/160, 57.5%), jaundice (94/160, 58.8%), hepatomegaly (73/160, 45.6%), ascites (26/160, 16.3%) and liver failure (5/160, 3.1%).

steps/28.description: Steatosis is the commonest finding on liver biopsy (70% of biopsied patients). The denominator is patients who had a biopsy, not the whole cohort.

evidence.snippet: Metabolic laboratory tests confirmed metabolic acidosis in 106/202 (52.5%) and hypoglycemia in 100/202 (49.5%) cases.
evidence.explanation: Metabolic acidosis in 52.5% of the whole cohort, which includes adult-onset cases.

evidence.snippet: Additional symptoms were: metabolic acidosis in 75/110 (68.2%), hypoglycemia in 67/110 (60.9%), failure to thrive in 40/110 (36.4%), feeding difficulties in 33/110 (30%), renal involvement in 10/110 (9.1%), hypothermia in 10/110 (9.1%)
evidence.explanation: Metabolic acidosis in 68% of the hepatocerebral subgroup.

steps/29.description: Metabolic acidosis over the course of illness in about half the whole cohort and 68% of the hepatocerebral subgroup (89% of the small hepatomyocerebral subgroup).

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI showed abnormal patterns in 25 out of 65 patients (38.5%).
evidence.explanation: Frequency among imaged patients.

evidence.snippet: Specifically, cortical/subcortical atrophy was reported in 8/25 (32%), cerebellar atrophy in 3/25 (12%), white matter abnormalities in 9/25 (36%), focal lesions in 4/25 (16%), vasogenic pattern and cerebral edema in 3/25 (12%), grey matter abnormalities in 2/25 (8%).
evidence.explanation: Breakdown of the abnormal scans.

steps/30.description: Brain MRI is abnormal in 38.5% of those imaged in the 2024 cohort (about half in a separate 2024 collation). The findings are heterogeneous: white matter abnormalities (9 of 25 abnormal scans), cortical or subcortical atrophy (8), focal lesions (4), cerebellar atrophy (3), oedema (3) and grey matter changes (2); MR spectroscopy showed a lactate peak in 6 of 8. Bound to the general brain-morphology term because no single pattern predominates.

evidence.snippet: Weakness or fatigue was reported in 33/159 patients (20.8%), ptosis in 22/159 (13.8%), progressive external ophthalmoplegia in 14/159 (8.8%), myalgia in 12/159 (7.5%), dysphagia in 12/159 (7.5%) and dysphonia in 8/159 (5.0%).
